docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is the first volume of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā. Its subject is the Vedic corpus: the four Saṃhitās of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda and Atharvaveda, with the poetry and myths of the hymns; the Brāhmaṇas and Āraṇyakas; the six Vedāṅgas and the later Upavedas; the solemn and domestic rituals; the oral tradition and the schools that preserved these texts for three thousand years; the world-view and society that they reveal; and their later history and legacy.

The volume tries to do two things at once. It presents the Vedas as the tradition has understood them—as Śruti, the foundation of Brahmanical learning and practice—and it presents them as historians and philologists read them, as compositions of many generations of poets and ritualists in north-western and northern India between roughly 1500 and 500 BCE. Where these perspectives differ, both are stated and labelled. Dates are given in the mainstream academic form first; traditional dates are identified as such.

Chapter 1 introduces the corpus, its dating and the history of its study; Chapters 2–7 describe the Saṃhitās and the literature that grew around them; Chapters 8–12 the rituals, the later scheme of applied sciences, the oral tradition and the schools; and Chapters 13–15 the world-view and society of the texts and their later history, including the responses of Buddhist, Jain and Tamil authors. A list of abbreviations, a map of places named in the volume, a glossary and a chronology are provided for reference.

This edition has been thoroughly revised. Quotations from the Vedic texts have been checked and, where they could not be verified, removed; doubtful or unsourced quotations from modern authors have been omitted; claims that the Vedas anticipated modern science have been replaced by an account of their genuine achievements in phonetics, grammar, geometry and calendrical astronomy; and contested questions—the date of the Ṛgveda, the Sarasvatī, the origins of the Indo-Aryan languages and the evidence of ancient DNA—are presented with the evidence on each side. The volume also treats honestly the origins of varṇa hierarchy and the position of women, which are part of the Vedic legacy and still matter today.

Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST), and Tamil words in the transliteration of the Madras Tamil Lexicon (Section 1.14). Translations are the author’s own unless otherwise indicated, and readers are encouraged to consult the critical editions and the scholarly translations listed in the Select Bibliography.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction to the Vedic Knowledge System
docs.text:
Invocatory Verse

vedāham etaṃ puruṣaṃ mahāntam ādityavarṇaṃ tamasaḥ parastāt I know this great Puruṣa (Supreme Being), luminous as the Sun, beyond all darkness. — Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8

docs.title: 1.1 What is Veda?
docs.text:
The word Veda is derived from the Sanskrit root vid, meaning “to know.” Within the tradition, and especially in the Mīmāṃsā school, Veda denotes not merely a collection of ancient texts but knowledge held to be eternal (nitya), intrinsically valid (svataḥ pramāṇa), and authorless (apauruṣeya). The Vedas are regarded as Śruti—that which was “heard” by the ancient seers (ṛṣis)—and were transmitted orally, with remarkable fidelity, for some three thousand years. Historians, for their part, treat the same texts as compositions of many generations of poets and ritualists, composed in north-western and northern India between roughly 1500 and 500 BCE (Witzel 2003; Jamison and Brereton 2014). This volume sets out both perspectives and marks clearly which is which.

The Vedic corpus is more varied than the English word “scripture” suggests. It includes:

  • Hymns and prayers — poetry of praise, petition and speculation addressed to the gods;

  • Ritual texts — formulas, chants and prose explanations for the solemn sacrifices (yajña);

  • Speculative dialogues — the riddles of the Ṛgveda and the philosophical discussions of the Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads;

  • Charms and spells — especially in the Atharvaveda, for healing, protection, love and prosperity;

  • Ancillary sciences — phonetics, grammar, metre, etymology, ritual geometry and calendrics, developed to preserve and perform the texts correctly.

The Threefold Meaning of Veda

In traditional thought the term Veda is understood at three levels:

  1. Cosmic level: The eternal knowledge inherent in the fabric of the universe, identified in Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta with the eternal Word or with Brahman itself.

  2. Revelatory level: The specific mantras and hymns “seen” (dṛṣṭa) by the seers (ṛṣis) during deep contemplation.

  3. Textual level: The four Saṃhitās and their associated literature, as preserved and transmitted across generations.

docs.title: 1.2 The Fourfold Division of the Vedas
docs.text:
The Vedic corpus, as it has come down to us, is traditionally divided into four Saṃhitās (collections), each associated with a specific aspect of the Vedic yajña (sacred ritual):

  1. Ṛgveda (Ṛk = praise, verse) — The Veda of hymns; contains verses of praise addressed to the gods (devas).

  2. Yajurveda (Yajus = sacrificial formula) — The Veda of ritual formulas; provides the prose mantras used in ceremonies.

  3. Sāmaveda (Sāman = melody, chant) — The Veda of melodies; sets verses, almost all of them found in the Ṛgveda, to melodies for chanting.

  4. Atharvaveda (Atharvan = the name of an ancient sage) — The Veda of practical and esoteric knowledge; addresses healing, daily life, and philosophical speculation.

Each of these four Vedas (Figure 1.1) was transmitted in several śākhās (recensions or “branches”), of which only a fraction survive. A traditional count, already found in Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya (c. 150 BCE), gives the Ṛgveda 21 śākhās, the Yajurveda 101, the Sāmaveda 1,000 and the Atharvaveda 9. These figures are conventional rather than historical; scholars can identify a few dozen schools with confidence, of which about a dozen survive (Witzel 1997).

The tradition explains the division into four by the work of the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, called Veda Vyāsa, “the arranger of the Veda”. According to the Purāṇas (e.g. Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4), Vyāsa, foreseeing the decline of human memory in the approaching Kali Yuga, divided a single primordial Veda into four collections and entrusted them to four pupils—the Ṛgveda to Paila, the Yajurveda to Vaiśampāyana, the Sāmaveda to Jaimini and the Atharvaveda to Sumantu—from whom the lineages of the schools descend. Historians read the story as a later explanation of a real process: the collection and arrangement of hymns and formulas by priestly schools, probably in the Kuru realm of the early first millennium BCE (Witzel 1997). The four collections answer to the four kinds of priest in the śrauta ritual (Section 8.3); the schools themselves, their numbers and their survival are the subject of Chapter 12 (Table 12.1).

Figure 1.1. The fourfold division of the Vedas with key attributes.

docs.title: 1.3 The Layers of Vedic Literature
docs.text:
Each of the four Vedas is not a monolithic text but a layered corpus. Tradition arranges it in four genres (Figure 1.2), and Vedānta reads them as a progression from external ritual to inner realisation. Historically the genres overlap: Brāhmaṇa-style prose already occurs in the Black Yajurveda Saṃhitās, and the oldest Upaniṣads are themselves parts of Brāhmaṇas or Āraṇyakas.

  1. Saṃhitā — The core collection of mantras, hymns, and formulas.

  2. Brāhmaṇa — Prose commentaries explaining the rituals and the significance of the mantras.

  3. Āraṇyaka — “Forest texts” intended for contemplation in solitude, bridging ritual and philosophy.

  4. Upaniṣad — The philosophical culmination, exploring the nature of Ātman (Self) and Brahman (Absolute Reality).

Figure 1.2. The four genres of Vedic literature as traditionally arranged, from external ritual to internal realisation.

docs.title: 1.3.1 The Vedic Corpus at a Glance
docs.text:
Table 1.1 lists the principal surviving texts of each Veda by genre. The Upaniṣads named are those embedded in, or traditionally attached to, the schools concerned; they are treated in Volume 2 of this series.

Table 1.1. Principal surviving texts of the four Vedas. docs.title: 1.3.2 The Auxiliary Sciences
docs.text: Around the four Vedas the later tradition grouped a set of auxiliary sciences. The six Vedāṅgas, “limbs of the Veda”—phonetics, metre, grammar, etymology, astronomy and calendar, and ritual procedure—grew up to preserve, understand and perform the texts correctly; they are the subject of Chapter 7. Later texts also attach to each Veda a “subsidiary Veda” (upaveda): medicine, warfare, music, and polity or architecture. That scheme is a post-Vedic classification which lent Vedic prestige to sciences whose content developed long after the Vedic period; it is discussed in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 1.4 The Concept of Apauruṣeya: Authorless Revelation
docs.text:
A distinctive doctrine of the later tradition is apauruṣeyatva—the claim that the Vedas are not the composition of any human or even divine author, but eternal. On this view the ṛṣis are not “authors” but “seers” who “saw” the hymns. The idea is old: Yāska’s Nirukta (c. 5th century BCE) explains the word ṛṣi from “seeing” (ṛṣir darśanāt, Nirukta 2.11).

The Seers in Yāska’s Nirukta

sākṣātkṛtadharmāṇa ṛṣayo babhūvuḥ The seers were those who had direct insight into dharma. — Nirukta 1.20

The Vedic poets themselves, however, often speak of “making” or “fashioning” their hymns (the verb takṣ, “to fashion as a carpenter does”), and the hymns name their poets and patrons. The full doctrine of authorlessness was worked out by the Mīmāṃsā school. Jaimini’s Mīmāṃsāsūtra (usually dated to the last centuries BCE) holds that the relation between a word and its meaning is “inborn” (autpattika, Mīmāṃsāsūtra 1.1.5), not conventional, and later Mīmāṃsakas such as Śabara and Kumārila argued that a text without an author is free of the defects that make human testimony fallible, and is therefore intrinsically valid (svataḥ pramāṇa). This is a reasoned philosophical position, not simply an appeal to faith; it was also contested in India itself by Buddhist, Jain and Cārvāka thinkers and, from a different angle, by Nyāya, which held the Vedas to be authoritative because they were composed by a reliable author, God.

docs.title: 1.5 The Seers and Their Hymns
docs.text: Each hymn of the Ṛgveda is assigned, in the later index called the Sarvānukramaṇī (attributed to Kātyāyana), to a seer (ṛṣi), a deity (devatā) and a metre (chandas). Some of these ascriptions reflect genuine family traditions, since the poets often name themselves or their clans in the hymns; others, especially for late hymns, are inferred from the content and should be treated as traditional rather than historical.

docs.title: 1.5.1 The Sapta Ṛṣis (Seven Great Seers)
docs.text:
Later tradition honours seven primordial seers (saptarṣi), whose names vary from text to text; the list of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (2.2.4) is:

  1. Atri — Seer of the fifth Maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda

  2. Bharadvāja — Seer of the sixth Maṇḍala

  3. Gautama — Ancestor of the Gautama clan, to which Vāmadeva, the seer of the fourth Maṇḍala, belongs

  4. Jamadagni — Father of Paraśurāma

  5. Kaśyapa — The primeval progenitor sage

  6. Vasiṣṭha — Seer of the seventh Maṇḍala; priest (purohita) of King Sudās (RV 7.18)

  7. Viśvāmitra — Seer of the third Maṇḍala; the seer of the Gāyatrī Mantra

docs.title: 1.5.2 Women Seers
docs.text: The Anukramaṇīs ascribe a number of Ṛgvedic hymns to women seers (ṛṣikās), among them Ghoṣā, Lopāmudrā and Vāk Āmbhṛṇī (Table 2.10), and the Upaniṣads show women in philosophical debate. These figures matter, but they should not be over-read. Some ascriptions are probably derived from the speaker of a hymn rather than from a historical poet—in RV 10.125 the speaker is the goddess Speech herself (Section 2.5.4)—and women appear in the ritual chiefly as the sacrificer’s wife (patnī), whose presence was required. In later centuries women’s access to Vedic study narrowed sharply: the Dharmaśāstras treat marriage as the equivalent of initiation for women and prescribe that their life-cycle rites be performed without Vedic mantras (Manusmṛti 2.66–67). The evidence, which is mixed and changes over time, is set out in Section 14.7.

docs.title: 1.6 Śruti and Smṛti
docs.text:
The later tradition built a careful framework for the authority of the Vedas. Its central idea is the distinction between Śruti and Smṛti. The related theory of the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), and the long debate between the philosophical schools about the authority of verbal testimony and of the Veda in particular, belong to the history of philosophy and are treated in Volume 3, Darśana Darpaṇa.

The distinction is that between Śruti (“that which is heard”) and Smṛti (“that which is remembered”). Śruti comprises the four Vedas and their associated Brāhmaṇas, Āraṇyakas, and Upaniṣads. Smṛti includes the Dharmaśāstras, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other secondary texts. The authority of Smṛti is always subordinate to Śruti; where there is a conflict, Śruti prevails.

The Primacy of Śruti

vedaḥ smṛtiḥ sadācāraḥ svasya ca priyam ātmanaḥ etac caturvidhaṃ prāhuḥ sākṣād dharmasya lakṣaṇam The Veda, tradition, the conduct of good people, and what is pleasing to oneself— these, they say, are the four visible marks of Dharma. — Manusmṛti 2.12

docs.title: 1.6.1 The Concept of Vidyā and Avidyā
docs.text: The Vedic tradition draws a fundamental distinction between vidyā (knowledge, specifically liberating knowledge) and avidyā (ignorance or incomplete knowledge). The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad further distinguishes between parā vidyā (higher knowledge leading to the realisation of Brahman) and aparā vidyā (lower knowledge, which it identifies as the four Vedas and the six Vedāṅgas, Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.4–5). Even the Veda itself is thus ranked below the knowledge of the imperishable; later thinkers extended the category of lower knowledge to all learning that does not directly lead to liberation.

docs.title: 1.7 The Vedic Chronological Framework
docs.text: When were the Vedic texts composed? The question matters for everything that follows, and it has been argued over for two centuries. It is best approached by separating three kinds of answer: the traditional chronology, which belongs to the religious tradition; the mainstream academic chronology, which rests on several independent lines of evidence; and alternative proposals for much earlier dates, which have a following in India but are not accepted by most specialists, Indian or foreign.

docs.title: 1.7.1 The Traditional Chronology
docs.text: In traditional reckoning the Vedas are beginningless (anādi) and authorless (apauruṣeya); on this view the question of “dating” them does not arise, only the question of when they were arranged in their present form. According to the Purāṇas, the present age, the Kali Yuga, began in 3102 BCE, and Vyāsa arranged the Veda into four Saṃhitās at the close of the preceding Dvāpara Yuga. The 3102 BCE epoch itself is first attested in the Āryabhaṭīya of Āryabhaṭa (499 CE), and it appears to be a back-calculated astronomical epoch rather than a historical record.

docs.title: 1.7.2 The Mainstream Academic Chronology
docs.text:
Most historians and Indologists date the Vedic texts relative to one another by their language, and then anchor that relative sequence to a few external fixed points (Witzel 2003; Jamison and Brereton 2014). The relative strata are set out in Table 1.2.

Table 1.2. Relative strata of Vedic literature and approximate academic dates (after Witzel and others). All dates are approximate and some are disputed. Stratum Texts Characteristic Features Approximate Date Early Ṛgvedic Family Books (Maṇḍalas 2–7) Most archaic language; frequent injunctive; rich verbal system c. 1500–1200 BCE Late Ṛgvedic Maṇḍalas 1, 8 (in part), 10 Newer forms and vocabulary; speculative hymns (e.g. RV 10.90, 10.129) c. 1200–1000 BCE Mantra language Atharvaveda, Sāmaveda and Yajurveda mantras First mention of iron (śyāma ayas); new vocabulary c. 1200–900 BCE Saṃhitā prose Black Yajurveda prose Earliest expository prose c. 900–800 BCE Brāhmaṇa prose Brāhmaṇas, Āraṇyakas, oldest Upaniṣads Developed prose; ritual exegesis c. 850–500 BCE Sūtra language Śrauta, Gṛhya, Dharma and Śulba Sūtras Compressed technical style c. 600–200 BCE

docs.title: 1.7.3 External Anchors
docs.text:
Three kinds of external evidence tie this relative sequence to absolute dates.

The Mitanni treaty (c. 1380 BCE).

The most important fixed point comes not from India but from northern Syria. A treaty between the Hittite king Šuppiluliuma I and Šattiwaza, king of Mitanni, preserved on clay tablets from the Hittite capital Ḥattuša and usually dated c. 1380 BCE (some chronologies place it a few decades later), calls on the Mitanni gods as witnesses. Among them appear Mi-it-ra, U-ru-wa-na, In-da-ra and the Na-ša-at-ti-ya—that is, Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra and the Nāsatyas (Aśvins), named in the same grouping as in the Ṛgveda. A horse-training manual from the same archive, attributed to a Mitanni trainer named Kikkuli, uses Indo-Aryan technical terms and numerals (aika-, tera-, pañza-, satta-, cf. Sanskrit eka, tri, pañca, sapta) for the number of laps. The Mitanni rulers also bore Indo-Aryan names. This shows that speakers of an early form of Indo-Aryan, worshipping the Ṛgvedic gods, had reached the Near East by the fourteenth century BCE, and that their language was, if anything, slightly older than Ṛgvedic Sanskrit. It is consistent with a Ṛgveda composed in the second half of the second millennium BCE; it does not support dates in the fourth or fifth millennium.

The Avestan comparison.

The language of the oldest part of the Zoroastrian scripture, the Old Avestan Gāthās, is so close to Ṛgvedic Sanskrit that whole lines can be converted from one to the other by regular sound changes. The two traditions share a common religious vocabulary: Avestan aša and Vedic ṛta (“truth, order”), haoma and soma, yasna and yajña, Mi\(\theta\)ra and Mitra, ahura and asura, daēva and deva (with reversed valuation). Indo-Iranian must therefore have been a single language not long before the Ṛgveda; the Gāthās are usually dated to the late second or early first millennium BCE, though their date is itself debated (Table 1.3).

Table 1.3. Some Vedic–Avestan correspondences. The pairs are cognate: they descend from common Indo-Iranian originals. Vedic Avestan Remarks deva daēva “God” in the Veda; “demon” in Zoroastrianism asura ahura “Lord”, a title of powerful gods; in Avestan the title of the supreme god, Ahura Mazdā ṛta aša Truth, cosmic order soma haoma The sacred plant and drink yajña yasna Worship, sacrifice hotṛ zaotar Priest who pours or recites atharvan ā\(\theta\)ravan Fire-priest Mitra Mi\(\theta\)ra God of contract Yama, son of Vivasvant Yima, son of Vīvahvant First mortal, king of a paradise Vṛtrahan Verethragna “Smiter of Vṛtra”, epithet of Indra; an Iranian god of victory sapta sindhavaḥ hapta hindu “Seven rivers” gāthā gā\(\theta\)ā Song, verse

The sound correspondences are regular: Vedic s corresponds to Avestan h (soma–haoma, sindhu–hindu), and Vedic h or j to Avestan z (hotṛ–zaotar). The reversal of values between deva and asura shows that the two traditions, once one, developed in rivalry.

The kinship extends beyond vocabulary to myths, ritual and social ideas. Both traditions know a dragon-slaying hero: the Ṛgvedic Trita Āptya, who kills the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ (RV 10.8), corresponds to the Avestan Thraētaona, son of Āthwya, who kills the three-headed dragon Aži Dahāka, and the Vedic epithet of Indra, vṛtrahan, survives in Iran as the name of a god of victory. Both have a pressed sacred drink with its own hymns—the Avestan Hōm Yašt (Yasna 9–11) is the counterpart of the ninth book of the Ṛgveda—and both a ritual fire tended by a priest who pours and recites (Section 8.8). The Avesta divides society into priests (ā\(\theta\)ravan), chariot-warriors (ra\(\theta\)aēštar) and herdsmen-farmers, a threefold scheme that matches the Ṛgveda’s brahman, kṣatra and viś before the fourth class appears in the Puruṣa Sūkta. At the same time the two traditions diverged sharply: the Zoroastrian reform condemned the daēvas and made one ahura supreme, while the Vedic tradition, which kept the devas, came to treat the asuras as their enemies. These shared inheritances and divergences are best explained by a common Indo-Iranian past not long before the composition of the oldest texts of each tradition.

Material culture and geography.

The Ṛgveda knows bronze or copper (ayas) but not iron; iron (“dark metal”, śyāma ayas or kṛṣṇāyas) first appears in the Atharvaveda. Iron working becomes widespread in northern India from c. 1200–1000 BCE, although some earlier dates have been claimed. The horse and the spoked-wheel chariot, central to the Ṛgveda, are well attested in South Asia only from the second millennium BCE. The Ṛgveda’s geography centres on the Greater Panjab (Sapta Sindhavaḥ) and the Sarasvatī; later Vedic texts shift eastward to the Kuru–Pañcāla country of the Ganga–Yamunā Doab and then to Videha. The Ṛgveda shows no knowledge of cities of the Harappan kind, of writing, or of seals.

Taken together, these lines of evidence led scholars such as Witzel, Jamison and Brereton, and many Indian historians, to place the bulk of the Ṛgveda c. 1500–1200 BCE (some allow c. 1700–1100 BCE) and the later Vedic texts in the first half of the first millennium BCE (Witzel 2003; Jamison and Brereton 2014; Thapar 2002). These dates are inferences, not certainties, and specialists continue to refine them.

docs.title: 1.7.4 Alternative Proposals for Earlier Dates
docs.text:
Several writers have proposed much earlier dates. Their arguments deserve to be stated fairly, together with the reasons most specialists do not accept them.

  1. Astronomical arguments. B. G. Tilak (The Orion, 1893) and, independently, Hermann Jacobi argued that Vedic references to the year beginning with the asterism Mṛgaśiras (Orion) reflect the position of the vernal equinox around 4500 BCE (Tilak 1893). In The Arctic Home in the Vedas (1903) Tilak went further, reading descriptions of long dawns as memories of an Arctic homeland. Critics point out that the passages are brief and ambiguous, that they may preserve old calendar conventions rather than contemporary observation, and that astronomical dates depend on which star and which season a phrase is assumed to mean.

  2. Numerical “codes”. Subhash Kak has argued that the numbers of hymns and verses in the Ṛgveda and the brick counts of fire altars encode astronomical constants. Because the numbers can be grouped and combined in many ways, such correspondences are easy to find and impossible to test; they are not accepted as evidence by specialists and are not used in this volume.

  3. The Sarasvatī argument. David Frawley, Kak and others argue that because the Ṛgveda praises the Sarasvatī as a mighty river, and the Ghaggar–Hakra (with which it is usually identified) had dwindled by c. 1900 BCE, the hymns must be older than that date. This is discussed below.

docs.title: 1.7.5 The Sarasvatī River
docs.text:
The Sarasvatī is celebrated in the Ṛgveda as “best of mothers, best of rivers, best of goddesses” (ambitame nadītame devitame sarasvati, RV 2.41.16), and a hymn of Vasiṣṭha describes her flowing “from the mountains to the sea”:

Praise of Sarasvatī — Ṛgveda 7.95.2

ekācetat sarasvatī nadīnāṃ śucir yatī giribhya ā samudrāt Sarasvatī, alone among the rivers, has taken notice, pure, flowing from the mountains to the sea. — Ṛgveda 7.95.2

Most scholars identify the Ṛgvedic Sarasvatī, at least in the later hymns, with the Ghaggar–Hakra system of Haryana, Rajasthan and Cholistan, whose dry bed is lined with Harappan sites; a minority identify the older Sarasvatī with the Helmand of Afghanistan (Avestan Haraxvaitī).

The geological picture is more complicated than the popular argument assumes. A major study by Giosan and colleagues found that the Ghaggar–Hakra was not fed by a large glacier-fed Himalayan river during Harappan times; it was a monsoon-fed river whose flow declined, together with the Harappan cities along it, as the monsoon weakened around 2000 BCE (Giosan et al. 2012). Later work dated the Sutlej’s shift away from this channel to about 8,000 years ago, long before the Harappan period (Singh et al. 2017). On this evidence there was no mighty snow-fed Sarasvatī for the Ṛgvedic poets to describe after the early Holocene, and the river’s drying cannot by itself fix a date for the hymns. The praise of the river may be religious and poetic rather than hydrological; the word samudra can mean a large body of water or a terminal lake rather than the ocean; and the late hymn RV 10.75 already lists the Sarasvatī as one river among many. The question remains open, but it is no longer reasonable to present the Sarasvatī as a proof that the Ṛgveda predates 1900 BCE (Figure 1.3).

Figure 1.3. Map of the Indus (Harappan) Civilisation in its mature phase (c. 2600–1900 BCE), showing the Ghaggar–Hakra channel. Whether and how this civilisation relates to the Vedic texts is discussed in Section 1.8. Map: Avantiputra7, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 1.8 Modern Academic Debates
docs.text: Several questions about the Vedas remain genuinely open. The most politically charged is the origin of the Indo-Aryan languages and of the people who composed the hymns.

docs.title: 1.8.1 Where Did the Indo-Aryan Languages Come From?
docs.text:
Sanskrit belongs to the Indo-European language family, together with Iranian, Greek, Latin, Germanic, Slavic and other languages. Since these languages share a common ancestor, its speakers must have lived somewhere, and its daughter languages must have spread from there. The debate is about where that homeland was and how Indo-Aryan reached South Asia. The main positions are:

  1. Migration from the Eurasian steppe. Most historical linguists, archaeologists and geneticists hold that Indo-Iranian developed in the steppe and Central Asia, and that Indo-Aryan speakers entered the north-west of the subcontinent in the second millennium BCE, through gradual movements of people over generations rather than a single “invasion”. Vedic culture on this view formed in South Asia, through interaction between incoming groups and the existing population; the Ṛgveda already contains words borrowed from local languages, and Vedic Sanskrit has the retroflex consonants typical of the South Asian linguistic area.

  2. Indigenous origin (“Out of India”). A minority of writers, mostly in India—among them K. D. Sethna, Shrikant Talageri, N. S. Rajaram and Koenraad Elst—argue that the Indo-Aryans were indigenous and that Indo-European languages spread outward from India, or that the Vedic people were the bearers of the Harappan Civilisation. This view has few supporters among specialists in historical linguistics.

It is important to see that this is not a division between “Indian” and “Western” scholarship. Leading Indian historians such as R. S. Sharma, Romila Thapar and Irfan Habib accept a second-millennium arrival of Indo-Aryan speech, while some Western writers argue for indigenous origins (Thapar 2002). The real division is between methods and kinds of evidence.

The evidence of ancient DNA.

Since 2018, genome-wide data from ancient skeletons have transformed the debate. The largest study, by Narasimhan and colleagues, analysed several hundred ancient individuals from Central and South Asia (Narasimhan et al. 2019). Its main findings are: (1) the population of the Harappan world was a mixture of ancestry related to ancient Iranian farmers and to indigenous South Asian hunter-gatherers, and lacked steppe ancestry; (2) ancestry derived from Middle-to-Late Bronze Age steppe populations entered South Asia in the first half of the second millennium BCE, c. 2000–1500 BCE; (3) most present-day South Asians descend from a mixture of these sources in varying proportions, and steppe-related ancestry is proportionally higher in some groups of traditionally priestly status and in speakers of Indo-European languages. A genome from the Harappan site of Rakhigarhi, published the same year, likewise showed no steppe ancestry (Shinde et al. 2019).

These results fit the migration model well. They are consistent with the arrival of Indo-Aryan languages with people moving from the north-west in the second millennium BCE, and hard to reconcile with an Indian origin of the Indo-European family. They do not show any “invasion” or conquest; they show admixture over many centuries. Nor do they make the Harappans “non-Indian” or Vedic culture “foreign”: both are chapters in the history of the subcontinent, and the population that composed and preserved the Vedas was a mixed one. The Harappan script remains undeciphered, and the language or languages of the Harappans are unknown.

docs.title: 1.8.2 Textual Criticism and Oral Tradition
docs.text: A second debate concerns how far Western textual-critical methods, developed for manuscript traditions, apply to an orally preserved corpus. The Vedic oral tradition has preserved the Ṛgveda with extraordinary fidelity (Chapter 11), so that variant readings of the kind found in manuscript traditions are almost absent. Scholars nevertheless detect earlier stages beneath the transmitted text: some features of the received Saṃhitā text, such as certain sandhi forms, are later than the hymns’ composition and must be undone to restore the original metre.

docs.title: 1.9 Vedic Manuscript Traditions
docs.text: The Vedas were composed and transmitted orally, and for a long time writing them down was positively discouraged; a passage of the Mahābhārata (13.24.70, critical edition) lists “those who write the Vedas” among those who will go to hell. Manuscripts were nevertheless made, as aids to teachers and ritualists. Because palm leaf, birch bark and paper decay quickly in the Indian climate, surviving Vedic manuscripts are late: very few are older than the eleventh century CE, and most were copied in the last four or five centuries.

docs.title: 1.9.1 Writing Materials and Scripts
docs.text:
Table 1.4 summarises the main writing materials and scripts.

Table 1.4. Writing materials used for Vedic manuscripts. Material Main Regions Typical Scripts Example Birch bark (bhūrjapatra) Kashmir Śāradā The Kashmir manuscript of the Paippalāda Atharvaveda, discovered in the 1870s and now in Tübingen Palm leaf (tālapatra) South India, Odisha, Nepal Grantha, Malayalam, Telugu, Odia Odia manuscripts of the Paippalāda Atharvaveda; South Indian Taittirīya texts Paper North and West India Devanāgarī Most Ṛgveda manuscripts used for the nineteenth-century editions

docs.title: 1.9.2 Major Manuscript Repositories
docs.text: Important collections of Vedic manuscripts are held by the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune; the Oriental Research Institute, Mysuru; the Adyar Library, Chennai; the Sarasvatī Mahal Library, Thanjavur; the Asiatic Society, Kolkata; the Sampurnanand Sanskrit University, Varanasi; and the National Archives of Nepal, Kathmandu. European libraries, especially in Oxford, London, Berlin and Tübingen, hold manuscripts collected in the colonial period. The Ṛgveda manuscripts in the Pune collection were inscribed in UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register in 2007.

docs.title: 1.9.3 The Relationship between Oral and Written Traditions
docs.text: The manuscript tradition was always secondary to the oral one. Manuscripts served as reference aids, not as the primary vehicle of transmission, and authentic Vedic learning is still considered incomplete without oral instruction from a qualified teacher (ācārya). This is why Vedic scholars can treat living reciters as witnesses to the text alongside the manuscripts.

docs.title: 1.10 The Place of the Vedas in Bhāratīya Civilisation
docs.text:
Within Brahmanical tradition the Vedas are the root authority from which later bodies of knowledge claim descent. Figure 1.4 shows this traditional self-understanding. It should be read as such: many of these traditions also drew on non-Vedic sources, the claimed descent is often nominal, and Buddhism, Jainism, many Tantric and devotional movements, and much of Tamil literature developed in dialogue with, or in opposition to, Vedic authority (Sections 15.2.1 and 15.2.2).

Figure 1.4. The Vedas as the root of later learning, as conceived in Brahmanical tradition. The claimed lines of descent are often nominal (Chapter 15); the lower box names traditions that stood outside the scheme or opposed it.

docs.title: 1.11 European Scholarship and Indian Responses
docs.text: The encounter between European scholarship and the Vedic tradition from the late 18th century onwards has had a profound and complex impact on the study of the Vedas. While European scholars made important contributions to textual scholarship, their work was also shaped by the ideological assumptions of the colonial era.

docs.title: 1.11.1 The Discovery of Sanskrit by Europe
docs.text: The systematic study of Sanskrit by European scholars began with Sir William Jones’s celebrated address to the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1786, in which he noted the structural similarities between Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin, thereby inaugurating the field of comparative philology. This discovery led to an explosion of interest in Sanskrit texts, including the Vedas.

docs.title: 1.11.2 Key European Scholars and Their Contributions
docs.text:
Table 1.5 lists the principal European Vedic scholars of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and their main contributions.

Table 1.5. Major European scholars of the Vedas and their contributions. Scholar Period Major Contribution Henry Thomas Colebrooke 1765–1837 First European to study the Vedas systematically; published essays on Vedic religion Friedrich Rosen 1805–1837 First European edition of part of the Ṛgveda (1838, posthumous) Rudolf Roth 1821–1895 Co-editor of the Sanskrit-Wörterbuch; foundational Vedic lexicography Friedrich Max Müller 1823–1900 Published the editio princeps of the Ṛgveda with Sāyaṇa’s commentary (6 vols.) Albrecht Weber 1825–1901 Extensive studies on Yajurveda and Vedic ritual Hermann Grassmann 1809–1877 Wörterbuch zum Rig-Veda (1873–75) and a German verse translation Ralph T.H. Griffith 1826–1906 Complete English translation of the Ṛgveda (1889–92), now dated but widely reprinted Karl Friedrich Geldner 1852–1929 German translation of the Ṛgveda (published 1951), the scholarly standard for decades Hermann Oldenberg 1854–1920 Die Religion des Veda (1894) (Oldenberg 1894); translation of the Gṛhyasūtras Arthur Berriedale Keith 1879–1944 Comprehensive studies on Brāhmaṇa literature and Vedic philosophy

docs.title: 1.11.3 Critiques of Colonial-Era Scholarship
docs.text:
Colonial-era scholarship laid the philological foundations on which all later work builds, but it has been criticised on several grounds, by Indian and Western scholars alike:

  1. Racial readings: Nineteenth-century writers often turned a linguistic category (speakers of Indo-European languages) into a racial one, and imagined the arrival of “Aryans” as the conquest of a dark-skinned native population by a fair-skinned invading race. This racial theory, and the picture of a violent “invasion”, are now rejected. Müller himself insisted that “Aryan” was a term of language, not of race, but the racial reading spread widely and was later exploited politically in Europe.

  2. Condescension: Some scholars treated the hymns as “primitive” nature worship and underestimated their poetic and intellectual sophistication.

  3. Neglect of Indian commentators: The Indian commentarial tradition, above all Sāyaṇa (14th century), was sometimes dismissed, although Müller’s edition printed Sāyaṇa’s commentary in full and Wilson’s translation followed it closely.

  4. Separation from the living tradition: Academic study tended to treat the Vedas as documents of the past, with little interest in the reciters and ritualists who still preserved them.

At the same time, many of the central results of nineteenth-century scholarship—the Indo-European language family, the relative order of the Vedic texts, the close kinship of Vedic and Avestan—have been confirmed by later research and are accepted by Indian and foreign specialists alike.

docs.title: 1.11.4 Indian Responses
docs.text:
Indian thinkers responded to colonial-era interpretations in different ways:

  • Dayānanda Sarasvatī (1824–1883), founder of the Ārya Samāj, read the Saṃhitās as monotheistic and as containing scientific knowledge, and rejected the authority of the Brāhmaṇas and Purāṇas.

  • B. G. Tilak (1856–1920) used astronomical references to argue for much earlier dates than those accepted by European scholars (Tilak 1893).

  • Sri Aurobindo (1872–1950), in The Secret of the Veda, read the Ṛgveda as a symbolic record of inner spiritual experience (Sri Aurobindo 1956).

  • Indian Sanskritists and historians also took up the philological method itself: R. G. Bhandarkar, V. S. Sukthankar and the editors of the Vaidika Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala’s critical edition of the Ṛgveda with Sāyaṇa’s commentary (Pune, 1933–1951) are examples.

docs.title: 1.11.5 Vedic Studies in the Twentieth Century
docs.text:
In the twentieth century the centres of Vedic philology multiplied. In Germany the tradition ran from Roth and Geldner to Paul Thieme and Karl Hoffmann; in the Netherlands J. C. Heesterman and above all Jan Gonda at Utrecht transformed the study of Vedic religion and ritual (Gonda 1975); in France Louis Renou devoted much of his life to Vedic grammar and poetics (Renou 1955–1969, 1965); in the United States Michael Witzel, Stephanie Jamison and Joel Brereton have shaped recent work; and in Japan scholars such as Yasuke Ikari have produced meticulous studies of the ritual texts.

Indian scholarship grew alongside, in modern universities and in institutions that bridge traditional and academic learning, such as the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute and the Vaidika Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala in Pune and the Vishveshvaranand Vedic Research Institute at Hoshiarpur. Its achievements include the Pune critical edition of the Ṛgveda with Sāyaṇa’s commentary, R. N. Dandekar’s Vedic Bibliography, C. G. Kashikar’s surveys of the śrauta ritual (Kashikar 1968) and the word-concordance Vaidika Padānukrama Koṣa begun by Vishva Bandhu (Section 12.7). The Vedas were also put into Indian languages. Dayānanda Sarasvatī’s commentary on the Yajurveda and the greater part of the Ṛgveda, in Sanskrit with a Hindi rendering, was left unfinished at his death in 1883; Romesh Chunder Dutt published a Bengali translation of the Ṛgveda in the 1880s; and S. D. Sātavalekar’s Svādhyāya Maṇḍala issued texts and Hindi translations of all four Saṃhitās. Translations and commentaries in Marathi, Gujarati, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and other languages followed during the twentieth century, though few of them rest on the critical scholarship of the period, and readable modern translations of many Vedic texts are still lacking (Section 15.10).

docs.title: 1.12.1 How Vedic Texts Are Cited
docs.text:
Vedic passages are cited by their traditional divisions, separated by full stops:

  • Ṛgveda (RV): book (maṇḍala), hymn, verse — e.g. RV 10.129.1;

  • Atharvaveda (AV, Śaunaka): book (kāṇḍa), hymn, verse — e.g. AV 12.1.12;

  • Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (VS): chapter, verse — e.g. VS 40.1;

  • Taittirīya Saṃhitā (TS): book, chapter (prapāṭhaka), section (anuvāka), paragraph — e.g. TS 4.5.2.1;

  • Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (ŚB): book, chapter, section, paragraph — e.g. ŚB 1.8.1.1;

  • Upaniṣads: chapter, section, verse or paragraph — e.g. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (BU) 1.4.10, Chāndogya Upaniṣad (ChU) 6.8.7.

docs.title: 1.12.2 Editions
docs.text: The first complete printed edition of the Ṛgveda was Max Müller’s, with Sāyaṇa’s commentary (1849–1874); Theodor Aufrecht published a transliterated text in 1861–1863, and B. A. van Nooten and G. B. Holland a “metrically restored” text that undoes later sandhi to recover the poets’ pronunciation (van Nooten and Holland 1994). The history of the editions of the whole corpus, from the first European editions to the Pune critical edition, the concordances and the digital texts now freely available, is told in Section 12.7.

docs.title: 1.12.3 Translations
docs.text: Complete translations of the Ṛgveda include those of H. H. Wilson (English, following Sāyaṇa, 1850–1888) (Wilson 1850–1888), Hermann Grassmann (German, 1876–77), R. T. H. Griffith (English, 1889–92; revised edition 1896) (Griffith 1896), K. F. Geldner (German, 1951) (Geldner 1951), Tatyana Elizarenkova (Russian, 1989–1999) (Elizarenkova 1989–1999) and Stephanie Jamison and Joel Brereton (English, 2014) (Jamison and Brereton 2014), whose companion volume is a good introduction to the text (Brereton and Jamison 2020); translations into Indian languages are noted above. Wendy Doniger’s selection of 108 hymns is a widely used introduction (O’Flaherty 1981). For the other texts, standard English translations include W. D. Whitney’s Atharvaveda (1905), A. B. Keith’s Taittirīya Saṃhitā (1914) (Keith 1914), Julius Eggeling’s Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa in the Sacred Books of the East (1882–1900) (Eggeling 1882) and Patrick Olivelle’s Upaniṣads and Dharma Sūtras. Because the Ṛgveda is difficult and allusive, translations differ greatly; readers should compare more than one. For the names, places and realia of the texts, Macdonell and Keith’s Vedic Index remains a standard tool (Macdonell and Keith 1912). The abbreviations used for texts in this volume are listed at the front of the book.

docs.title: 1.13 Why Study the Vedas Today?
docs.text: The Vedas are the oldest body of Indian literature and the foundation of much later Indian religion, law and thought; India’s later history cannot be understood without them, including those parts of their legacy, such as the origins of varṇa hierarchy, that later generations have rightly questioned. Their speculative hymns, and the Upaniṣads that grew out of the same schools, raise questions about being, the self and the origin of the world that remain of philosophical interest. The effort to preserve and perform them produced real achievements in phonetics, grammar, metrics, ritual geometry and calendrical astronomy. The Ṛgveda is among the oldest poetry in any Indo-European language, and much of it is poetry of high quality; Vedic Sanskrit is one of the chief witnesses for the reconstruction of Indo-European, and the Indian analysis of it, culminating in Pāṇini, is a landmark in the history of linguistics. Finally, the Vedas are still recited and used in ritual. Their recitation is kept alive by a comparatively small number of traditional schools and families, several of whose branches are now endangered (Chapters 11 and 12).

docs.title: 1.14 Transliteration and Conventions
docs.text:
Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST). Long vowels carry a macron (ā, ī, ū); retroflex consonants an underdot (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ); the palatal sibilant is written ś, the visarga ḥ, the anusvāra ṃ and the velar nasal ṅ. Tamil words follow the transliteration of the Madras Tamil Lexicon. Vedic accents are not marked in quotations, except in the specimen given in Section 11.4.

Sanskrit terms are set in italics and in lower case (deva, ṛṣi, śākhā, yajña). Capitals are kept for the names of persons, gods, peoples and places; for the titles and classes of texts (Ṛgveda, Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa, Upaniṣad, Śruti, Smṛti); and for a few words that have become English, such as Veda and Brahmin. Dates follow the conventions stated in the Preface. Translations are the author’s own unless otherwise indicated.

Note: Living Texts

The Vedas are not only objects of historical study. For many people in India and elsewhere they are living texts, recited daily in homes and temples, learnt under the guidance of teachers, and regarded as the highest religious authority. This volume tries to describe that tradition accurately and with respect for those who maintain it, while applying to the texts the same historical and philological methods that are applied to any other ancient literature. Readers of every background—practitioners, students and scholars—are invited to approach the texts in that spirit of careful and open enquiry.

Scholarly Note: Quotations about the Vedas

Popular books often quote famous Western figures in praise of the Vedas. Many of these quotations cannot be traced. The often-repeated line attributed to J. Robert Oppenheimer (“Access to the Vedas is the greatest privilege this century may claim…”) has no identifiable source and is omitted here. Arthur Schopenhauer’s celebrated praise is genuine but concerns the Upaniṣads, which he read in Anquetil-Duperron’s Latin translation of a Persian version (the Oupnek’hat); he wrote that their study had been the consolation of his life and would be that of his death (Parerga and Paralipomena, vol. II, §185). Versions in which he speaks of “the Vedas” are later distortions. This volume quotes modern authors only where the source can be named.

docs.title: 1.15 The Structure of This Volume
docs.text:
The present volume, Veda Prakāśa, is organised into fifteen chapters (Table 1.6). Chapters 2–5 take the four Saṃhitās in turn, and Chapters 6 and 7 the prose and auxiliary literature that grew around them. Chapters 8 and 9 describe the solemn and domestic rituals as systems, and Chapter 10 the later scheme of “subsidiary Vedas”. Chapters 11 and 12 turn to the oral tradition and to the schools that preserved the texts, Chapters 13 and 14 to the world-view and society that the texts reveal, and Chapter 15 to the later history of the Veda, including its Buddhist, Jain and Tamil critics and admirers. A list of abbreviations precedes this chapter; a glossary and a chronology follow the bibliography.

Table 1.6. Chapter overview of Veda Prakāśa. Ch. Title Subject Matter 1 Introduction The corpus, its dating and transmission, and the history of its study 2 Ṛgveda The ten books, the gods and myths, the landmark hymns, Vedic poetics 3 Yajurveda The Black and White branches, their Saṃhitās, the Agnicayana, the Śatapatha 4 Sāmaveda Verse collections and song-books, chant and notation, the Chāndogya 5 Atharvaveda The two recensions, charms and healing, speculative hymns 6 Brāhmaṇas & Āraṇyakas Ritual exegesis, correspondences, narratives, the inner sacrifice 7 Vedāṅgas Phonetics, metre, grammar, etymology, calendar and ritual geometry 8 Śrauta Ritual The solemn sacrifices: manuals, ritual ground, principal rites, history 9 Gṛhya Ritual The domestic rites and the life-cycle rites in the Gṛhyasūtras 10 Upavedas The scheme of four “subsidiary Vedas” as a classification 11 Oral Tradition Teacher and pupil, the recitation patterns, the accent 12 Vedic Schools The śākhās: geography, history, survival, editions 13 Vedic Worldview Cosmogony, ṛta and dharma, the gods, death, nature 14 Vedic Society Archaeology, varṇa, priesthood, women, economy, polity 15 Legacy & Relevance The later gods, critics and admirers, modern readings, living traditions

docs.title: Chapter 2: The Ṛgveda: The Veda of Praise
docs.text:
Invocatory Verse

agnim īḷe purohitaṃ yajñasya devam ṛtvijam hotāraṃ ratnadhātamam I praise Agni, the household priest, the god of the sacrifice, the officiant, the invoker, who best bestows treasure. — Ṛgveda 1.1.1

docs.title: 2.1 Introduction to the Ṛgveda
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda (ṛc, “verse of praise” + veda, “knowledge”) is the oldest of the four Vedas and the oldest substantial text in any Indo-Aryan language. Composed in the north-west of the subcontinent over several centuries, probably c. 1500–1200 BCE for its core and somewhat later for its latest parts (see Section 1.7), it was preserved orally with extraordinary accuracy for some three thousand years (Jamison and Brereton 2014; Witzel 2003).

The Ṛgveda Saṃhitā consists of 10,552 verses (ṛc) in 1,028 hymns (sūkta), grouped into ten books (maṇḍala). The hymns are addressed mainly to the gods (devas)—powers of nature, of the ritual and of social order—and were recited by the hotṛ priest at the sacrifice. They are also highly crafted poetry, full of word-play, riddles and allusion, composed by hereditary families of poets who prized verbal skill and competed for the favour of gods and patrons.

Key Facts about the Ṛgveda

Maṇḍalas (books): 10 Sūktas (hymns): 1,028 (including the 11 Vālakhilya hymns) Ṛcs (verses): 10,552 Words: about 153,800 (traditional count) Commonest metres: Triṣṭubh, Gāyatrī, Jagatī Most-invoked deities: Indra, Agni, Soma Surviving recension: Śākala

docs.title: 2.2 The Ten Maṇḍalas: Structure and Organisation
docs.text:
Scholars distinguish between the “family books” (Maṇḍalas 2–7), each the collection of a particular clan of poets, and the books added around them (Maṇḍalas 1, 8, 9 and 10), as Figure 2.1 shows.

Figure 2.1. Overview of the ten Maṇḍalas of the Ṛgveda. Verse counts follow the standard edition and total 10,552.

docs.title: 2.2.1 The Family Books (Maṇḍalas 2–7)
docs.text:
The family books form the oldest nucleus of the Ṛgveda. Each is the collection of one poetic clan, and within each book the hymns are arranged on a consistent plan: first by deity (Agni first, then Indra, then other gods), and within each deity-group by decreasing number of verses per hymn. Hymns that break this pattern are often later additions—one of the clues used by scholars to identify the growth of the collection (Witzel 1997). Table 2.1 lists the six family books.

Table 2.1. The Family Books of the Ṛgveda. Maṇḍala Poet Family Sūktas Verses Notable Feature II Gṛtsamada 43 429 Smallest family book III Viśvāmitra 62 617 Contains the Gāyatrī (3.62.10); Viśvāmitra and the rivers (3.33) IV Vāmadeva 58 589 Rich in Indra hymns V Atri 87 727 Third largest family book VI Bharadvāja 75 765 Second largest family book VII Vasiṣṭha 104 841 Largest family book; Battle of the Ten Kings (7.18)

By number of verses the family books rank: VII (841), VI (765), V (727), III (617), IV (589), II (429). The books are arranged broadly in order of increasing size, from the small second book to the large seventh, though the order is not strict.

docs.title: 2.2.2 The Added Maṇḍalas (1, 8, 9 and 10)
docs.text:
Maṇḍala 1, with 191 hymns and 2,006 verses, is the longest book. It brings together collections by several poets, including Madhucchandas, Medhātithi, Kutsa, Gotama Rāhūgaṇa and Dīrghatamas, whose riddle hymn (1.164) is one of the most difficult and influential compositions in the Ṛgveda.

Maṇḍala 8 is associated chiefly with the Kāṇva family. It contains the Vālakhilya hymns (8.49–59), a supplementary group of eleven hymns, and is notable for its pragātha strophes, in which verses in different metres are combined in pairs.

Maṇḍala 9 is devoted entirely to Soma Pavamāna, “self-purifying Soma”. Its hymns were gathered from the family collections and arranged by metre. They describe the Soma juice flowing through the woollen filter (pavitra), likened to a racing horse, a bellowing bull and a stream of light.

Maṇḍala 10 is the latest book. It contains many of the speculative hymns (the Nāsadīya, Puruṣa and Hiraṇyagarbha hymns), the funeral and wedding hymns, charms closer in character to the Atharvaveda, and several dialogue hymns.

docs.title: 2.2.3 Internal Ordering Principles
docs.text:
The arrangement of the Ṛgveda reflects careful editorial work by its redactors (Table 2.2):

  1. Within the family books: hymns are arranged by deity and then by decreasing length, as described above.

  2. The family books themselves: broadly in order of increasing size.

  3. The Aṣṭaka system: an alternative division into eight aṣṭakas of eight adhyāyas each, subdivided into short vargas, used for teaching and memorisation. It cuts across the boundaries of the Maṇḍalas.

Table 2.2. Overview of all ten Maṇḍalas of the Ṛgveda. Maṇḍala Principal Poet(s) Sūktas Verses Special Features I Several (Madhucchandas, Dīrghatamas, etc.) 191 2,006 Longest book; riddle hymn 1.164 II Gṛtsamada 43 429 Smallest family book III Viśvāmitra 62 617 Gāyatrī (3.62.10) IV Vāmadeva 58 589 Rich Indra mythology V Atri 87 727 Hymns to Mitra–Varuṇa and the Maruts VI Bharadvāja 75 765 Hymns to Indra and Agni; Pūṣan VII Vasiṣṭha 104 841 Battle of the Ten Kings; Varuṇa hymns VIII Kāṇvas and others 103 1,716 Vālakhilya hymns; pragātha strophes IX Various (arranged by metre) 114 1,108 Entirely devoted to Soma Pavamāna X Various 191 1,754 Speculative hymns; latest layer Total 1,028 10,552

docs.title: 2.3 The Principal Deities of the Ṛgveda
docs.text: The Ṛgveda addresses a large pantheon. Roughly a quarter of the hymns are addressed to Indra, nearly a fifth to Agni and over a tenth to Soma; the remainder are distributed among many deities, among them Varuṇa and Mitra, the Aśvins, Uṣas, Sūrya and Savitṛ, the Maruts, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, the Viśvedevas and the goddesses Sarasvatī and Aditi (Macdonell 1900).

docs.title: 2.3.1 Indra: King of the Gods
docs.text: Indra is the warrior god par excellence, the slayer of the serpent Vṛtra who had confined the waters, the breaker of the Vala cave that held the cattle and the dawns, and the patron of the Ārya in battle. Strengthened by Soma and armed with the vajra, he kills Vṛtra and releases the waters; the myth is told many times, most fully in RV 1.32. Naturalistic interpreters read it as the release of rain or of rivers; Sri Aurobindo read it as the victory of illumined consciousness over obstruction.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Agni: The Sacred Fire
docs.text: Agni is the fire in its many forms—domestic, sacrificial, lightning and sun—and above all the messenger between humans and gods, who carries the offerings to heaven. He is the household priest (purohita) of the gods and the model of the human priest, and his hymns open each of the family books.

docs.title: 2.3.3 Soma: The Sacred Drink
docs.text: Soma is at once a plant, the drink pressed from it, and a god. The pressed juice, filtered and mixed with milk, was offered to the gods and drunk by the priests, and it was believed to give inspiration, strength and a sense of immortality (amṛta): “We have drunk the Soma; we have become immortal” (RV 8.48.3, apāma somaṃ amṛtā abhūma). The identity of the original plant is unknown; ephedra is a leading candidate among many that have been proposed.

docs.title: 2.3.4 Varuṇa: The Guardian of Ṛta
docs.text: Varuṇa, often paired with Mitra, is the sovereign guardian of ṛta and of oaths. He binds wrongdoers with his fetters, and the hymns addressed to him in Book 7 (7.86–89) contain the Ṛgveda’s most personal expressions of guilt and prayers for forgiveness.

docs.title: 2.3.5 Other Gods and Goddesses
docs.text:
Beyond these four, the Ṛgveda addresses a large and varied company of deities. Hymn counts are approximate, since many hymns are addressed to several gods at once (Macdonell 1897; Jamison and Brereton 2014).

The Ādityas.

Varuṇa and Mitra head a group of gods called the Ādityas, sons of the goddess Aditi (“boundlessness”). RV 2.27.1 names six of them—Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga, Varuṇa, Dakṣa and Aṃśa—and RV 10.72.8 speaks of eight sons of Aditi. They personify aspects of social order: contract (Mitra), hospitality and the customs of marriage (Aryaman), and the fair portion (Bhaga, Aṃśa). Later texts count twelve Ādityas and equate them with the months of the year (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.5).

Gods of light.

Sūrya, the sun, is the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa, who sees the deeds of mortals (RV 1.115). Savitṛ, the “impeller”, rouses all beings in the morning and sends them to rest at evening (RV 2.38); the Gāyatrī is addressed to him. Uṣas, the Dawn, receives some twenty hymns (Section 2.16). Pūṣan, protector of roads, travellers and herds, who finds lost cattle and conducts the dead, has a group of hymns in Book 6 (RV 6.53–58).

Viṣṇu.

Viṣṇu receives only a handful of hymns, but his characteristic deed is celebrated repeatedly: with three strides he measured out the earthly realms and the heavens (RV 1.154.1–3), and in his highest step there is a spring of honey (1.154.5). A much-recited verse says that “the wise always see that highest step of Viṣṇu” (tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padaṃ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ, RV 1.22.20). In the Brāhmaṇas he is identified with the sacrifice (ŚB 1.1.2.13) and appears as the dwarf who wins the worlds for the gods (ŚB 1.2.5.5); in the epics and Purāṇas he becomes one of the two supreme gods of Hinduism.

Rudra and the Maruts.

Rudra is addressed in only three complete hymns (RV 1.114, 2.33, 7.46). He is a fierce archer whose anger brings disease and death to people and cattle, and at the same time a healer, called “the best physician among physicians” (RV 2.33.4), whose remedies are prayed for. The Yajurvedic Śatarudrīya (Section 3.7) appeals to his “kindly form” (śivā tanūḥ); the euphemistic epithet śiva, “auspicious”, later became the name of the great god Śiva. Rudra’s sons, the Maruts, a troop of young storm-gods with lances and golden ornaments, are Indra’s companions in the fight against Vṛtra and receive some thirty hymns.

The Aśvins.

The twin horsemen, also called the Nāsatyas (the name found in the Mitanni treaty, Section 1.7), receive more than fifty hymns. They drive a chariot at dawn and are above all rescuers and healers: the poets recall how they made the aged seer Cyavāna young again, gave the warrior woman Viśpalā a metal leg (jaṅghām āyasīm, RV 1.116.15; on ayas see Section 1.7), and brought Bhujyu home from the sea (RV 1.116). They are usually compared with the divine twins of Greek and Baltic tradition.

Other gods.

Bṛhaspati or Brahmaṇaspati, “lord of the sacred formula”, is the divine priest who splits the Vala cave with his chant. Vāyu and Vāta are the wind; Parjanya is the thunder-cloud that brings rain (RV 5.83); Tvaṣṭṛ is the divine craftsman who fashioned Indra’s vajra (RV 1.32.2); the Ṛbhus are artisans who won immortality by their skill; Yama is king of the dead (Section 13.7); Heaven and Earth (Dyāvāpṛthivī) are praised as a parental pair; and the Viśvedevas, the “All-Gods”, are invoked as a collective.

Goddesses.

Goddesses are fewer and less prominent than gods. Besides Uṣas, Aditi and Sarasvatī, the Ṛgveda addresses Rātrī, the Night (RV 10.127), Araṇyānī, the lady of the forest (RV 10.146), Pṛthivī, the Earth, and Vāk, Speech (RV 10.125); the wives of the gods, such as Indrāṇī, receive offerings but have little mythology of their own. The great goddesses of later Hinduism are largely post-Vedic, though Vedic names and motifs, such as Śrī in the Śrī Sūkta (a supplementary hymn) and Ambikā as Rudra’s sister in the Yajurveda (VS 3.57), became points of departure for them.

The relative standing of these gods changed greatly over time. Indra and Varuṇa, central in the Ṛgveda, became minor figures in later Hinduism, while Viṣṇu and Rudra–Śiva, comparatively marginal in the hymns, rose to supremacy (Section 15.3).

docs.title: 2.4 The Myths of the Ṛgveda
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda contains a large body of myth, but it rarely tells a story from beginning to end. The poets allude to deeds that their audience knew, celebrating them in a phrase or a verse and then moving on (Section 2.9). The myths must therefore be pieced together from scattered allusions, with the help of the Brāhmaṇas, Yāska’s Nirukta, the Bṛhaddevatā and Sāyaṇa, which often supply a narrative—sometimes, it seems, one constructed to explain an obscure verse. Several myths were retold in the epics and Purāṇas, and comparison with the Avesta and other Indo-European traditions shows that some are older than the hymns. The main ones are listed in Table 2.3.

Indra’s deeds.

The central myth is Indra’s victory over Vṛtra, the serpent who held back the waters (RV 1.32; Section 2.3). Around it cluster other deeds that make Indra a creator as well as a warrior: he made firm the quaking earth, settled the mountains, measured out the midspace and propped up the sky (RV 2.12.2), and he begot the sun and the dawn (2.12.7). A dialogue hymn (RV 4.18) tells of his strange and violent birth, in which he insists on coming out sideways, through his mother’s flank (4.18.2), and a later verse asks who made his mother a widow and which god showed him mercy when he seized his father by the foot and struck him down (4.18.12). Another hymn (RV 10.8.8–9) tells how Trita Āptya, urged on by Indra, fought the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ, and how Indra cut off his three heads and released his cows. Its Avestan counterpart, noted in Section 1.7, shows that the myth is older than the separation of the Indian and Iranian traditions; in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā the three-headed Viśvarūpa has become a Brahmin, and his killing a sin (Section 15.3).

The cave of Vala.

In the second great myth the cows—and with them the dawns and the light—have been shut up in a rock cave, Vala, by the Paṇis, a group of stingy, non-sacrificing beings. Indra with the Aṅgiras seers, or Bṛhaspati with his chant, breaks the cave open, and the dawns and cows come out (RV 3.31; 10.67–68). The divine bitch Saramā tracks down the cows, and in a dialogue hymn (RV 10.108) she demands them from the Paṇis, who try in vain to bribe her. Where the Vṛtra myth is a battle, the Vala myth is a ritual victory won by the sacred word, and the poets identify themselves with the Aṅgiras who opened the cave with their song. Michael Witzel has compared it with the Japanese myth of the sun goddess who hides in a rock cave until she is lured out, and suggests that both continue a very old myth of the hidden sun (Witzel 2005).

Fire and Soma brought from afar.

Both the substances of the sacrifice are said to have come from elsewhere. Mātariśvan brought Agni, who had been hidden, from far away, churned out from among the gods (RV 3.9.5), and in another myth Agni flees from his priestly duty into the waters and must be coaxed back by the gods (RV 10.51). Soma was fetched from heaven by a falcon, who escaped the arrows of the archer Kṛśānu at the cost of a feather (RV 4.26–27). The epic story of Garuḍa stealing the nectar of immortality from the gods, told in the first book of the Mahābhārata, is a later development of the same theme.

The first mortals.

Yama, son of Vivasvant, is the first mortal to die and the one who found the path to the world of the fathers, which all the dead now follow (RV 10.14.1–2); his twin sister Yamī proposes that they unite to continue the human race, and he refuses (RV 10.10). Their mother is the subject of one of the most enigmatic myths of the collection. Two verses of a funeral hymn (RV 10.17.1–2) say that Tvaṣṭṛ held a wedding for his daughter; the mother of Yama, the wife of Vivasvant, disappeared; the gods hid the immortal woman from mortals, made one “of the same kind” (savarṇā) and gave her to Vivasvant; and Saraṇyū bore the Aśvins and abandoned the twins. Yāska and the Bṛhaddevatā expand this into a story in which Saraṇyū takes the form of a mare and Vivasvant that of a stallion, and the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa retells it as the story of Saṃjñā, the Sun’s wife, who leaves her “shadow” (Chāyā) in her place. Wendy Doniger has traced the long history of this myth of the substitute wife (Doniger 1999). Manu, Yama’s brother, is the first sacrificer and the ancestor of humankind.

Gods made by skill.

The Ṛbhus were craftsmen who, by making four cups out of the one cup of Tvaṣṭṛ, renewing their aged parents and fashioning a cow and a chariot, won a share in the sacrifice and immortality (RV 1.161; 4.33–37). The myth expresses in divine terms the poets’ own claim that skilled work wins a place among the gods.

Table 2.3. Principal myths of the Ṛgveda and their later development. Myth Main hymns Later development Indra slays Vṛtra 1.32; 2.12 Vṛtra counted a Brahmin; Indra’s guilt (Mahābhārata, Udyogaparvan) Trita and the three-headed one 10.8.8–9 Avestan Thraētaona; Viśvarūpa as a Brahmin (TS 2.5.1) Opening of the Vala cave 3.31; 10.67–68; 10.108 Parallel: the Japanese hidden-sun myth (Witzel) Mātariśvan brings fire 3.9.5 — Agni hides in the waters 10.51 Retold in the Brāhmaṇas The falcon brings Soma 4.26–27 Garuḍa steals the nectar (Mahābhārata 1) Viṣṇu’s three strides 1.154 The dwarf Vāmana Yama, Yamī and the first death 10.10; 10.14 Yama as judge of the dead Saraṇyū and the substitute wife 10.17.1–2 Saṃjñā and Chāyā (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa) Puruṛavas and Urvaśī 10.95 Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.5.1; Kālidāsa’s Vikramorvaśīya The Ṛbhus’ four cups 1.161; 4.33–37 —

How the myths should be understood has been debated since the nineteenth century. Max Müller and the “nature-myth” school read them as poetic accounts of sun, storm and dawn; others read them as reflections of the ritual, or of the conflicts of the Vedic clans. F. B. J. Kuiper argued that the Vṛtra and Vala myths together form a cosmogony, in which the world of order and light is won from an undifferentiated primordial state, and that the ritual, especially at the turn of the year, re-enacted it (Kuiper 1983). These readings are not exclusive: a myth recited at the Soma sacrifice could at once recall a cosmic event, model the ritual being performed, and promise the patron the same victory.

docs.title: 2.5.1 The Nāsadīya Sūkta (Hymn of Creation) — RV 10.129
docs.text:
This short hymn of seven verses is one of the most celebrated speculative poems in world literature. It begins by denying that either being or non-being existed at the beginning:

Nāsadīya Sūkta — Ṛgveda 10.129.1

nāsad āsīn no sad āsīt tadānīṃ nāsīd rajo no vyomā paro yat kim āvarīvaḥ kuha kasya śarmann ambhaḥ kim āsīd gahanaṃ gabhīram There was neither non-existence nor existence then; there was neither the realm of space nor the sky beyond. What stirred? Where? In whose protection? Was there water, unfathomably deep? — Ṛgveda 10.129.1

The hymn goes on to describe “That One” breathing without breath, born by the power of heat (tapas), and desire (kāma) as the first seed of mind. It then turns to doubt: the gods came later than this creation (v. 6), so who knows whence it arose? It ends: “he who is its overseer in the highest heaven surely knows—or perhaps he does not know” (v. 7).

docs.title: 2.5.2 The Gāyatrī Mantra — RV 3.62.10
docs.text:
The most widely recited verse of the Vedic tradition, also called the Sāvitrī, is attributed to Viśvāmitra and addressed to Savitṛ, the god who “impels” all beings:

Gāyatrī Mantra — Ṛgveda 3.62.10

tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt We meditate on that desirable radiance of the god Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts.

In later tradition the verse was taught at initiation (upanayana) and recited daily in the sandhyā rite. For most of its history it was restricted to initiated men of the three upper varṇas; in modern times reformers such as the Ārya Samāj opened it to all.

docs.title: 2.5.3 The Puruṣa Sūkta — RV 10.90
docs.text:
The Puruṣa Sūkta describes the sacrifice of a primordial cosmic Man (puruṣa) by the gods, from whose dismembered body the world was made: the moon from his mind, the sun from his eye, Indra and Agni from his mouth, the wind from his breath. Verse 12 derives the four social classes (varṇas) from his body:

Puruṣa Sūkta — Ṛgveda 10.90.12

brāhmaṇo ’sya mukham āsīd bāhū rājanyaḥ kṛtaḥ ūrū tad asya yad vaiśyaḥ padbhyāṃ śūdro ajāyata The Brahmin was his mouth; his two arms were made the Rājanya; his two thighs, that was the Vaiśya; from his feet the Śūdra was born.

Linguistic and stylistic evidence shows that the hymn belongs to the latest layer of the Ṛgveda, and this is the only passage in the Ṛgveda that names all four varṇas. Its image of a body in which the mouth is higher than the feet became the classic charter of a hierarchical social order, cited again and again in later law books. For this reason it has also been the target of sustained criticism, most powerfully by B. R. Ambedkar, who argued in Who Were the Shudras? (1946) that the verse was a late interpolation used to sanctify inequality (Ambedkar 1946). The hymn is discussed further in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 2.5.4 The Vāk Sūkta — RV 10.125
docs.text:
In this hymn Speech (Vāk) speaks in the first person as the power that supports the gods: she moves with the Rudras, Vasus and Ādityas, bears Mitra and Varuṇa, Indra and Agni, and makes whomever she loves powerful, a seer or a sage. The tradition ascribes the hymn to Vāk, daughter of the seer Ambhṛṇa:

Vāk Sūkta — Ṛgveda 10.125.3

ahaṃ rāṣṭrī saṃgamanī vasūnāṃ cikituṣī prathamā yajñiyānām I am the queen, the gatherer of riches, the knowing one, first of those worthy of worship.

docs.title: 2.5.5 The Hiraṇyagarbha Sūkta — RV 10.121
docs.text: This hymn celebrates a “Golden Embryo” (Hiraṇyagarbha), the first-born lord of creation. Nine verses end with the refrain kasmai devāya haviṣā vidhema—“To which god shall we offer worship with oblation?”; a final verse, generally regarded as a later addition, answers the question by naming Prajāpati.

docs.title: 2.6 Philosophical Themes in the Ṛgveda
docs.text: The Ṛgveda is primarily a liturgical collection, but its later layers in particular contain genuine philosophical enquiry.

docs.title: 2.6.1 Ṛta (Cosmic Order)
docs.text: Ṛta denotes the order of the world—the regularity of nature, the correct ritual, and truthful conduct. The gods, especially Mitra and Varuṇa, uphold it; sacrifice supports it; and human conduct should conform to it (Section 13.3).

docs.title: 2.6.2 Unity behind the Many Gods
docs.text:
While the Ṛgveda addresses many gods, some late hymns suggest that the many are names of one reality:

Ekam Sat — Ṛgveda 1.164.46

ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti agniṃ yamaṃ mātariśvānam āhuḥ The inspired poets speak of the one Being in many ways; they call it Agni, Yama, Mātariśvan. — Ṛgveda 1.164.46

This verse, from Dīrghatamas’s riddle hymn, became central to later Hindu thought, which read it as a statement of the unity of the divine behind many names. Within the Ṛgveda itself such statements are rare and late; most hymns treat the gods as distinct persons.

docs.title: 2.6.3 The Spirit of Enquiry
docs.text: The interrogative mood of several hymns—“To which god shall we offer?”, “Who truly knows?”—shows a philosophical curiosity that prefigures the Upaniṣads. The riddle hymn RV 1.164 poses dozens of enigmas about the year, speech, the sun and the origin of the world, many of which are still debated.

docs.title: 2.7 The Śākala Recension and the Khilas
docs.text:
Of the twenty-one schools of the Ṛgveda traditionally enumerated, only the Śākala recension survives complete. It is the text on which all editions and translations are based. Other schools, such as the Bāṣkala, Āśvalāyana and Śāṅkhāyana, are known through their ancillary literature and through a few variants in the number and order of hymns.

A collection of supplementary hymns, the Khilāni or Khilas, was transmitted alongside the Ṛgveda, notably in a Kashmiri birch-bark manuscript. It includes the Śrī Sūkta to the goddess Śrī–Lakṣmī, which became very popular in later worship.

The text is divided in two ways:

  • Maṇḍala system: ten books, hymns and verses; the standard scholarly arrangement (e.g. RV 10.129.1).

  • Aṣṭaka system: eight aṣṭakas, each of eight adhyāyas, divided into vargas of about five verses; used in traditional teaching.

docs.title: 2.8 Literary and Poetic Features
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda is poetry of a highly developed kind. Its techniques include (for the metres see Table 2.4):

  1. Imagery: dawn as a radiant young woman, the rivers as cows or mares, fire as a messenger and as a horse.

  2. Metre: verses are built of lines with a fixed number of syllables and a partly regular rhythm, especially in the cadence.

  3. Dialogue hymns: dramatic exchanges such as Yama and Yamī (10.10) or Puruṛavas and Urvaśī (10.95).

  4. Riddles and enigmas: some hymns are built of riddles, a form linked to the ritual verbal contest (brahmodya).

  5. Ring composition, refrain and repetition, serving both artistic and liturgical ends.

Table 2.4. Principal metres of the Ṛgveda. Proportions are rough estimates. Metre Syllables per Line Lines per Verse Share of Verses Triṣṭubh 11 4 (44 syllables) about two-fifths Gāyatrī 8 3 (24 syllables) about one-quarter Jagatī 12 4 (48 syllables) about one-eighth Anuṣṭubh 8 4 (32 syllables) smaller share; becomes the classical śloka Uṣṇih 8+8+12 3 (28 syllables) minor Bṛhatī 8+8+12+8 4 (36 syllables) minor

docs.title: 2.9 The Poet’s Craft: Vedic Poetics
docs.text: The list above names some of the devices of the hymns. This section asks how the Vedic poets understood their own work, in what setting they composed, what they did with their language, and how modern readers have tried to follow them. The metres themselves, and their later history, are treated in Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā, in the chapter on prosody; the classical theory of poetry (alaṅkāraśāstra), which drew very little on the Veda, is the subject of Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā.

docs.title: 2.9.1 Seer and Maker
docs.text:
The later tradition calls the composers of the hymns ṛṣis, “seers” (Section 1.4). The hymns themselves use a richer vocabulary. The poet is a kavi, a word for a person of insight and wisdom that is applied also to the gods, above all to Agni, Soma and Varuṇa, and that became the ordinary word for a poet of classical kāvya. He is a vipra, usually explained as “the quivering one”, the inspired poet stirred by his vision; the word later came to mean simply a Brahmin. He is a jaritṛ or stotṛ, a “singer” or “praiser”, and a kāru, a “bard” who celebrates the gods. What he produces is a dhī (“insight, visionary thought”), a mati or manīṣā (“thought, conception”), a brahman (“formulation”, the word from which the later brahman and brāhmaṇa descend), a stoma or uktha (“praise, recitation”), or a sūkta, literally “well spoken”.

This vocabulary holds together two ideas that later thought separated. On the one hand the poem is received: it is a vision granted by the gods, kindled by Soma, and the most famous of all Vedic verses, the Gāyatrī (RV 3.62.10, Section 2.5), is a prayer that Savitṛ may “impel our insights” (dhiyaḥ). Jan Gonda’s study of dhī and related words showed how central this idea of a visionary faculty is to the poets’ self-description (Gonda 1963). On the other hand the poem is made. The poets describe their work in the language of the crafts: a poet of the fifth book says that he has fashioned his praise for Agni “as a skilled and steady craftsman fashions a chariot” (rathaṃ na dhīraḥ svapā atakṣam, RV 5.2.11), and others speak of weaving, polishing and adorning their hymns like a bride. Again and again they offer the god a “new” hymn (navya), composed in an inherited manner but in fresh words. Novelty within tradition was the poet’s ideal.

The Mīmāṃsā school, which defended the authorlessness of the Veda, was aware of the difficulty. Jaimini’s sūtras state the objection that the Vedas bear the names of persons and mention beings who lived and died (Mīmāṃsāsūtra 1.1.27–28), and answer that names such as Kāṭhaka come from expounding a text, not from composing it (ākhyā pravacanāt, 1.1.30), and that apparent references to historical persons are only similarities of sound (1.1.31). In the tradition’s view the ṛṣi named in the Anukramaṇī is the one to whom a mantra first appeared. The historian, reading the same hymns, sees named poets and families at work over several centuries. Both readings take seriously the poets’ claim that their words came to them from beyond themselves.

docs.title: 2.9.2 Poets, Patrons and Contest
docs.text:
The hymns were composed for performance at sacrifices sponsored by patrons—chiefs and wealthy householders, often called sūri or maghavan (“bountiful”, an epithet also of Indra). Many sacrificers might be calling on the same god on the same day, and the poet’s task was to make his patron’s invitation the one the god accepted. The hymns therefore have a competitive edge. They refer to rival poets and rival sacrifices, and to a verbal contest (vivāc) in which the better formulation “won” the god and the prize. F. B. J. Kuiper’s study of this “verbal contest” showed how much of the hymns’ language belongs to it (Kuiper 1960). The reward is recorded in the “praises of the gift” (dānastuti) that close many hymns (Section 2.19; on the priests’ fee see Chapter 8).

The poets reflected on their art. RV 10.71, addressed to Bṛhaspati, the lord of the sacred formulation, describes how the wise “made speech with their mind, sifting it like groats through a sieve” (saktum iva titaunā punantaḥ, 10.71.2), and how in that speech companions recognise their companionship; the hymn goes on to mock those who hear speech without understanding it and those who master its outward form without its meaning. Mastery of the formulation bound poets into a fellowship and set them apart from those who lacked it. The families of poets in the family books (Section 2.2) were the institutions in which this mastery was taught and passed on.

docs.title: 2.9.3 Language and Technique
docs.text:
The Vedic poets used every level of their language. Tatyana Elizarenkova’s study of the language and style of the hymns shows how they exploited sound, word-formation, case and syntax for poetic effect (Elizarenkova 1995). A god’s name may be declined through a series of cases in successive verses; a root may be repeated in different forms within a line; words are placed in unusual orders, and verbs or subjects are left to be supplied by the hearer. Many hymns allude to myths without telling them, as if the audience knew the story and wanted only to hear it evoked in a new way; the straightforward narrative of Indra’s fight with Vṛtra in RV 1.32 is an exception. Words are often chosen because they can be read in two ways, one referring to the ritual taking place and the other to the cosmic or mythic event it re-enacts. Later Vedic texts made a principle of this indirectness: “the gods love the cryptic, as it were, and dislike the obvious” (parokṣapriyā iva hi devāḥ pratyakṣadviṣaḥ), says the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4.2.2), explaining the name Indra as a veiled form of Indha, “the kindler”.

The hymns are also carefully built. Besides refrain and ring composition, in which a hymn ends by returning to the words of its beginning, verses are often linked by catchwords, and some hymns are arranged symmetrically around a central verse that carries their deepest or most enigmatic statement, a structure that Jamison and Brereton call an “omphalos” (navel) (Jamison and Brereton 2014). The metres set the frame (Table 2.4): within a fixed number of syllables, and with a regular cadence at the end of the line, the poet had considerable freedom in the opening of each line.

docs.title: 2.9.4 Hymn and Rite: The Āprī Hymns
docs.text: The Āprī hymns show particularly clearly how poetry, ritual and family identity were bound together.
