The Brāhmaṇas and Āraṇyakas are the prose texts that stand between the Saṃhitās and the Upaniṣads. The Brāhmaṇas explain the solemn (śrauta) rituals: how they are to be performed, why each act is done as it is, and what it means. The Āraṇyakas (“forest books”) deal with rites and teachings considered too dangerous or secret to be learnt in the village, and they contain, or shade into, the earliest Upaniṣads. Most of this literature was composed c. 850–500 BCE (Table 1.2), as Vedic culture spread eastward from the Kuru–Pañcāla country into Kosala and Videha (Witzel 1997; Gonda 1975).

Older accounts presented the Brāhmaṇas as arid ritualism. Modern scholarship has recovered their intellectual seriousness: they develop a systematic way of thinking about correspondences between ritual, cosmos and person, and much of the vocabulary and many of the questions of the Upaniṣads come directly from them.

docs.title: 6.2.1 Nature and Purpose
docs.text:
The word brāhmaṇa here means an “explanation” or “pronouncement” concerning brahman, the power of the sacred formula. The later Mīmāṃsā tradition distinguishes two main kinds of statement in them:

  1. Vidhi — injunctions prescribing what is to be done;

  2. Arthavāda — explanatory and laudatory passages, including myths and legends, that give the reasons for the rite.

The Brāhmaṇas also contain etymologies of ritual terms, discussions between ritualists holding different views, and many narratives.

docs.title: 6.2.2 Major Brāhmaṇa Texts
docs.text:
The principal surviving Brāhmaṇas of each Veda are listed in Table 6.1 and described below.

Table 6.1. Principal Brāhmaṇa texts associated with each Veda. Veda Brāhmaṇa Notable Features Ṛgveda Aitareya Duties of the hotṛ; Soma ritual; royal consecration; Śunaḥśepa Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) Parallel to the Aitareya, more systematic Sāmaveda Pañcaviṃśa (Tāṇḍya) 25 books; the chants and the Soma sessions Jaiminīya Very large; rich in legends White Yajurveda Śatapatha 100 adhyāyas; the most extensive; ends with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Black Yajurveda Taittirīya Supplements the Taittirīya Saṃhitā Atharvaveda Gopatha The only Atharvavedic Brāhmaṇa; comparatively late

docs.title: 6.2.3 The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa
docs.text: The Śatapatha (“hundred paths”) Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda is the largest and most important Brāhmaṇa. Its Mādhyandina version has 100 adhyāyas in 14 books. Its early books are associated with Yājñavalkya, while Books 6–10, on the Agnicayana, are linked with the ritualist Śāṇḍilya. It covers the major śrauta rituals in detail, contains cosmogonic myths of Prajāpati, the flood story of Manu, the legend of Puruṛavas and Urvaśī, and the account of Videgha Māthava carrying the sacrificial fire eastward, and it ends with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

docs.title: 6.2.4 The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa
docs.text: The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa of the Ṛgveda, attributed to Mahidāsa Aitareya, has 40 adhyāyas grouped in eight pañcikās. Most of it explains the Soma sacrifice from the point of view of the hotṛ, who recites the śastras. The last two pañcikās concern royal ritual: the story of Śunaḥśepa (7.13–18), recited at the royal consecration; the “great consecration of Indra” (aindra mahābhiṣeka), with a list of kings said to have been so consecrated; and the role of the royal chaplain (purohita).

docs.title: 6.2.5 The Sāmavedic Brāhmaṇas
docs.text: The Pañcaviṃśa (“twenty-five-fold”) or Tāṇḍya Mahābrāhmaṇa of the Kauthuma school explains the chants (stotras) of the Soma rituals and the long Soma sessions (sattras), including the twelve-day rite and the year-long gavām ayana. It also describes the vrātyastomas (PB 17.1–4), rites by which vrātyas—Aryans living outside Brahmanical norms—could be admitted to Vedic society. The Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, of the Jaiminīya school, is a very large text whose many narratives, often told with vivid detail, are not found elsewhere.

docs.title: 6.2.6 The Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa
docs.text: The Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, in three books with 8, 8 and 12 chapters, supplements the Taittirīya Saṃhitā with further formulas and explanations. Among other things it contains material on the Aśvamedha and the Puruṣamedha, lists of the lunar asterisms (nakṣatras), and, in its final “Kāṭhaka” chapters, rites such as the Nāciketa fire, together with a version of the story of Naciketas and Death that was later developed in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad.

docs.title: 6.2.7 The Gopatha Brāhmaṇa
docs.text: The Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, the only Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda, is later than the others and draws heavily on them. Its main concern is to establish the authority of the Atharvaveda and the claim that the brahman priest of the śrauta ritual should be an Atharvavedin.

docs.title: 6.3.1 Bandhu: Correspondence
docs.text:
The central intellectual method of the Brāhmaṇas is the search for bandhus, “connections” or “equivalences”, between three levels: the ritual, the cosmos, and the human person. To know these connections is to have power over what they connect. Some of the most frequent equivalences are:

  • “The sacrifice is Viṣṇu” (yajño vai viṣṇuḥ, ŚB 1.1.2.13), and “the sacrifice is the man” (puruṣo vai yajñaḥ, ŚB 1.3.2.1);

  • Prajāpati, the creator, is the year, and the fire altar is both Prajāpati and the year;

  • the three fires correspond to the three worlds, and the metres, chants and offerings to gods, seasons and parts of the body.

Such correspondences can seem arbitrary to a modern reader, but they rest on a coherent idea: that the world is a system of homologies, and that the ritual is a model of it which can be manipulated. The Upaniṣads inherit this method and turn it toward the self (ātman), asking what single reality underlies all equivalences.

docs.title: 6.3.2 The Symbolism of Numbers
docs.text:
Numbers are an important part of this system:

  • 3: the three worlds, three fires, three Vedas, three Soma pressings;

  • 5: the five seasons (in the Vedic count), five layers of the fire altar, five breaths;

  • 7: the seven metres, seven hotrās (reciting priests);

  • 12: the twelve months, the twelve-day rite;

  • 17: Prajāpati is “seventeenfold”;

  • 33: the thirty-three gods—eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Ādityas, and two others, named in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (3.9.2) as Indra and Prajāpati;

  • 360 and 10,800: the days of the ritual year and its muhūrtas, used in the symbolism of the fire altar.

docs.title: 6.3.3 The Five Great Sacrifices (Pañca Mahāyajñas)
docs.text:
The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (11.5.6.1) names five “great sacrifices” to be performed daily by the householder:

  1. Brahmayajña — to Brahman (the Veda), by daily recitation (svādhyāya);

  2. Devayajña — to the gods, by an oblation in the fire;

  3. Pitṛyajña — to the ancestors, by offerings of water and food;

  4. Manuṣyayajña — to human beings, by hospitality to guests;

  5. Bhūtayajña — to all beings, by food offerings (bali) for animals, birds and spirits.

These domestic duties extend the idea of sacrifice into daily life, and they became a fixed part of the householder’s duties in the law books.

docs.title: 6.4.1 Prajāpati
docs.text: The creator god Prajāpati (“lord of offspring”) dominates the cosmogony of the Brāhmaṇas. Desiring to multiply, he heats himself with tapas and emits the worlds, the gods and creatures; having emitted them, he is left exhausted and “unstrung”, and the gods restore him through sacrifice. The Agnicayana, in which the altar is built as Prajāpati’s body, re-enacts this restoration. The myth anticipates the Upaniṣadic idea that the many derive from, and can be reunited with, a single source.

docs.title: 6.4.2 The Flood Story
docs.text:
The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.8.1) contains the earliest Indian version of the flood story. A small fish comes into Manu’s hands with his washing water and asks to be protected, promising to save him. Manu rears it until it is full-grown. It warns him of a coming flood; Manu builds a ship and ties it to the fish’s horn, and the fish draws it to a northern mountain. When the waters subside Manu, alone of all creatures, offers a sacrifice, from which a woman, Iḍā, is born, and through her he begets the human race.

The story has striking parallels with the Mesopotamian flood narratives (in the Atrahasis epic and the Epic of Gilgamesh), which are older; whether the Indian version derives from them or developed independently is debated. In the Purāṇas, the fish becomes the first incarnation (avatāra) of Viṣṇu.

docs.title: 6.4.3 Śunaḥśepa
docs.text: The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (7.13–18) tells how King Hariścandra, who had obtained a son from Varuṇa by promising to sacrifice him, delayed the sacrifice. The son, Rohita, eventually bought a Brahmin boy, Śunaḥśepa, from his impoverished father Ajīgarta to take his place. Ajīgarta himself offered, for a further fee, to bind and kill his son. Bound to the post, Śunaḥśepa prayed to a series of gods with Ṛgvedic verses; as he praised Uṣas, his fetters fell away. He refused to return to his father and was adopted by Viśvāmitra. The story, recited at the royal consecration, raises sharp questions about human sacrifice, the sale of children and paternal duty.

docs.title: 6.4.4 Gods and Asuras
docs.text: Many Brāhmaṇa narratives begin “The gods and the Asuras, both offspring of Prajāpati, were contending…” (e.g. BU 1.3.1). The gods win because they discover the correct ritual, or speak the truth, while the Asuras rely on force or falsehood. The stories explain why a rite is performed in a particular way.

docs.title: 6.5.1 Nature and Purpose
docs.text:
The Āraṇyakas (from araṇya, “wilderness, forest”) take their name from the rule that they were to be studied outside the village. The traditional explanation is that they were meant for contemplation in solitude; modern scholars note that much of their content concerns rites regarded as dangerous or secret, such as the Pravargya (the hot milk offering) and the Mahāvrata, which had to be learnt away from the settlement. They contain (the principal texts are listed in Table 6.2):

  1. explanations of these special rites;

  2. meditations (upāsanā) on the hidden meaning of ritual acts and formulas;

  3. discussions of breath (prāṇa) as the essence of life and of the ritual;

  4. passages that develop into the earliest Upaniṣads.

Table 6.2. Principal Āraṇyakas and their Vedic affiliations. Āraṇyaka Veda Notable Contents Aitareya Ṛgveda Mahāvrata rite; contains the Aitareya Upaniṣad Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) Ṛgveda Contains the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad Taittirīya Black Yajurveda Pravargya; funeral rites; contains the Taittirīya and Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣads Bṛhadāraṇyaka White Yajurveda The last book of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; mostly Upaniṣad Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa Sāmaveda (Jaiminīya) Also called the Talavakāra Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa; serves as the school’s Āraṇyaka; contains the Kena Upaniṣad

docs.title: 6.5.2 The Aitareya Āraṇyaka
docs.text:
Its structure is set out in Table 6.3.

Table 6.3. Structure of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka. Book Contents I The Mahāvrata rite and its interpretation II Meditations on breath; chapters 4–6 form the Aitareya Upaniṣad III The Saṃhitopaniṣad, on the mystical meaning of the forms of recitation IV The Mahānāmnī verses V The niṣkevalya recitation of the Mahāvrata

The Aitareya Upaniṣad ends with the statement prajñānaṃ brahma, “Brahman is cognition” (AU 3.3), later counted among the “great sayings” of Vedānta.

docs.title: 6.5.3 The Taittirīya Āraṇyaka
docs.text:
The Taittirīya Āraṇyaka has ten chapters (prapāṭhakas). The first, the Aruṇa Praśna, is chanted today in many places with the Hindu Sun-salutation (sūrya-namaskāra); chapters 4–5 concern the Pravargya and chapter 6 the funeral rites; chapters 7–9 form the Taittirīya Upaniṣad; and chapter 10 is the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad, a collection of meditations and formulas much used in later worship (Figure 6.1).

Figure 6.1. Upaniṣads embedded in Āraṇyakas and Brāhmaṇas, with a characteristic teaching of each.

docs.title: 6.6 Internalising the Sacrifice
docs.text:
A key development of this period is the internalisation of ritual: the sacrifice comes to be understood as something that can take place within the person. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (5.19–24) teaches that a person who knows the “universal self” (vaiśvānara ātman) offers the Agnihotra simply by eating, the first mouthfuls being oblations to the breaths. The Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad (2.5) describes an “inner Agnihotra” in which one continually offers speech into breath and breath into speech. Later texts call this the prāṇāgnihotra, “fire-offering in the breaths” (Table 6.4).

Table 6.4. Ways of interpreting ritual in the Āraṇyakas and early Upaniṣads. Principle Sanskrit Term Description Correspondence Bandhu Ritual, cosmic and bodily elements are linked by hidden equivalences Bodily application Adhyātma Ritual and cosmic elements are identified with faculties of the person Meditation Upāsanā Contemplating the meaning of a rite or formula, sometimes in place of performing it Breath-sacrifice Prāṇāgnihotra The fire-offering is performed in the breaths, as in eating

This development did not mean that ritual was abandoned—the śrauta and domestic rites continued, and continue today—but it opened the way for the Upaniṣads’ emphasis on knowledge, and for later ideas such as the Bhagavadgītā’s “sacrifice of knowledge” (jñānayajña).

docs.title: 6.7 The Great Sayings (Mahāvākyas)
docs.text:
Later Advaita Vedānta selected four sentences, one from an Upaniṣad of each Veda, as “great sayings” summing up the identity of self and Brahman. The grouping is a later scholastic convention, not a Vedic one, but the sentences themselves are Upaniṣadic (see Volume 2, Upaniṣad Dīpikā) (Table 6.5):

Table 6.5. The four Mahāvākyas of Advaita Vedānta and their sources. Mahāvākya Meaning Source Veda Prajñānaṃ brahma “Brahman is cognition” Aitareya Up. 3.3 Ṛgveda Ahaṃ brahmāsmi “I am Brahman” Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 1.4.10 White Yajurveda Tat tvam asi “That you are” Chāndogya Up. 6.8.7 Sāmaveda Ayam ātmā brahma “This self is Brahman” Māṇḍūkya Up. 2 Atharvaveda

Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10

brahma vā idam agra āsīt tad ātmānam evāvet ahaṃ brahmāsmīti tasmāt tat sarvam abhavat In the beginning this world was Brahman, and it knew only itself: “I am Brahman.” As a result, it became the Whole. — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10

docs.title: 6.8 Language, History and Science in the Brāhmaṇas
docs.text: The Brāhmaṇas are the oldest substantial body of Indian prose, and among the oldest prose in any Indo-European language (only Hittite prose is clearly older). Their language bridges the Vedic of the Saṃhitās and the Sanskrit described by Pāṇini. They are also an essential source for the social history of the later Vedic period, for the eastward spread of Vedic culture, and for the growth of priestly specialisation.

docs.title: 6.8.1 Mathematics and Astronomy
docs.text:
The construction of altars presupposes the practical geometry later set out in the Śulba Sūtras (Chapter 7). The Brāhmaṇas also contain calendrical material: lists of the nakṣatras, the twelve months and their intercalation, and the five-year cycle of named years.

One passage has played a large part in debates about dating. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (2.1.2.3) says that the Kṛttikās (Pleiades) “do not swerve from the eastern quarter”. S. B. Dikshit argued in the nineteenth century that this describes the Pleiades rising due east, which would place the observation around 3000 BCE. Others reply that the statement may be approximate, or may preserve an older tradition, and that the language of the Śatapatha belongs clearly to the early first millennium BCE. The passage illustrates both the value and the limits of astronomical dating.

docs.title: 6.9 Summary
docs.text:
The Brāhmaṇas are easily mistaken for commentaries on ritual and nothing more. Read as a whole, they are the first Indian attempt to think systematically: to ask why an act is done, to answer by finding the hidden equivalence (bandhu) that links it to the cosmos and the person, and to argue with other teachers about the answer. Their prose, their myths and their debates are also the richest source for the society of the later Vedic period. The Āraṇyakas show the same method applied to dangerous and secret rites, and then turned inward, until the knowledge of the equivalences mattered more than the act; that is the point at which the Upaniṣads begin.

Closing Verse

yo ha vai jyeṣṭhaṃ ca śreṣṭhaṃ ca veda jyeṣṭhaś ca ha vai śreṣṭhaś ca bhavati He who knows the eldest and the best becomes the eldest and the best. — Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.1.1

docs.title: Chapter 7: The Six Vedāṅgas: Limbs of the Veda
docs.text:
Invocatory Verse

chandaḥ pādau tu vedasya hastau kalpo ’tha paṭhyate jyotiṣām ayanaṃ cakṣur niruktaṃ śrotram ucyate śikṣā ghrāṇaṃ tu vedasya mukhaṃ vyākaraṇaṃ smṛtam Metre is said to be the feet of the Veda, ritual its hands, astronomy its eyes, etymology its ears, phonetics its nose, and grammar its mouth. — Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 41–42

docs.title: 7.1 Introduction to the Vedāṅgas
docs.text:
The Vedāṅgas (“limbs of the Veda”) are six auxiliary sciences that grew up to preserve, understand and correctly perform the Vedic texts: phonetics (śikṣā), metre (chandas), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), astronomy and calendar (jyotiṣa) and ritual procedure (kalpa). The list of six is already given in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad (1.1.5); Figure 7.1 shows the later image of them as the limbs of the Veda’s body. Most of the surviving Vedāṅga texts are composed in the terse sūtra style and date from c. 600 BCE to the early centuries CE.

These disciplines are among the most remarkable intellectual achievements of ancient India. The need to preserve sacred sound exactly produced phonetics of great precision; the need to understand archaic texts produced etymology and grammar; the need to build altars and to time rituals produced geometry and calendrical astronomy. This chapter introduces them as aids to the Veda; phonetics, grammar and etymology are treated in full in Volume 10 of this series, Śabda Vidyā, the geometry of the Śulba Sūtras and Piṅgala’s combinatorics in Volume 11, Gaṇita, and the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa in Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa.

Figure 7.1. The Veda as a body with six limbs, after the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā.

docs.title: 7.2 Śikṣā: Phonetics
docs.text:
Śikṣā is the science of correct pronunciation. Since the power of a mantra was believed to depend on its exact sound, it was of the first importance. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (1.2) lists its six topics:

  • Varṇa — the sounds (vowels, stops, semivowels, sibilants);

  • Svara — the pitch accents (udātta, anudātta, svarita);

  • Mātrā — quantity (short, long, prolonged);

  • Bala — effort of articulation;

  • Sāma — even delivery;

  • Santāna — the connection of sounds in continuous recitation (sandhi).

The oldest phonetic treatises are the Prātiśākhyas, manuals attached to particular schools (the Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya, the Taittirīya Prātiśākhya and others). They describe the place and manner of articulation of every sound and the rules for converting the word-by-word recitation into the continuous text. Their analysis of the sounds of language—arranged by place of articulation from the throat to the lips—underlies the order of the Indian alphabets to this day, and modern phoneticians have praised it highly. Later and shorter manuals bear the name Śikṣā, such as the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā, whose attribution to Pāṇini is doubtful.

Note: The Story of Indraśatru

The ritual prose texts (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.4.12.1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.6.3.8–10) tell how Tvaṣṭṛ, wishing for a son who would kill Indra, pronounced the compound indraśatru; the grammarians explain that he gave it the wrong accent (Patañjali, Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśā). Instead of meaning “slayer of Indra” it came to mean “he whose slayer is Indra”, and Indra killed the son, Vṛtra. The story is often cited to show why the accent mattered.

docs.title: 7.3 Chandas: Metre
docs.text:
Chandas is the study of metre; the word is also used as a name for the Vedic texts themselves. The foundational surviving text is the Chandaḥsūtra of Piṅgala (dated variously between c. 300 BCE and the early centuries CE), which treats both Vedic and classical metres. Lists of Vedic metres also appear in the Prātiśākhyas and in the Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas themselves (Table 7.1).

Table 7.1. Principal Vedic metres. Metre Syllables per Pāda Pādas Remarks Gāyatrī 8 3 The Gāyatrī verse (RV 3.62.10) Uṣṇih 8+8+12 3 Anuṣṭubh 8 4 Develops into the classical śloka Bṛhatī 8+8+12+8 4 Paṅkti 8 5 Triṣṭubh 11 4 The commonest metre of the Ṛgveda Jagatī 12 4

Piṅgala and Combinatorics

Piṅgala’s treatment of metres includes rules (pratyaya) for listing every possible sequence of light (laghu) and heavy (guru) syllables of a given length, for finding the position of a given pattern in that list, and for counting how many patterns contain a given number of heavy syllables. Historians of mathematics note that, if light and heavy are written as 1 and 0 (or 0 and 1), his procedure for numbering the patterns is equivalent to writing numbers in binary, and his counting rule leads to the binomial coefficients. The triangular arrangement of these coefficients (the “Mount Meru” diagram, meru-prastāra) is described explicitly by the commentator Halāyudha (10th century CE), and the sequence later called “Fibonacci” appears in the counting of metres based on syllable-length (mātrā) by Virahāṅka and later writers (Plofker 2009). These are genuine and early achievements in combinatorics; they were developed for prosody, not as a general theory of number.

docs.title: 7.4 Vyākaraṇa: Grammar
docs.text: Grammar was regarded as the chief of the Vedāṅgas. Its supreme text, Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī (“eight chapters”, c. 4th century BCE), describes the Sanskrit of Pāṇini’s day, with notes on Vedic forms, in nearly 4,000 short rules (sūtras). By means of technical abbreviations, meta-rules governing the application of other rules, and an ordered system of derivation, it generates correct word-forms from roots and suffixes. It is widely regarded as one of the greatest achievements of linguistic analysis in any culture. Modern linguists and computer scientists have compared its techniques with formal grammars and with notations used to specify programming languages; such comparisons are illuminating analogies, not claims that Pāṇini anticipated computers. Pāṇini himself names earlier grammarians, so he stands at the end of a long tradition.

docs.title: 7.4.1 Key Grammatical Texts
docs.text:
The principal works are listed in Table 7.2; Figure 7.2 shows the line of transmission.

Table 7.2. Major texts of the Pāṇinian grammatical tradition. Text Author (date) Significance Aṣṭādhyāyī Pāṇini (c. 4th c. BCE) The foundational grammar Vārttikas Kātyāyana (c. 3rd c. BCE) Critical supplements to Pāṇini Mahābhāṣya Patañjali (c. 150 BCE) The “great commentary” Vākyapadīya Bhartṛhari (5th c. CE) Philosophy of language Siddhāntakaumudī Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita (17th c. CE) Topical rearrangement for teaching Figure 7.2. The lineage of the Pāṇinian grammatical tradition.

docs.title: 7.5 Nirukta: Etymology and Interpretation
docs.text:
Nirukta is the explanation of the meanings of Vedic words, especially obscure ones. Its foundational text is Yāska’s Nirukta (c. 5th century BCE), a commentary on an older word-list, the Nighaṇṭu. Yāska’s work:

  1. is one of the oldest surviving works on etymology in any language;

  2. preserves the views of earlier interpreters, such as Śākapūṇi and Aurṇavābha, and of rival schools (ritualists, “etymologists”, “historians”);

  3. classifies words into four kinds: nouns (nāma), verbs (ākhyāta), preverbs (upasarga) and particles (nipāta) (Nirukta 1.1);

  4. defends the principle, against the grammarian Gārgya, that all nouns are derived from verbal roots.

Yāska determines meaning by derivation from a verbal root, by the context of the hymn and the ritual, and by the tradition of earlier interpreters. He also records the view of one Kautsa, who argued that the Vedic mantras are meaningless (anarthaka) and effective only as sound, and he rebuts it point by point (Nirukta 1.15–16), insisting that the mantras have meanings that can be recovered by careful study—one of the earliest recorded debates about the interpretation of a sacred text.

docs.title: 7.6 Jyotiṣa: Astronomy and Calendar
docs.text:
Jyotiṣa served to fix the times of rituals, which depended on the phases of the moon, the seasons and the positions of the sun and moon among the nakṣatras. Its foundational text, the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa attributed to Lagadha, survives in a Ṛgvedic recension of 36 verses and a Yajurvedic recension of 43 verses.

The Pre-eminence of Jyotiṣa

yathā śikhā mayūrāṇāṃ nāgānāṃ maṇayo yathā tadvad vedāṅgaśāstrāṇāṃ jyotiṣaṃ mūrdhani sthitam As the crest on the heads of peacocks, as the gems on the heads of serpents, so is Jyotiṣa at the head of the sciences of the Vedāṅgas. — Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, Ārca recension 35

The Yājuṣa recension (verse 4) has the same verse but reads gaṇitaṃ (“calculation”) for jyotiṣaṃ.

Key Parameters of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa

  • A five-year cycle (yuga) of 1,830 days

  • 62 synodic months in the cycle, so that two intercalary months are needed

  • 67 sidereal months in the cycle

  • The winter solstice at the beginning of the nakṣatra Śraviṣṭhā (Dhaniṣṭhā), the summer solstice in the middle of Āśleṣā

  • Time measured with a water clock in units of nāḍikās

The solstice positions given by the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa correspond to the sky of roughly 1400–1150 BCE. The language and style of the text, however, are much later, and many scholars date its composition to the last centuries BCE. Either it preserves an older tradition of observation, or its data were conventional and approximate; this is a further example of the caution needed in using astronomy to date texts (Plofker 2009). The twenty-seven nakṣatras on which the system rests are listed in Table 7.3.

Table 7.3. The twenty-seven nakṣatras and their deities, in the order of the Taittirīya texts (beginning with Kṛttikā). Some deities vary between sources. No. Nakṣatra Deity No. Nakṣatra Deity 1 Kṛttikā Agni 15 Anurādhā Mitra 2 Rohiṇī Prajāpati 16 Jyeṣṭhā Indra 3 Mṛgaśīrṣa Soma 17 Mūla Pitṛs / Nirṛti 4 Ārdrā Rudra 18 Pūrvāṣāḍhā Āpaḥ (Waters) 5 Punarvasu Aditi 19 Uttarāṣāḍhā Viśvedevas 6 Tiṣya (Puṣya) Bṛhaspati 20 Śroṇā (Śravaṇa) Viṣṇu 7 Āśleṣā Sarpas (Serpents) 21 Śraviṣṭhā Vasus 8 Maghā Pitṛs (Fathers) 22 Śatabhiṣaj Varuṇa 9 Pūrva Phalgunī Aryaman 23 Pūrva Proṣṭhapadā Aja Ekapād 10 Uttara Phalgunī Bhaga 24 Uttara Proṣṭhapadā Ahi Budhnya 11 Hasta Savitṛ 25 Revatī Pūṣan 12 Citrā Indra (later Tvaṣṭṛ) 26 Aśvayuj (Aśvinī) Aśvins 13 Svāti Vāyu 27 Apabharaṇī (Bharaṇī) Yama 14 Viśākhā Indra and Agni

In some lists a twenty-eighth asterism, Abhijit, is inserted between Uttarāṣāḍhā and Śravaṇa. Later Indian astronomy, from the early centuries CE, adopted the twelve zodiacal signs and planetary theory from Hellenistic astronomy and combined them with the older nakṣatra system.

docs.title: 7.7 Kalpa: Ritual Procedure
docs.text:
Kalpa (from kḷp, “to arrange”) is the systematic description of ritual. It is the most extensive of the Vedāṅgas, and its sūtras were composed by the schools of each Veda. They fall into four groups (Figure 7.3):

Figure 7.3. The four kinds of Kalpa Sūtra.

The Śrauta Sūtras systematise the solemn rituals described in the Brāhmaṇas. The Gṛhya Sūtras prescribe the domestic rites of the householder, including the life-cycle rites (saṃskāras) from conception to death. The Dharma Sūtras of Āpastamba, Gautama, Baudhāyana and Vasiṣṭha (c. 3rd–1st centuries BCE) are the earliest Indian law books; they codify the duties of the social classes and stages of life, and with them the hierarchy of varṇa and the disabilities of Śūdras and women that later law books developed further (Olivelle 1999). The Śulba Sūtras give the geometry needed to build the altars.

docs.title: 7.7.1 The Śulba Sūtras: Vedic Geometry
docs.text:
The Śulba Sūtras (from śulba, “cord”) of Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, Kātyāyana and Mānava are the earliest Indian mathematical texts. Using cords and pegs, they show how to construct right angles, squares and rectangles of given area; how to combine two squares into one or subtract one from another; how to turn a square into a circle of nearly equal area and back; and how to build bird-shaped and other altars from bricks of standard sizes. Their key results include:

  • a general statement of the theorem now called Pythagorean (see Section 3.10);

  • lists of integer right triangles, such as (3, 4, 5) and (5, 12, 13);

  • an approximation of \(\sqrt{2}\) correct to five decimal places;

  • approximate circle–square conversions, which imply values of \(\pi\) that depend on the rule and on how it is read: about 3.00 for the simplest rule of Baudhāyana and about 3.09 for his more accurate one, with some readings of other rules giving slightly higher values (Plofker 2009).

The diagonal theorem was known in practice in Old Babylonian mathematics centuries earlier (lists of Pythagorean triples appear on the tablet Plimpton 322, c. 1800 BCE); the Śulba Sūtras contain among the earliest explicit general statements of it, and are a distinctive tradition of constructive geometry developed for ritual (Plofker 2009). The principal texts and their approximate dates are given in Table 7.4.

Table 7.4. The principal Śulba Sūtras. Dates are approximate and disputed. Śulba Sūtra Approximate Date Key Mathematical Content Baudhāyana c. 800–500 BCE General statement of the diagonal theorem; \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1 + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3\cdot 4} - \frac{1}{3\cdot 4\cdot 34}\); circle–square transformations Mānava c. 750–350 BCE Circle–square transformations Āpastamba c. 600–300 BCE Refined constructions; area transformations Kātyāyana c. 400–200 BCE Further constructions and generalisations

docs.title: 7.8 Summary
docs.text:
The Vedāṅgas show how a religious need can generate a science. Each began as a service to the Veda—to pronounce it, to measure its verses, to understand its words, to time and build its rites—and each grew beyond that service into a discipline with its own methods: the phonetic analysis that still orders Indian scripts, a grammar that modern linguists study as a formal system, a constructive geometry and a calendar. The same process had a darker side. The Kalpa literature that codified the rites also produced, in the Dharma Sūtras, the first codifications of a hierarchical social order whose legacy India is still debating.

Closing Reflection

anādinidhanaṃ brahma śabdatattvaṃ yad akṣaram vivartate ’rthabhāvena prakriyā jagato yataḥ Brahman, without beginning or end, the imperishable essence of the Word, which manifests itself as things, and from which the world proceeds. — Bhartṛhari, Vākyapadīya 1.1

docs.title: Chapter 8: The Śrauta Ritual: The Solemn Sacrifices
docs.text:
Invocatory Verse

ṛcāṃ tvaḥ poṣam āste pupuṣvān gāyatraṃ tvo gāyati śakvarīṣu brahmā tvo vadati jātavidyāṃ yajñasya mātrāṃ vi mimīta u tvaḥ One sits bringing the abundance of verses to flourish; one sings a song in Śakvarī metres; one, the brahman, tells the knowledge of what has come to be; another measures out the measure of the sacrifice. — Ṛgveda 10.71.11

docs.title: 8.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The verse above was read by Yāska (Nirukta 1.8) as a description of the four priests of the solemn sacrifice: the hotṛ, who recites the verses of the Ṛgveda; the udgātṛ, who sings the chants; the brahman, who knows the whole; and the adhvaryu, who “measures out” the ritual with his hands. These rites are called śrauta, “belonging to śruti”, because they are prescribed by the Veda itself, in contrast to the domestic (gṛhya) rites, whose authority the tradition traces to remembered custom (Chapter 9). A śrauta rite requires three sacred fires, professional priests from more than one Vedic school, and a sponsor (yajamāna) who has formally established those fires and whose wife takes part with him.

Earlier chapters have described parts of this system: the formulas of the Yajurveda (Chapter 3); the Agnicayana (Section 3.10); the chants of the Sāmaveda and the seven forms of the Soma sacrifice (Section 4.12); and the Brāhmaṇas’ explanations of the rites (Chapter 6). This chapter presents the śrauta ritual as a whole: its manuals, its ritual ground, the logic by which its rites are built from a few models, the principal rites in the order in which a sacrificer would undertake them, its history after the Vedic period, and the ways in which tradition and modern scholarship have tried to understand it. The standard modern surveys are those of Alfred Hillebrandt, Jan Gonda and C. G. Kashikar, and the detailed reconstructions of individual rites by Willem Caland and others (Hillebrandt 1897; Gonda 1977; Kashikar 1968).

docs.title: 8.2 The Śrautasūtras
docs.text:
The Brāhmaṇas explain the ritual but do not set it out in order; they assume that the reader already knows the procedure and comment on its meaning. The procedure itself was codified in the Śrautasūtras, manuals composed by the ritual schools of each Veda between about the sixth and the second century BCE, the oldest of them perhaps earlier. Each sūtra prescribes the rites from the point of view of the priest whose Veda it belongs to: the Ṛgvedic sūtras describe what the hotṛ and his assistants recite, the Sāmavedic sūtras what the chanters sing, and the Yajurvedic sūtras, the most comprehensive, what the adhvaryu does and says (Table 8.1).

Table 8.1. The principal Śrautasūtras by Veda and school. Veda School Śrautasūtras Ṛgveda Śākala; Kauṣītaki Āśvalāyana; Śāṅkhāyana (Kauṣītaki) Sāmaveda Kauthuma, Rāṇāyanīya, Jaiminīya Lāṭyāyana (Kauthuma); Drāhyāyaṇa (Rāṇāyanīya); Jaiminīya. The Ārṣeyakalpa of Maśaka lists the chants used in each rite Black Yajurveda Taittirīya Baudhāyana, Vādhūla, Bhāradvāja, Āpastamba, Hiraṇyakeśin (Satyāṣāḍha), Vaikhānasa Maitrāyaṇīya Mānava, Vārāha Kaṭha Kāṭhaka (known only from fragments) White Yajurveda Vājasaneyin Kātyāyana Atharvaveda Śaunaka Vaitāna

The manuals differ in age and style. The Baudhāyana Śrautasūtra, generally regarded as the oldest, is written in a discursive prose close to that of the Brāhmaṇas, and often reports the opinions of named teachers. Later sūtras, such as those of Āpastamba and Kātyāyana, are terse lists of rules, which presuppose general rules of interpretation (paribhāṣā) stated once at the beginning. The Vaitāna Sūtra of the Atharvaveda is late and largely derivative: it exists to support the Atharvavedic claim to the office of the brahman (Section 5.9). Because each sūtra belongs to a school, a sacrificer traditionally follows the sūtra of his own branch (svasūtra); the schools are discussed in Chapter 12.

Alongside the sūtras stand the mantra collections (the Saṃhitās), the Brāhmaṇas that explain the rites, and a large later literature of handbooks (prayoga, paddhati) that set out the actual sequence of acts and words for a particular school. It is largely through such handbooks, and through families of practising ritualists, that the rites have been performed in recent centuries (Smith 1987).

docs.title: 8.3 Fires, Priests and the Ritual Ground
8.3.1 Establishing the Fires
docs.text:
A householder becomes eligible for the śrauta rites by the agnyādheya, the “placing of the fires”. The Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa assigns the rite to different seasons for the different classes—spring for a Brahmin, summer for a Kṣatriya, autumn for a Vaiśya—and the fire is produced by friction, with two kindling sticks (araṇi) of the aśvattha tree, ideally one that has grown upon a śamī tree. Once established, the fires are to be maintained for life; the man who keeps them is an āhitāgni, “one who has set up the fires”, and at his death he is cremated in them (Section 9.5.4). If the fires are lost or the rite fails, they can be re-established (punarādheya).

The three fires are laid out on an east–west axis (Figure 8.1). The gārhapatya, the “householder’s fire”, is in the west and is round; from it the other fires are kindled and on it the offerings are cooked. The āhavanīya, the “fire for offering”, is in the east and is square; into it most oblations are poured. The dakṣiṇāgni, the “southern fire”, is semicircular and lies to the south; it is associated with the ancestors and with protection against hostile powers. The distance between the western and eastern fires varies with the class of the sacrificer: the sūtras give eight steps (prakrama) for a Brahmin, eleven for a Kṣatriya and twelve for a Vaiśya, numbers that match the syllables of the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh and Jagatī metres with which the classes are associated. Some schools add two further fires, the sabhya (“of the assembly hall”) and the āvasathya (“of the dwelling”), giving the “five fires” of the fullest form of the system.

Between the fires lies the vedi, a shallow, grass-strewn hollow in the ground, broad at its ends and narrow in the middle; the texts compare its shape to that of a woman, with “shoulders” to the east and “hips” to the west. The offerings are set down on it, and the earth dug from it is heaped to the north on the utkara, the place for discarded material. The geometry of the altars, and its codification in the Śulbasūtras, has been described in Section 3.10 and in Chapter 7.

Figure 8.1. Simplified plan of the ritual ground. Left: the hall with the three fires of the regular offerings—G, gārhapatya (round); Ā, āhavanīya (square); D, dakṣiṇāgni (semicircular)—and the small waisted vedi between them. Right: the great altar (mahāvedi) laid out for the Soma sacrifice, a trapezium 36 steps long and 30 and 24 steps wide at its western and eastern ends, with the shed for the priests’ seats (sadas), the shed for the Soma carts (havirdhāna), the raised fire-altar (uttaravedi), the sacrificial post (yūpa), and two subsidiary sheds standing half inside and half outside the altar ground, the āgnīdhrīya to the north and the mārjālīya to the south. The outline of the great altar is drawn approximately to scale; everything else is schematic.

docs.title: 8.3.2 The Priests and Their Texts
docs.text:
The number of priests depends on the rite. An iṣṭi, the simplest offering of cakes, milk or ghee, needs four: the adhvaryu, who acts; the hotṛ, who recites; the āgnīdh, who tends the fire and answers the adhvaryu’s calls; and the brahman, who watches in silence. An animal sacrifice adds two more, the maitrāvaruṇa, who directs the hotṛ, and the pratiprasthātṛ, the adhvaryu’s assistant. The Soma sacrifice requires the full set of sixteen, in four groups of four (Figure 8.2): the hotṛ, who recites the verses of the Ṛgveda, with the maitrāvaruṇa, acchāvāka and grāvastut; the adhvaryu, who performs the ritual actions with Yajurvedic formulas, with the pratiprasthātṛ, neṣṭṛ and unnetṛ; the udgātṛ, who sings the Sāmavedic chants, with the prastotṛ, pratihartṛ and subrahmaṇya; and the brahman, who oversees the rite in silence, with the brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, āgnīdhra and potṛ. The Atharvavedic schools later claimed the office of the brahman for themselves (Section 5.9). Some schools add a seventeenth, the sadasya, who supervises from the sadas, and several minor officiants such as the cup-bearers (camasādhvaryu).

Each group works from its own texts. The hotṛ and his assistants recite Ṛgvedic verses in prescribed sequences, the śastras, which are assembled from many hymns and are not simply the hymns of the Saṃhitā in their original order. The chanters sing sāmans from the song-books of their school, adapted (ūha) to the verses and occasions of the rite. The adhvaryu mutters Yajurvedic formulas as he acts and gives orders (praiṣa) to the other priests. The brahman, according to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (4.17), repairs any fault in the rite with the three “utterances” bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, as a goldsmith joins gold with a flux; his knowledge of the whole is the sacrifice’s protection.

Figure 8.2. The sixteen priests of the Soma sacrifice and the sponsor.

The co-operation of the priests is regulated by fixed calls and responses. When an oblation is to be offered, the adhvaryu calls ā śrāvaya (“make [the gods] listen”), the āgnīdh answers astu śrauṣaṭ (“so be it, may they hear”), the adhvaryu instructs the hotṛ to recite the offering verse, and the hotṛ begins with ye yajāmahe (“we who worship”) and ends with the exclamation vauṣaṭ, at which the oblation is poured. Whatever their literal sense, these formulas work as signals that co-ordinate the priests, and their exact form is part of the knowledge that each school preserved.

docs.title: 8.3.3 The Sacrificer and His Wife
docs.text: The sponsor, the yajamāna, is the beneficiary of the rite and pays the priests’ fees (dakṣiṇā). He must be a married twice-born man; the Śūdra is excluded, although the texts make a much-discussed exception for the chariot-maker (rathakāra), who may establish the fires in the rainy season. His wife (patnī) is a necessary participant. She has her own place near the gārhapatya, is girded with a cord at the start of the rite, looks at the melted butter, is present at the offerings to the wives of the gods (patnīsaṃyāja), and in the animal sacrifice washes the victim’s body. Stephanie Jamison has shown how much the ritual texts reveal about the wife’s role, which the Brāhmaṇas treat as both indispensable and dangerous (Jamison 1996). A widower, or a man whose wife cannot take part, faces real difficulties in continuing the rites, and the texts discuss substitutes.

docs.title: 8.3.4 The Priests’ Fee
docs.text:
Every śrauta rite ends with the giving of the dakṣiṇā, the fee for the priests. The word is usually explained as originally designating a productive cow, and cows remained the standard measure of the fee, with gold, garments, horses, chariots and, in the great royal rites, land and enormous herds. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (2.2.2.6) explains the logic: there are two kinds of gods, the gods in heaven and the learned Brahmins who have studied the Veda, who are “human gods”; the oblation is given to the first, the fee to the second, and the sacrifice is complete only when both are satisfied. The fee was not a wage in the modern sense but a gift that the rite itself required, and the texts prescribe its amount and kind for each rite, from a single cow or a garment for a small offering to thousands of cows for a royal consecration.

The gift economy of the sacrifice is already visible in the Ṛgveda, where many hymns end with “praises of the gift” (dānastuti) celebrating a patron’s generosity in cattle, horses and slave women (see Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra). Heesterman argued that the fee preserves the logic of an older system of exchange between rival patrons and their priests, in which giving and receiving created bonds and obligations (Heesterman 1993). The giving of all one’s possessions (sarvavedasa) was the fee of certain rites, and it is such a rite that opens the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, where the boy Naciketas watches his father give away worn-out cows in the name of total generosity and asks to whom he himself will be given. The scale of the fees also explains why the great rites were sponsored mainly by kings and wealthy patrons, and why inscriptions such as that of Nāneghāṭ record the fees as carefully as the rites themselves (Section 8.7).

docs.title: 8.4 The Logic of the System: Models and Variants
docs.text:
The śrauta ritual comprises hundreds of named rites, but it is not a loose collection. It is built from a small number of model rites (prakṛti) of which the others are variants (vikṛti). The new- and full-moon offerings are the model for all iṣṭis; the animal sacrifice (paśubandha) for all animal offerings; and the Agniṣṭoma for all Soma sacrifices. A variant rite is described only by its differences from its model, and everything that is not specified is carried over (atideśa): “the variant is performed like the model” (prakṛtivad vikṛtiḥ kartavyā) is the basic rule. The Mīmāṃsā school of philosophy built a large part of its theory of interpretation on the problems that this transfer raises—what exactly is transferred, what is modified, and what is dropped—and Jaimini’s Mīmāṃsāsūtra devotes several of its books to them (see Volume 3, Darśana Darpaṇa).

The rites are also nested. A Soma sacrifice contains several iṣṭis and animal offerings within it, each performed according to its own model, and the Agnicayana is in turn built round a Soma sacrifice. The resulting structures can be described as hierarchies of embedded units. Frits Staal, who studied the Agnicayana closely, compared them with the recursive structures of grammar and argued that the ritual is governed by rules of a syntactic kind (Staal 1989).

The tradition classifies the obligatory śrauta rites into seven haviryajñas (offerings of milk, ghee, grain and cakes, together with the animal sacrifice and the Sautrāmaṇī) and seven forms (saṃsthā) of the Soma sacrifice; the list appears in the Gautama Dharmasūtra (chapter 8) among the forty “sacraments” (saṃskāra), together with seven “cooked” domestic offerings. The seven Soma forms, from the Agniṣṭoma to the Aptoryāma, are distinguished mainly by the number of chants and are listed in Table 4.2. Soma rites are also classified by length: one-day rites (ekāha); rites of two to twelve pressing days (ahīna); and “sessions” (sattra) of twelve days or more, of which the longest commonly described is the year-long gavām ayana. In a sattra all the officiants are themselves sacrificers, and no fees are paid.

Table 8.2 sets out the regular rites in the order in which a sacrificer would normally take them up.

Table 8.2. The principal śrauta rites of a sacrificer, in the usual order of undertaking. Rite When performed Place in the system Agnyādheya Once, to establish the fires; repeated (punarādheya) if they fail Precondition of all śrauta rites Agnihotra Every evening and morning for life An independent daily rite Darśapūrṇamāsa At every new and full moon Model of all iṣṭis Āgrayaṇa At the rice and barley harvests An iṣṭi Cāturmāsya At the start of each of the three seasons A series of iṣṭis Nirūḍhapaśubandha Once or twice a year Model of all animal sacrifices Agniṣṭoma At least once, traditionally in spring Model of all Soma sacrifices Other Soma rites, Agnicayana, royal rites For particular aims or persons Variants of the Soma model

The rites are tied to time. The new- and full-moon offerings require knowledge of the exact moment of the lunar phase, the seasonal rites and the establishment of the fires depend on the seasons, and the year-long sessions on a correct reckoning of the year with its intercalary month. The calendrical science of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa was composed, by its own account, to determine the proper times of the sacrifice (Section 7.6), and the Brāhmaṇas’ discussions of the year, the seasons and the lunar asterisms belong to the same practical concern.

docs.title: 8.5.1 The Agnihotra
docs.text:
The agnihotra is the simplest and most frequent of the śrauta rites: an offering of hot milk into the āhavanīya, made every evening after sunset and every morning around sunrise, for as long as the sacrificer lives. It is the stock example of an obligatory (nitya) rite: “he offers the agnihotra as long as he lives” (yāvajjīvam agnihotraṃ juhoti). The milk is drawn from a cow milked for the purpose, heated on the gārhapatya and offered with a special ladle, with a short formula: in the evening “Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā”, in the morning “Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā” (VS 3.9). A second, silent oblation follows each.

The Brāhmaṇas devote surprisingly long discussions to this small rite. They debate whether the morning offering should be made before or after sunrise, and they interpret it as the means by which the sun, which “enters the fire” at sunset, is reborn each morning; by offering, the sacrificer takes part in sustaining the alternation of night and day. H. W. Bodewitz’s study of the agnihotra in the Brāhmaṇas, especially the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, shows how much of the later theory of ritual, including the idea of the sacrifice as an internal act, grew out of reflection on this daily offering (Bodewitz 1976). The “agnihotra in the breaths” (prāṇāgnihotra), in which eating itself becomes the offering, is described in Section 6.6.

docs.title: 8.5.2 The New- and Full-Moon Offerings
docs.text:
The darśapūrṇamāsa is the model (prakṛti) of all iṣṭi offerings. Its central sequence on the day of offering is:

  1. Prayājas — five fore-offerings of ghee

  2. Principal oblations — cakes (puroḍāśa) and other offerings to Agni and other deities

  3. Sviṣṭakṛt and Iḍā — the offering to Agni “who makes the offering well”, and the priests’ consumption of a portion

  4. Anuyājas — three after-offerings

  5. Sūktavāka and Śaṃyuvāka — concluding recitations

  6. Patnīsaṃyājas — offerings to the wives of the gods, in the presence of the sacrificer’s wife

The rite takes two days at each new and full moon. The first is a day of preparation (upavasatha), on which the sacrificer and his wife observe restraints; at the new moon, a sacrificer who has already performed a Soma sacrifice also separates the calves from the cows so that the milk can be offered the next morning. On the second day the adhvaryu digs and strews the vedi, husks and grinds the rice or barley, and bakes the cakes (puroḍāśa) on potsherds: on eight potsherds for Agni, and for the second principal offering on eleven for Agni and Soma at the full moon and on twelve for Indra and Agni at the new moon.

The hotṛ’s part begins with the eleven “kindling verses” (sāmidhenī), recited as the fire is fed with sticks, with the first and last verses repeated three times to make fifteen. He then “chooses” Agni as the divine hotṛ by naming the ancestral seers of the sacrificer’s lineage (the pravara)—one of the places where the system of exogamous clans (gotra) enters the ritual. After the principal oblations, the priests and the sacrificer eat a share of the offering called iḍā, which is invoked as a goddess and identified with the cow and with nourishment, and the brahman receives a portion of his own. The rite ends with the offerings to the wives of the gods, in which the sacrificer’s wife takes part, and with the discarding of the remains. Because the darśapūrṇamāsa is the model of all iṣṭis, its every detail matters for the whole system, and the sūtras describe it first and at greatest length.

docs.title: 8.5.3 The Seasonal Offerings
docs.text:
The cāturmāsya, the “four-monthly” offerings, divide the year into three seasons of four months, each opened by a sacrifice on a full-moon day (Einoo 1988). The Vaiśvadeva, in spring, is offered to the All-Gods and many other deities. The Varuṇapraghāsa, at the beginning of the rains, is an expiatory rite to Varuṇa, the god who binds wrongdoers: figures of a ram and a ewe made of barley dough are offered, and the sacrificer’s wife is asked, in a striking episode of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (2.5.2.20), to name any lovers she has had, since an unconfessed wrong would harm her family. The Sākamedha, in autumn, includes a great offering to the ancestors (mahāpitṛyajña) and the tryambaka offering of cakes to Rudra, made at a crossroads and outside the settlement, with a verse that is still among the best known of all Vedic mantras (VS 3.60, also RV 7.59.12):

The Tryambaka Verse — Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 3.60

tryambakaṃ yajāmahe sugandhiṃ puṣṭivardhanam urvārukam iva bandhanān mṛtyor mukṣīya māmṛtāt We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, who increases prosperity. Like a cucumber from its stalk, may I be freed from death, not from immortality.

In its ritual setting the verse belongs to an offering meant to send the dangerous god away from the household; it later became the “death-conquering” (mṛtyuñjaya) mantra of Śaiva devotion. A fourth offering, the Śunāsīrīya, addressed to the ploughshare and the plough, closes the yearly cycle.

To these regular offerings belong the āgrayaṇa, the offering of the first fruits of the rice and barley harvests before the new grain may be eaten, and the independent animal sacrifice (nirūḍhapaśubandha), performed once or twice a year. In the animal sacrifice the victim, usually a goat, is bound to a wooden post (yūpa) and killed outside the vedi by suffocation, so that no blood is shed at the altar; the texts call the killing a “quieting” (saṃjñapana), and the hotṛ recites a long litany addressed to the slaughterers (the adhrigu formula). The texts’ unease about the killing, and the later replacement of animal victims, are discussed in Section 3.9. The omentum (vapā) is offered first, then prescribed portions of the body; the remainder is eaten by the priests.

docs.title: 8.6 The Soma Sacrifice Step by Step
docs.text:
The Agniṣṭoma, the model of all Soma sacrifices, lasts five days in its basic form and requires sixteen priests; it is outlined in Table 8.3.

Table 8.3. Outline of the five-day Agniṣṭoma. Day Name Principal Activities 1 Dīkṣā Consecration of the sacrificer (yajamāna) and his wife; vows of restraint 2–4 Upasad days Purchase of the Soma; the Upasad offerings (twice daily); building of the Soma altar (mahāvedī); animal offering on the fourth day 5 Sutyā (pressing day) Soma pressed three times (morning, midday, evening); twelve chants (stotra) and twelve recitations (śastra); gifts to the priests (dakṣiṇā); concluding bath (avabhṛtha)

Its full description in the sūtras runs to hundreds of pages; Caland and Henry’s reconstruction of it from the texts, published in 1906–07, remains the classic study (Caland and Henry 1906). The main sequence is as follows.

Choice of priests and consecration.

The sacrificer formally chooses (varaṇa) his sixteen priests, and the area of the sacrifice is prepared: the hall with its three fires and, to the east, the great altar (Figure 8.1). He then undergoes the consecration (dīkṣā). He is shaved, bathed and anointed, puts on a new garment and a black antelope skin, and receives a staff; he must keep his hands closed in fists, speak little, live on milk and, according to the Śatapatha, scratch himself only with a black antelope’s horn. The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (1.3) explains the consecration as a rebirth: the consecrated man is an embryo, his hut the womb, his garment the caul. His wife is consecrated with him.

The purchase and reception of Soma.

The Soma plant is bought from a seller in a mock bargain: a young cow is led forward, its footprint is dug up and kept, the price is haggled over item by item, and in some texts the seller is struck and the payment taken back. The Soma is then carried on a cart to the sacrificial ground and received as a royal guest (ātithya). The priests and the sacrificer swear an oath of mutual loyalty, the tānūnaptra, by touching a dish of ghee together. On the days that follow, the upasad offerings (“sieges”) are made twice a day, and in many performances the pravargya, a rite in which a clay pot (mahāvīra) is heated until it glows and fresh milk is poured into it, so that a column of flame rises. The pravargya is regarded as secret and dangerous; its mantras and its explanation are transmitted in the Āraṇyakas (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 4–5), and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (14.1.1) tells how it restores the severed head of the sacrifice (Houben 1991).

The great altar.

During these days the great altar is measured out, the sadas and the shed for the Soma carts (havirdhāna) are built, and the fire is carried forward from the hall to a raised altar (uttaravedi) at the eastern end, which becomes the new āhavanīya; the old āhavanīya of the hall now serves as the gārhapatya. On the day before the pressing a he-goat is offered to Agni and Soma (agnīṣomīya), and water for the pressing (vasatīvarī) is drawn and kept overnight.

The pressing day.

Before dawn the hotṛ recites the long “morning litany” (prātaranuvāka). The Soma stalks are then crushed with stones on boards placed over sound-holes dug in the havirdhāna, mixed with water and strained through wool, and the juice is drawn into a series of cups (graha) dedicated to particular gods: Vāyu and Indra, Mitra and Varuṇa, the Aśvins, and others. The Soma is pressed three times in the day, at the morning, midday and third pressings (savana), each with its own offerings, chants and recitations. The day’s chanting begins outside the sadas with the bahiṣpavamāna stotra, for which the priests creep out in a line, each holding the one in front; the remaining chants are sung inside it.

The chants follow a fixed numerical plan. Each stotra is sung on a group of verses expanded by repetition to a set total (stoma); in the Agniṣṭoma the totals rise through the day from nine to fifteen, seventeen and finally twenty-one. Each stotra is answered by a śastra, recited by the hotṛ or one of his assistants. The rite takes its name from its last chant, the agniṣṭoma sāman, the “praise of Agni”. The priests’ fees, which in the texts consist chiefly of cows, are distributed at the midday pressing. At the third pressing the wives of the gods receive offerings, and the sacrificer’s wife has a part to play.

Conclusion.

The rite ends with the offering of a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa (anūbandhyā), the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in which the sacrificer, his wife and the implements stained with Soma are washed in flowing water, and concluding iṣṭis, after which the sacrificer returns to ordinary life.

Scholarly Note: What Was Soma?

The identity of the original Soma plant is unknown. Ephedra, which grows in the mountains of Afghanistan and Iran and is used in the Zoroastrian haoma rite, is the candidate most widely favoured; the fly agaric mushroom, proposed by R. Gordon Wasson in 1968 (Wasson 1968), and various other plants have also been suggested. The Brāhmaṇas already permit substitutes when true Soma cannot be had, and in modern performances a leafless creeper gathered in the hills, identified botanically as a species of Sarcostemma, is commonly used.

docs.title: 8.7.1 Sessions and the Ritual Year
docs.text: The sattras extend the Soma sacrifice over many days. The year-long gavām ayana, the “course of the cows”, is built from standard blocks of six-day periods arranged symmetrically around a central day, the viṣuvat; its penultimate day is the mahāvrata, a festival with music, a swing for the hotṛ, ritual abuse and a mock combat (Table 14.4). Such sessions, performed by groups of consecrated men who all count as sacrificers, are probably the most archaic form of the Soma rite, and some scholars have connected them with the life of the vrātya bands mentioned in the Atharvaveda and Brāhmaṇas. In historical times they were rarely performed.

docs.title: 8.7.2 The Vājapeya
docs.text: The vājapeya, the “drink of strength”, is a Soma sacrifice of the saṃsthā with seventeen chants, and the number seventeen pervades it: seventeen cups of Soma and seventeen of surā, seventeen animals for Prajāpati, seventeen drums and seventeen chariots. Its distinctive episodes are a chariot race, which the sacrificer is made to win, and the climbing of the sacrificial post: the sacrificer and his wife mount a ladder to its top and reach towards the sky before descending to be seated on a throne and sprinkled. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (5.1.1) presents the rite as one that gives the status of paramount ruler (samrāj), higher than that of a king (rājan) consecrated by the rājasūya; it was open to Brahmins as well as Kṣatriyas.

docs.title: 8.7.3 The Rājasūya
docs.text:
The royal consecration, described in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, is not a single ceremony but a long series of rites spread over more than a year. Its principal episodes include:

  • Ratnināṃ haviṃṣi: offerings in the houses of the king’s “jewels” (ratnins)—officials and members of his household—marking their support;

  • Abhiṣeka: anointing of the king with waters gathered from many sources;

  • symbolic acts such as a cattle raid, a chariot drive and a game of dice, which the king is made to win.

J. C. Heesterman’s analysis of its Yajurvedic sources showed that its structure reproduces a cycle of conception, birth and growth, through which the king is ritually reborn, and that its contests—the cattle raid on a kinsman’s herd, the game of dice—preserve traces of an older, agonistic ritual in which the king’s position had to be won against rivals (Heesterman 1957). After the anointing, the hotṛ recites to the king the story of Śunaḥśepa (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 7.13–18; Section 6.4). Theodore Proferes has traced how the imagery of these rites draws on the Ṛgvedic association between the sacred fire, the unity of the clans and the person of the ruler (Proferes 2007).

docs.title: 8.7.4 The Aśvamedha
docs.text:
The horse sacrifice, described in Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 22–25, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13 and the sūtras, was the most prestigious of the royal rites (Dumont 1927). A selected stallion was released in spring to wander for a year, guarded by an armed escort of young men; any territory it entered without resistance was claimed for the king. During the year the priests performed daily offerings, and a cycle of narratives (pāriplava ākhyāna) was recited over ten days and repeated throughout the year, each day devoted to a legendary king and a class of beings, before an audience of the king’s subjects (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.4.3). When the horse returned, a three-day Soma rite was held, during which the horse and many other animals were sacrificed. The priests exchanged riddles (brahmodya) about the nature of the world—“Who moves alone? … The sun moves alone” (VS 23.9–10)—and the chief queen lay beside the slain horse under a cover while the priests and the women of the court exchanged obscene verses, a fertility rite that later commentators found embarrassing. The texts’ interpretation identifies the horse with the cosmos and with Prajāpati, and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad opens by describing the dawn as the head of the sacrificial horse (BU 1.1.1).

The aśvamedha remained a claim to sovereignty long after the Vedic period. The Ayodhyā inscription of Dhanadeva describes the Śuṅga king Puṣyamitra (2nd century BCE) as the performer of two horse sacrifices; the Nāneghāṭ inscription of the Sātavāhana queen Nāyanikā (1st century BCE) lists the śrauta rites performed by the royal family, including the aśvamedha and the rājasūya, with the fees given; Samudragupta (4th century CE) struck gold coins showing a horse before a sacrificial post, and his successors’ inscriptions describe him as the restorer of the long-neglected horse sacrifice; the Vākāṭaka king Pravarasena I is styled the performer of four, and the Cālukya king Pulakeśin I is recorded as having performed one in the sixth century. These performances show the śrauta ritual being used, as it was in the Kuru realm, to proclaim a king’s power (see also Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra, on the coins).

docs.title: 8.7.5 Other Special Rites
docs.text: The sautrāmaṇī, offered to Indra “the good protector” (sutrāman), the Aśvins and Sarasvatī, uses cups of surā, a fermented grain drink, alongside milk; it is performed independently, or as a remedy for one who has vomited Soma, or as part of the royal consecration and the Agnicayana. The “human sacrifice” (puruṣamedha) of Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 30–31 consists, in the Śatapatha’s account, of a long list of human “victims” of every occupation who are bound and then released, and its historicity as an actual killing is doubtful. The Agnicayana, the greatest of the composite rites, has been described in Section 3.10.

docs.title: 8.8 The Indo-Iranian Background
docs.text: Several elements of the śrauta ritual are older than the Veda itself. The Zoroastrian high liturgy, the Yasna, which is still performed by Parsi priests in India, offers the closest comparison. It is conducted by two priests, the chief of whom is called the zōt (Avestan zaotar, cognate with Vedic hotṛ); it centres on the pounding of twigs of the haoma plant (Vedic soma) with water and milk; it requires a bundle of twigs, the barsom, comparable to the Vedic bundle of grass (veda) and strewing (barhis); and it is performed before a ritual fire. The Old Avestan Gāthās themselves are embedded in the text of the Yasna, much as Ṛgvedic hymns are embedded in the śrauta liturgy (Boyce 1979). The Indo-Iranian vocabulary listed in Table 1.3—yajña/yasna, hotṛ/zaotar, atharvan/ā\(\theta\)ravan—thus corresponds to shared ritual practice and not only to shared words. What is distinctively Indian is the vast elaboration of the ritual in the Brāhmaṇa period, the division of labour between priests of different Vedas, and the fire altar of the Agnicayana, which has no Iranian counterpart.

docs.title: 8.9 Interpreting the Sacrifice
docs.text:
The tradition itself offered several kinds of explanation. The Brāhmaṇas interpret each act through correspondences (bandhu) between the ritual, the cosmos and the person, and present the sacrifice as the means by which Prajāpati, exhausted after creation, is reassembled and the world renewed (Chapter 6). The Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads internalised it, treating breath, speech and thought as the true sacrifice. The Mīmāṃsā school took the opposite course: it held that the Vedic injunction—the stock example is “one who desires heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma”—is authoritative in itself, that the rite produces an unseen potency (apūrva) which bears fruit later, and that the gods named in the mantras matter chiefly as recipients designated by the text (see Volume 3, Darśana Darpaṇa).

Modern scholarship has been equally divided. Henri Hubert and Marcel Mauss, in their classic essay on sacrifice, drew heavily on the Vedic animal sacrifice to describe sacrifice as a mediation between the sacred and the profane through a victim (Hubert and Mauss 1964). Heesterman argued that the classical śrauta ritual is the product of a deliberate reform: an older, agonistic sacrifice, in which rival patrons competed in feasts and contests, was transformed into a closed, individual rite in which the sacrificer has no opponent and every act is fixed by rule (Heesterman 1993). Staal went further, arguing in a celebrated article that ritual is “pure activity” without meaning, governed by rules that can be studied like the rules of grammar, and that the Brāhmaṇas’ explanations are later and secondary (Staal 1979, 1989). Critics have replied that the explanations are as old as the codification of the rites and that ritual cannot be separated from what its participants believe it does. These debates show at least that the śrauta ritual is one of the best-documented ritual systems in the world, and one that has shaped the general theory of ritual.

docs.title: 8.10 The Śrauta Ritual after the Vedic Period
docs.text:
After the Vedic period the śrauta rites became the preserve of a small number of specialist families, while domestic rites, temple worship and devotion became the centre of most people’s religious life. They never ceased, however. Medieval land grants frequently describe their Brahmin recipients as performers of Soma sacrifices, and family names in many parts of India still record the ritual status of an ancestor: Agnihotri, Dīkṣit (one consecrated for a Soma rite), Somayājī or Somayājulu, Vājapeyī, Yājñik. Among the Nambūdiri Brahmins of Kerala, a man who has performed a Soma sacrifice is styled Somayājippāṭ, and one who has performed the Agnicayana Akkittiri, from Sanskrit agnicit.

In the twentieth century śrauta traditions were found chiefly in Kerala, coastal Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Maharashtra, and occasionally elsewhere. C. G. Kashikar and Asko Parpola surveyed them for Staal’s Agni (Staal 1983), and David Knipe has recorded the lives and practice of families of āhitāgnis in the Godavari delta of Andhra Pradesh (Knipe 2015). The twelve-day Atirātra–Agnicayana performed by Nambūdiri ritualists at Panjal, Kerala, in April 1975, filmed and documented by Staal and his colleagues, was the first such rite to be recorded by scholars in this detail; at the insistence of local opinion the goats were replaced by figures made of rice flour, a substitution that itself has a long history in the tradition.

In this combined rite the Agnicayana is built round an Atirātra, a Soma sacrifice whose chanting continues through the night. Over the twelve days the ritualists built the five-layered, bird-shaped brick altar described in Section 3.10, performed the pravargya, chanted and recited the Śatarudrīya and the other litanies of the rite, and on the final night completed the cycle of chants; at the end, following Kerala practice, the ritual enclosure was set on fire. Staal’s two-volume publication of the performance, with contributions by many specialists, recordings of the recitations and photographs, and the film Altar of Fire made with Robert Gardner, remain the fullest documentation of a Vedic rite in performance. Kerala families have performed further Atirātra–Agnicayana rites in later decades. In all these communities the rites survive through a few families, depend on patronage and on the long training of the priests, and are, like the recitation traditions on which they rest, under threat (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 8.11 Summary
docs.text:
What makes the śrauta ritual distinctive is less its scale than its system. A few model rites, endlessly varied and nested inside one another, generate hundreds of ceremonies, and the rules for transferring them from model to variant became the starting point of Indian hermeneutics in the Mīmāṃsā. The same rites served very different ends: the daily offering of a householder, the sovereignty of a king, the livelihood of priestly families. That is why they could survive the end of the Vedic period as a royal claim in inscriptions and on coins, and survive the end of royal patronage as the inherited practice of a few families, whose performances have in turn made the system one of the best documented in the comparative study of ritual.

Closing Verse

iyaṃ vediḥ paro antaḥ pṛthivyā ayaṃ yajño bhuvanasya nābhiḥ ayaṃ somo vṛṣṇo aśvasya reto brahmāyaṃ vācaḥ paramaṃ vyoma This altar is the farthest end of the earth; this sacrifice is the navel of the world; this Soma is the seed of the stallion; this sacred formulation is the highest heaven of speech. — Ṛgveda 1.164.35

docs.title: Chapter 9: The Gṛhya Ritual: Domestic Rites in the Gṛhyasūtras
docs.text:
Invocatory Verse

gṛbhṇāmi te saubhagatvāya hastaṃ mayā patyā jaradaṣṭir yathāsaḥ bhago aryamā savitā puraṃdhir mahyaṃ tvādur gārhapatyāya devāḥ I take your hand for good fortune, so that with me as your husband you may reach old age. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ and Puraṃdhi, the gods, have given you to me for the householder’s life. — Ṛgveda 10.85.36

docs.title: 9.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Alongside the solemn rites of the previous chapter, which required three fires and a team of priests, the Vedic householder performed a large number of simpler rites in his own house, in a single domestic fire, usually by himself or with one priest. These are the gṛhya (“domestic”) rites. They include daily offerings, rites of the month and the seasons, rites for the house, the cattle and the fields, and the life-cycle rites (saṃskāra) from conception to death. Because they touched every family and every stage of life, they have had a far longer and wider afterlife than the śrauta ritual: much of what Hindus today recognise as “Vedic” ritual—the wedding round the fire, the thread ceremony, the funeral and the offerings to the ancestors—comes down from them.

The rites are prescribed in the Gṛhyasūtras, the domestic manuals of the Vedic schools, which belong with the Śrauta-, Dharma- and Śulbasūtras to the Kalpa Vedāṅga (Section 7.7). The tradition classes them as smārta, based on remembered tradition rather than directly on the Veda, but their mantras are drawn from the Vedic Saṃhitās and their procedures are modelled on the śrauta rites. This chapter describes the rites as the Gṛhyasūtras present them; the legal side of the life-cycle rites—the age of initiation, the forms of marriage, inheritance and impurity—belongs to the Dharmaśāstras and is treated in Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra, and the initiation as the beginning of education in Volume 22, Manas and Śikṣā. The standard modern accounts are Jan Gonda’s survey of the “non-solemn” rites, the second volume of P. V. Kane’s History of Dharmaśāstra, and Raj Bali Pandey’s study of the saṃskāras (Gonda 1980; Kane 1941; Pandey 1969).

docs.title: 9.2 The Gṛhyasūtras
docs.text:
Each Vedic school had, at least in principle, its own Gṛhyasūtra, and the surviving texts are listed in Table 9.1. Most were composed between about the sixth and the third century BCE, and several are closely related: the Khādira Gṛhyasūtra is an abridgement of the Gobhila, and the Taittirīya sūtras share much material. Some schools collected the mantras needed for the domestic rites into separate books, such as the Mantrapāṭha of the Āpastambins and the Mantrabrāhmaṇa of the Sāmavedins, so that the sūtra itself need cite only the opening words. Seven of the most important texts were translated into English by Hermann Oldenberg in the Sacred Books of the East (Oldenberg 1886).

Table 9.1. The principal Gṛhyasūtras by Veda and school. Veda School Gṛhyasūtras Ṛgveda Śākala; Kauṣītaki Āśvalāyana; Śāṅkhāyana and Kauṣītaka (Kauṣītaki) Sāmaveda Kauthuma, Rāṇāyanīya, Jaiminīya Gobhila (Kauthuma); Khādira (Rāṇāyanīya); Jaiminīya; mantras in the Mantrabrāhmaṇa Black Yajurveda Taittirīya Baudhāyana, Bhāradvāja, Āpastamba (mantras in the Mantrapāṭha), Hiraṇyakeśin, Vaikhānasa, Āgniveśya, Vādhūla Maitrāyaṇīya Mānava, Vārāha Kaṭha Kāṭhaka (also called Laugākṣi) White Yajurveda Vājasaneyin Pāraskara (also called Kātīya) Atharvaveda Śaunaka Kauśika Sūtra

The sūtras differ in the rites they include, in their order and in many details. Most begin with marriage, because it is at marriage that the domestic fire is normally established; others begin with general rules or with the daily offerings. Their variety is itself significant. The Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra, for example, introduces its account of the wedding by observing that the customs of different regions and villages vary and that they should be followed (1.7.1–2), and several sūtras close a description by referring the householder to the practice of his family or region. The domestic ritual was thus never a single uniform system: the sūtras codified a common Brahmanical frame and left room for local custom within it.

docs.title: 9.3 The Domestic Fire and the Model Offering
docs.text:
The centre of the domestic cult is a single fire, variously called the gṛhya, aupāsana, āvasathya or “marriage” (vaivāhika) fire. According to Pāraskara and others it is set up at the time of marriage, or, in the view of some teachers, when a son takes his share of the family property on its division. A householder who later established the three śrauta fires kept the domestic fire as well. Into it he and his wife offered every morning and evening a small oblation of grain or rice—the domestic counterpart of the agnihotra—and in it were performed the other domestic rites.

The basic domestic rite is the pākayajña, the “cooked offering”. Its model is the sthālīpāka, a pot of rice or barley cooked in milk or water on the domestic fire and offered at new and full moon to Agni and other gods, just as the cakes of the śrauta new- and full-moon offerings are offered in the āhavanīya. The frame of the rite is a miniature version of the śrauta iṣṭi: the fire is enclosed and the grass strewn; a Brahmin may be seated in the place of the brahman; two streams of ghee are poured; the two “ghee portions” are offered to Agni and Soma; then come the principal oblations, the offering to Agni “who makes the offering good” (sviṣṭakṛt), and the concluding acts. Once the frame is known, each particular rite is described only by its special features—the same principle of model and variant that governs the śrauta ritual (Section 8.4).

Āśvalāyana opens his Gṛhyasūtra by distinguishing three kinds of pākayajña: those offered in the fire (huta); those offered outside the fire, as bali portions set down for spirits, animals and beings (prahuta); and those “offered in a Brahmin”, that is, the feeding of Brahmins. The third kind shows how the gift of food to learned men came to be treated as a sacrifice in its own right, a development that shaped later Hindu ritual and charity. The Gautama Dharmasūtra lists seven pākayajñas: the aṣṭakā, the pārvaṇa (new- and full-moon), the śrāddha for the ancestors, and four rites named after the full moons of the months Śrāvaṇa, Mārgaśīrṣa (āgrahāyaṇī), Caitra and Āśvayuja. Alongside them stand the five daily “great sacrifices” to the Veda, the gods, the ancestors, human beings and all creatures, described in Section 6.3.

docs.title: 9.4 The Domestic Year
docs.text:
The Gṛhyasūtras attach rites to the seasons and to the work of the household and the farm. At the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, at the height of the rains, the householder makes the śravaṇā offering and sets out bali for the serpents, a rite continued each evening until the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa; then, in the āgrahāyaṇī rite, the family “descends” (pratyavarohaṇa) from the raised beds used during the season of snakes to sleep again on the ground. At the full moon of Āśvayuja offerings are made for the welfare of the cattle, and at harvest the first fruits of the new grain are offered (āgrayaṇa) before it may be eaten. The aṣṭakās, on the eighth days of the dark halves of the winter months, are offerings to the ancestors which in some sūtras include the killing of a cow or goat. The śūlagava, the “spit-ox”, is a sacrifice of an ox to Rudra performed outside the village, an example of the many rites in which the dangerous god is honoured at a distance (cf. the tryambaka rite of the śrauta ritual, Section 8.5).

The study of the Veda also had its annual calendar. In the rainy season the students and teachers “opened” the year’s study with the upākaraṇa, and some months later closed it with the utsarjana; the sūtras also lay down days on which recitation is forbidden (anadhyāya), such as the days of the new and full moon and times of storm or of impurity. The opening rite survives as the Upākarma, observed in Śrāvaṇa by many Brahmin communities, when the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) is renewed; in Tamil Nadu it is known as Āvaṇi Aviṭṭam. Other rites accompany the building of a house, with offerings to Vāstoṣpati, the “lord of the dwelling” already invoked in the Ṛgveda (RV 7.54–55); the later development of these rites into the vāstu tradition is treated in Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa.

docs.title: 9.5 The Life-Cycle Rites
docs.text:
The number of life-cycle rites varies. The Gautama Dharmasūtra (chapter 8) counts forty “sacraments”, including the śrauta rites, while later tradition settled on sixteen, in lists that differ in detail; a commonly cited list is given in Table 9.2. That list is a later standardisation. The Gṛhyasūtras themselves do not use a fixed number, and they treat some rites at length and others briefly or not at all.

Table 9.2. A common list of the sixteen saṃskāras (lists vary between texts).
