No. Saṃskāra Purpose and Occasion 1 Garbhādhāna Rite for conception 2 Puṃsavana Rite to obtain a male child, in early pregnancy 3 Sīmantonnayana Parting of the pregnant wife’s hair 4 Jātakarma Birth rite; honey and ghee given to the newborn 5 Nāmakaraṇa Naming (commonly on the tenth or twelfth day) 6 Niṣkramaṇa First outing; the child is shown the sun 7 Annaprāśana First solid food (sixth month) 8 Cūḍākaraṇa First tonsure 9 Karṇavedha Ear-piercing 10 Vidyārambha Beginning of learning the alphabet 11 Upanayana Initiation into Vedic study (for males of the three upper varṇas) 12 Vedārambha Beginning of Vedic study 13 Keśānta First shaving of the beard 14 Samāvartana Return home at the end of study 15 Vivāha Marriage 16 Antyeṣṭi Funeral rites

Their accounts show what the rites consisted of, and which Vedic mantras accompanied them. Table 9.3 shows where the principal mantras of the life-cycle rites come from.

Table 9.3. Some Vedic sources of the mantras of the domestic life-cycle rites. Rite Principal Vedic sources Marriage RV 10.85 (the wedding of Sūryā); Atharvaveda book 14 Conception RV 10.184 (“May Viṣṇu prepare the womb”) Initiation The Sāvitrī verse, RV 3.62.10 House-building RV 7.54–55 (to Vāstoṣpati); Atharvaveda 3.12 Funeral RV 10.14–18; Atharvaveda book 18

docs.title: 9.5.1 Marriage
docs.text: Most Gṛhyasūtras describe the wedding first. Its mantras come above all from the great wedding hymn of the Ṛgveda (RV 10.85), which tells of the marriage of Sūryā, the daughter of the Sun, and from the corresponding fourteenth book of the Atharvaveda. The groom takes the bride’s hand with RV 10.85.36, the verse that opens this chapter; she treads on a stone, to be firm; parched grain, poured into her hands by her brother, is offered in the fire; the couple walk round the fire and take seven steps together; and in the evening the groom shows her the pole star (dhruva) and the star Arundhatī as emblems of constancy. These elements, described more fully in Volume 18 (in the chapter on family and law), recur in nearly every sūtra, but their order differs, and the sūtras include many local elements: Āśvalāyana, for instance, describes a test in which the girl chooses one of several lumps of earth taken from different places, from which her future is foretold. After the wedding the couple keep continence for three nights, and the marriage is consummated on the fourth (caturthīkarman) with further verses from RV 10.85.

docs.title: 9.5.2 Conception, Pregnancy and Birth
docs.text:
The rites of the first years are concerned above all with the safe birth and survival of children, at a time when both were uncertain. The garbhādhāna accompanies conception with verses such as RV 10.184 (“May Viṣṇu prepare the womb, may Tvaṣṭṛ shape the forms”). The puṃsavana, in the third month of pregnancy, is intended to secure a male child: in several sūtras the juice of a banyan shoot is placed in the right nostril of the pregnant woman. In the sīmantonnayana, the “parting of the hair”, the husband parts his wife’s hair with a porcupine quill and other objects, and in some sūtras lute-players are asked to sing. At birth, before the cord is cut, the father performs the jātakarman: he gives the child honey and ghee, sometimes from a golden spoon, whispers into its ear, and prays for its intelligence and long life; a secret name may be given at this time, and the public name on the tenth or twelfth day.

These rites also show the preferences of the society that produced them. Prayers are overwhelmingly for sons; and several sūtras state that the rites of childhood are to be performed for a daughter without the Vedic mantras. In this the domestic manuals anticipate the Dharmaśāstras’ exclusion of women from Vedic ritual (see Section 14.7 and Volume 18).

docs.title: 9.5.3 Childhood and Initiation
docs.text:
The first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana) takes place in the sixth month, and the sūtras recommend particular foods for the qualities they are believed to confer. The first tonsure (cūḍākaraṇa), in the third year or according to family custom, leaves locks of hair arranged in the manner of the child’s lineage; the godāna or keśānta, the first shaving of the beard, follows at about sixteen.

The initiation (upanayana) is described in the Gṛhyasūtras as a rite of passage into the teacher’s care. The teacher asks the boy’s name, takes his hand and entrusts him to Savitṛ and other gods; he invests him with a girdle, a staff and an upper garment or skin, and teaches him the Sāvitrī verse (RV 3.62.10), in some sūtras first by quarter-verses, then by half-verses, then as a whole. The boy then lays fuel on the fire (samidādhāna), a duty he repeats daily as a student, and begins to beg his food. Some sūtras prescribe special observances (vrata) before the study of particular parts of the Veda, such as the Mahānāmnī verses of the Sāmaveda or the esoteric portions of the Āraṇyakas. The return home at the end of study (samāvartana) is marked by a bath, after which the young man is a snātaka, “one who has bathed”, bound by a code of conduct that the Gṛhyasūtras list in detail, and eligible to marry. The legal rules on the age and eligibility for initiation, and its denial to Śūdras and women, are discussed in Volume 18 and Volume 22.

docs.title: 9.5.4 Death and the Ancestors
docs.text:
The funeral rites draw their mantras from the funeral hymns of the Ṛgveda (10.14–18) and the eighteenth book of the Atharvaveda; their religious background is discussed in Section 13.7. An āhitāgni, one who has kept the śrauta fires, is cremated in them: his body is laid on the pyre between the three fires, and his sacrificial implements are placed on the different parts of his body, so that he goes to the next world equipped for sacrifice. The body may be covered with the limbs and fat of a cow or goat, recalling RV 10.16.7 (“wrap yourself in the armour of Agni with the cows”). The widow lies down beside the body and is called back to life with RV 10.18.8, “Rise, woman, to the world of the living”. In the funeral hymn the fire is asked not to destroy the dead man but to carry him, “cooked”, to the Fathers (RV 10.16.1–2). After the cremation the mourners pour water for the dead, observe a period of impurity, and on a later day gather the bones into an urn, which is buried; the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (13.8) describes the building of a burial mound over the remains.

The dead are then sustained by offerings. The śrauta ritual includes a monthly piṇḍapitṛyajña, in which balls of rice are offered to the father, grandfather and great-grandfather; the domestic śrāddha, at which Brahmins representing the ancestors are fed, developed alongside it and became, in the Dharmaśāstras, one of the most elaborately regulated of all Hindu rites (Volume 18). The Gṛhyasūtras thus mark the point at which Vedic ancestor worship turns into the classical system of śrāddha and sapiṇḍa kinship.

docs.title: 9.6 Women and the Domestic Rites
docs.text:
The domestic rites gave the wife a larger part than the śrauta ritual. The domestic fire is established at marriage and belongs to the couple; the wife tends it, prepares the offerings and takes part in the daily oblations, and Gobhila’s Gṛhyasūtra permits her to make the morning and evening offerings herself. The bali offerings of food for the household spirits and creatures were in practice largely in women’s hands. Several rites, including parts of the wedding, the rites of pregnancy and those of childhood, were performed in the presence of, and partly by, the women of the family, and their songs and customs accompanied them. The Āpastamba Dharmasūtra closes by reporting the view that whatever has not been laid down should be learned from women and from people of all classes—an acknowledgement that the Sanskrit manuals recorded only part of what was actually done.

At the same time, the domestic manuals reflect the narrowing of women’s access to the Veda. The Vedic mantras of the rites are recited by men; for daughters several rites are to be performed without mantras; and the later Dharmaśāstras made marriage the only “initiation” for a woman (Section 14.7). Jamison’s study of the wife in Vedic ritual shows how the texts combine a real ritual role for the woman with anxiety about her sexuality and her loyalty, and how the hospitality of the household, over which she presided, was itself conceived as a kind of sacrifice (Jamison 1996). The history of women in the domestic rites is therefore neither one of simple exclusion nor one of equality, but of participation within limits set by men’s control of the sacred word.

docs.title: 9.7 The Kauśika Sūtra and the Atharvavedic Rites
docs.text: The domestic manual of the Śaunaka school of the Atharvaveda, the Kauśika Sūtra, is unlike the others. Besides the usual domestic rites it gives the ritual use (viniyoga) of the Atharvavedic hymns: how a charm against fever is to be recited while the patient is sprinkled or given a drink, how an amulet (maṇi) of a particular wood is to be bound on, how rain is to be brought, how a rival is to be driven away or an enemy harmed. It is therefore the key to understanding how the hymns described in Chapter 5 were used in practice. Maurice Bloomfield edited the text with extracts from its medieval commentaries in 1890, and Willem Caland translated its central sections on “magical” ritual (Bloomfield 1890). The sūtra shows that healing, protection and sorcery were part of the same domestic world as the wedding and the funeral, and that the boundary between “religion” and “magic” drawn by nineteenth-century scholars does not match the texts’ own categories.

docs.title: 9.8 From the Gṛhyasūtras to Living Practice
docs.text:
The Gṛhyasūtras are the remote ancestors of present-day Hindu domestic ritual, but the line of descent passes through two thousand years of change. The Dharmaśāstras and their medieval digests (nibandha) added rules on who might perform which rite; handbooks (prayoga, paddhati) composed for each school and region set out the actual sequence of acts and words; and Purāṇic and Āgamic elements were added, such as the preliminary worship of Gaṇeśa, the invocation of auspiciousness (puṇyāhavācana) and offerings to the Mother goddesses. Regional custom and the songs and practices of women, which the sūtras themselves acknowledged, shaped the rites at least as much as the Sanskrit texts.

The question of who was entitled to the Vedic mantras of the domestic rites remained contested. Medieval authorities generally held that women’s and Śūdras’ rites should be performed without Vedic mantras, or with Purāṇic substitutes; the seventeenth-century Śūdrakamalākara of Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa is a well-known manual of this kind. In the nineteenth century Dayānanda Sarasvatī’s Saṃskāravidhi, first published in the 1870s, set out the sixteen saṃskāras with Vedic mantras for all members of the Ārya Samāj, women included, and several later reform movements followed this lead. Today the wedding, the thread ceremony, the funeral and the ancestral offerings are the domestic rites most widely performed with Vedic mantras, often in shortened form and by a family priest; their study shows both the remarkable continuity of the Vedic tradition and the many ways in which it has been reshaped.

docs.title: 9.9 Summary
docs.text:
The domestic manuals are where the Vedic ritual meets the ordinary household. Their authors adapted a priestly system to a single fire and a single family, and in doing so they recorded, more than any other Vedic texts, what people hoped for and feared: the safe birth of children, the marriage of daughters, the health of the herd, the welfare of the dead. They also show the Brahmanical frame tightening around that life, as the Vedic mantras were reserved for twice-born men, and at the same time loosening, as the sūtras themselves conceded that region, family and women’s custom decided much of what was actually done. Both tendencies run through the later history of Hindu domestic ritual.

Closing Verse: Blessing of the Couple

ihaiva stam mā vi yauṣṭaṃ viśvam āyur vy aśnutam krīḷantau putrair naptṛbhir modamānau sve gṛhe Stay here, do not be parted; attain the full span of life, playing with sons and grandsons, rejoicing in your own home. — Ṛgveda 10.85.42

docs.title: Chapter 10: The Four Upavedas: The Applied Sciences and the Veda
docs.text:
Invocatory Verse

dharme cārthe ca kāme ca mokṣe ca bharatarṣabha yad ihāsti tad anyatra yan nehāsti na tat kvacit On dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation, O bull of the Bharatas, what is here is found elsewhere; what is not here is found nowhere. — Mahābhārata 1.56.33 (critical edition)

docs.title: 10.1 The Scheme of the Upavedas
docs.text:
The term upaveda (“subsidiary Veda”) denotes a group of practical sciences that later tradition attached to the four Vedas, so as to give them Vedic standing. Whereas the Vedāṅgas served the Vedic texts themselves, the Upavedas are sciences of the world: medicine, warfare, music, and either polity or architecture. The scheme is post-Vedic; it appears in texts such as the Caraṇavyūha, and the lists vary:

  1. Āyurveda — medicine; attached to the Ṛgveda in the Caraṇavyūha, but to the Atharvaveda in the medical texts themselves;

  2. Dhanurveda — archery and warfare; attached to the Yajurveda;

  3. Gāndharvaveda — music and the performing arts; attached to the Sāmaveda;

  4. Arthaśāstra (polity) or Sthāpatyaveda (architecture) — attached to the Atharvaveda.

This chapter is concerned with the scheme itself: where it comes from, what it claims, and what it shows about the way Brahmanical scholars ordered knowledge. The sciences have their own volumes in this series—Āyurveda in Volume 13, music, dance and drama in Volume 9 (Saṅgīta–Nāṭya), architecture in Volume 16 (Vāstu–Śilpa), polity in Volume 18 (Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra) and warfare in Volume 20 (Yuddha and Dhanurveda)—and are described here only in outline (Figure 10.1).

Figure 10.1. The four Upavedas and their traditional Vedic associations, after the Caraṇavyūha. The dashed line shows the alternative attachment of Āyurveda to the Atharvaveda, preferred by the medical texts.

The scheme belongs to a wider effort to arrange all learning around the Veda. The Yājñavalkya Smṛti (1.3) counts fourteen “seats of knowledge” (vidyāsthāna): the four Vedas, the six Vedāṅgas, Purāṇa, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā and Dharmaśāstra. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa (3.6) adds Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharva and Arthaśāstra to make eighteen, and the sixteenth-century Advaitin Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, in his Prasthānabheda, used these eighteen headings to survey every branch of learning as an aid, direct or indirect, to the Veda. The Upavedas are the part of this system that reached furthest from the ritual.

docs.title: 10.2 Vedic Antecedents
docs.text:
The idea of calling a body of practical lore a “Veda” is older than the Upaveda lists. In the horse sacrifice, the cycle of narratives recited over ten days (Section 8.7) declares on successive days that the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Atharvan and Āṅgirasa lore, the knowledge of snakes, the lore of other beings, sorcery, itihāsa, purāṇa and the Sāmans are “the Veda” (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.4.3), and the list of subjects in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (7.1.2) places grammar, calculation, the knowledge of portents, of snakes and of the stars beside the four Vedas (Section 14.10). Late Vedic culture thus already treated many kinds of specialist knowledge as Veda in a wider sense.

There are also real continuities of content, though none amounts to a line of descent. The healing charms of the Atharvaveda share vocabulary, named diseases and some plants with classical medicine (Section 5.7). The Sāmaveda is the oldest documented Indian tradition of sacred song, and the Nāradīya Śikṣā relates its tones to those of secular music (Section 4.6). The Ṛgveda has a hymn to the warrior’s weapons—armour, bow, bowstring, quiver, chariot and arrows (RV 6.75)—and the Atharvaveda war charms for the king’s army (Section 5.6). The measured construction of altars and ritual enclosures, codified in the Śulbasūtras (Section 7.7), and the domestic rites for a new house addressed to Vāstoṣpati (Section 9.4) stand at the beginning of the architectural tradition; and the royal consecrations and the purohita’s counsel to the king (Section 14.5) belong to the prehistory of Indian political thought.

docs.title: 10.3.1 Āyurveda
docs.text:
Āyurveda (āyus, “life” + veda) is the classical Indian system of medicine. Its medical texts present it as a limb of the Atharvaveda (Suśruta Saṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna 1.6), but classical Āyurveda took shape around the beginning of the Common Era. The Caraka Saṃhitā (redacted c. 100 BCE–200 CE and completed by Dṛḍhabala), the Suśruta Saṃhitā (in its present form by c. 500 CE) and Vāgbhaṭa’s Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya (c. 600 CE) form the “great triad” (bṛhattrayī) of its literature. They divide medicine into eight branches—internal medicine, surgery, diseases of the head, paediatrics, toxicology, the treatment of possession and mental illness, rejuvenation and virility—and their central theories, the three doṣas, the seven bodily tissues and a rational therapeutics based on diet, regimen and drugs, are new. Some scholars have argued that early Buddhist and śramaṇa healers played an important part in their formation (Zysk 1991).

Health and Safety Note

This section describes the history and ideas of a traditional medical system; it is not medical advice. The effectiveness and safety of Āyurvedic treatments must be judged by modern clinical evidence, which for most remedies is limited. Some Āyurvedic products, especially mineral and metal preparations (rasaśāstra, bhasma), have been found to contain dangerous levels of lead, mercury and arsenic (Saper et al. 2004, 2008). Consult a qualified medical practitioner before using any remedy.

docs.title: 10.3.2 Dhanurveda
docs.text: Dhanurveda (dhanus, “bow” + veda) is the science of archery and, more broadly, of arms and warfare. No early independent treatise survives. Its traditions are known from chapters of the Agni and Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇas, from the descriptions of weapons, training and battle formations in the epics, from the military books of Kauṭilya’s Arthaśāstra, and from medieval compilations. A common classification divides weapons into those released from the hand (mukta, such as arrows and javelins), those held (amukta, such as swords and maces), those both thrown and retained (muktāmukta), and those released by machines (yantramukta); some lists have instead weapons “released by mantra” (mantramukta), reflecting the epic idea of divine weapons.

docs.title: 10.3.3 Gāndharvaveda
docs.text: Gāndharvaveda, named after the Gandharvas, the celestial musicians, is the science of music, and by extension of dance and drama. Its foundational text is the Nāṭyaśāstra ascribed to Bharata, compiled over several centuries (c. 200 BCE–200 CE), which treats drama, dance, music, staging and the theory of aesthetic experience. Its doctrine that a performance produces in the spectator a “taste” (rasa) of one of eight kinds—to which later theorists, championed by Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016), added a ninth, the tranquil—became one of the most original Indian contributions to aesthetics. Mataṅga’s Bṛhaddeśī, which first defines rāga, and Śārṅgadeva’s Saṅgītaratnākara (13th century) carried the musical tradition forward. The gāndharva music of the Nāṭyaśāstra is, however, a system distinct from Sāman chant (Section 4.6).

docs.title: 10.3.4 Arthaśāstra and Sthāpatyaveda
docs.text: The fourth place is given in some lists to polity, in others to architecture. The Arthaśāstra ascribed to Kauṭilya, a composite text of c. 50 BCE–300 CE, treats government, law, diplomacy and war as a science of its own, with only a nominal debt to the Veda. Sthāpatyaveda (sthāpatya, “the builder’s art”), also called Vāstuśāstra or Śilpaśāstra, covers architecture, town-planning, sculpture and iconography. Its earliest systematic treatments appear in Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th century CE) and in works such as the Mānasāra, the South Indian Mayamata and King Bhoja’s Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra (11th century). Central to these texts is the vāstupuruṣa maṇḍala, a square grid, commonly of \(8\times8\) or \(9\times9\) cells, over which a cosmic being is imagined lying, with deities assigned to the cells and Brahmā at the centre. The texts combine practical knowledge of building with religious symbolism and rules of auspiciousness; modern claims that vāstu rules channel “cosmic” or “magnetic” energies are not found in them and have no scientific basis.

docs.title: 10.4 Summary
docs.text: The Upaveda scheme is best read as an act of classification rather than as a history. Its lists disagree about which science belongs to which Veda, and even about which sciences qualify; the medical writers preferred the Atharvaveda, whose healing charms gave them a natural ancestor, while the Caraṇavyūha pairs medicine with the Ṛgveda. What the lists share is a claim: that the practical sciences, whatever their actual sources, Vedic and non-Vedic, belong within a single order of knowledge whose root is the Veda. That claim gave medicine, music, warfare, polity and building a place in Brahmanical learning and a share in its prestige. It did not determine their content, which each science developed on its own terms over many centuries, as the volumes devoted to them describe.

docs.title: Chapter 11: The Oral Tradition: Śruti, Pāṭha, and the Art of Preservation
docs.text:
Invocatory Verse

yad eṣām anyo anyasya vācaṃ śāktasyeva vadati śikṣamāṇaḥ When one of them repeats the speech of the other, as a pupil repeats his teacher’s… — Ṛgveda 7.103.5 (the hymn of the frogs)

docs.title: 11.1 Introduction: Oral Transmission
docs.text:
For most of their history the Vedic texts were preserved not in writing but by oral transmission from teacher to pupil, over some three thousand years. The name śruti, “what is heard”, is literal. In the Ṛgveda’s humorous hymn to the frogs (RV 7.103), the croaking of frogs at the start of the rains is compared to pupils repeating their teacher’s words—a glimpse of Vedic schooling already in the oldest text.

Writing came late to India. Apart from the undeciphered Harappan script, the earliest Indian writing is in the Brāhmī and Kharoṣṭhī scripts of the inscriptions of Aśoka (3rd century BCE), long after the Vedic texts were composed. When writing did come into use, the Vedic schools continued to treat oral learning as primary.

The fidelity of this transmission is well documented. The Ṛgveda is recited today, across India, in a form that agrees almost syllable for syllable, and accent for accent, with the oldest manuscripts and with the analysis of the Prātiśākhyas composed more than two thousand years ago. Linguists rely on it as a faithful record of a language spoken in the second millennium BCE (Staal 1986; Witzel 1997).

Vedic Oral Transmission in Brief

  • The Vedas were transmitted orally for well over two thousand years before manuscripts were made, and orally alongside manuscripts ever since.

  • The Ṛgveda alone has over 10,500 verses, all memorised with their accents.

  • Several recitation methods (pāṭhas) provide cross-checks against error.

  • The tradition of Vedic chanting was proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2003 and inscribed on the Representative List in 2008.

docs.title: 11.2 The Guru–Śiṣya Paramparā
docs.text:
The foundation of Vedic transmission is the teacher–pupil lineage (guru–śiṣya paramparā). In the classical model, set out in the Gṛhya and Dharma Sūtras, it proceeds through several stages:

  1. Upanayana — initiation, in the classical law books at age 8 for a Brahmin, 11 for a Kṣatriya and 12 for a Vaiśya;

  2. Brahmacarya — studentship, traditionally twelve years or more for one Veda, living in the teacher’s household;

  3. Svādhyāya — daily recitation of the text learnt;

  4. Samāvartana — the ceremonial return home at the end of study.

This system was also a system of exclusion. Initiation, and therefore Vedic study, was restricted in the law books to boys of the three upper varṇas; Śūdras were forbidden even to hear the Veda, and women’s initiation, if it ever existed, had disappeared by the time of the Dharma Sūtras. In practice Vedic learning became concentrated in Brahmin families. In recent times some institutions have opened Vedic instruction to girls and to students of all backgrounds, a change that remains contested within the tradition (Figure 11.1).

Figure 11.1. The cycle of Vedic education in the teacher–pupil lineage.

docs.title: 11.3 The Pāṭha System: Methods of Recitation
docs.text: The best-known technique of Vedic preservation is the system of recitation methods (pāṭhas), in which the words of a text are recited in different orders and combinations.

docs.title: 11.3.1 The Natural Recitations (Prakṛtipāṭhas)
docs.text:
1. Saṃhitā pāṭha — the continuous text, with the sound changes (sandhi) between words applied.

  2. Pada pāṭha — the text word by word, with sandhi undone and compounds divided; for the Ṛgveda this analysis is ascribed to Śākalya. It amounts to a grammatical analysis of the whole text.

  3. Krama pāṭha — consecutive pairs of words: 1–2, 2–3, 3–4, and so on.

docs.title: 11.3.2 The Modified Recitations (Vikṛtipāṭhas)
docs.text:
Eight more complex “modified” recitations are traditionally listed: jaṭā, mālā, śikhā, rekhā, dhvaja, daṇḍa, ratha and ghana. The best known are:

  • Jaṭā (“braid”): 1–2, 2–1, 1–2; 2–3, 3–2, 2–3; …

  • Śikhā (“crest”): 1–2, 2–1, 1–2–3; 2–3, 3–2, 2–3–4; …

  • Ghana (“dense”): 1–2, 2–1, 1–2–3, 3–2–1, 1–2–3; 2–3, 3–2, 2–3–4, 4–3–2, 2–3–4; …

The other patterns vary in detail between traditions. Few reciters today master the full set; a reciter who has learnt the ghana of a Veda is honoured with the title ghanapāṭhin (Figure 11.2).

Figure 11.2. The pāṭha system: from the continuous text to the ghana recitation.

Note: Why the Pāṭhas Work

Each recitation preserves the same words in a different arrangement. The word-by-word text fixes the form of every word; the pair-wise and braided recitations fix their order and the sandhi between them; and because the sandhi must be applied anew in each arrangement, an error introduced in one would clash with the others. Modern writers sometimes compare this redundancy with error-detecting methods in information technology. The comparison is a useful analogy for the principle of cross-checking, but the pāṭhas are a memory discipline, not a mathematical theory of codes.

docs.title: 11.4 The Accent (Svara)
docs.text:
Every syllable of the Ṛgveda, and of most other Vedic texts, carries an inherited pitch accent, and reciters preserve it exactly. The tradition distinguishes three accents (Table 11.1):

Table 11.1. The three Vedic accents (svaras). Svara Pitch Description Udātta Raised The accented syllable of a word Anudātta Not raised Low syllables, especially the one preceding an udātta Svarita Falling The tone that follows an udātta

In Ṛgveda manuscripts the anudātta is marked by a line beneath the syllable and the svarita by a vertical stroke above, while the udātta is left unmarked (Figure 2.2 shows these marks in red); other schools use other systems. Western editions write the udātta with an acute accent instead. The first verse of the Ṛgveda, in its continuous (saṃhitā) and word-by-word (pada) forms, then reads:

Saṃhitā: agním īḷe puróhitaṃ yajñásya devám ṛtvíjam hótāraṃ ratnadh\(\acute{\bar{ a}}\)tamam Pada: agnim īḷe puraḥ-hitam yajñasya devam ṛtvijam hotāram ratna-dhātamam (accents not shown)

Each acute marks the raised syllable of a word; the syllable that follows it is the falling svarita, and unaccented syllables are in principle low. The verb īḷe, “I praise”, has no accent, as finite verbs in a main clause normally have none. In the pada text the compounds purohita and ratnadhātama are divided into their members, and the sandhi of the continuous text is undone. In recitation the accents are accompanied by hand and head movements that help the reciter keep them correct. The Vedic accent is also of great importance for historical linguistics, since it continues the accent of Proto-Indo-European.

docs.title: 11.5 The Vedic Pāṭhaśālās
docs.text: Vedic schools (pāṭhaśālās) continue to operate across India, though their number is small and many struggle for support. A typical day includes early-morning recitation; the learning of new material, in which the teacher recites a passage and the pupils repeat it many times; revision of earlier lessons; group recitation; individual testing by the teacher; and evening revision.

docs.title: 11.6 Why Were the Vedas Not Written Down?
docs.text:
Several reasons combined:

  1. Historical: the Vedic texts were composed before writing was in use in India, and their schools developed oral methods that worked.

  2. The primacy of sound: the power of a mantra was thought to lie in its exact pronunciation, including accent and quantity, which early scripts did not record well.

  3. Control of sacred knowledge: oral teaching kept the Veda within initiated lineages. Later texts condemn those who sell or write the Veda.

  4. The teacher–pupil relationship: learning was understood as a personal transmission, not merely a transfer of information.

docs.title: 11.7 The Transition to Writing
docs.text: The Vedas were eventually written down, though when this began is uncertain. Because of the Indian climate, the oldest surviving Vedic manuscripts date only from about the eleventh century CE, though copying certainly began earlier. Even after the adoption of writing, oral instruction remained primary, and manuscripts were aids to it.

docs.title: 11.8 Modern Preservation Efforts
docs.text:
• Government support: the Maharshi Sandipani Rashtriya Veda Vidya Pratishthan (Ujjain) and state bodies support Vedic schools and teachers.

  • Recording: systematic audio and video recording of master reciters by research institutes and private foundations.

  • UNESCO recognition: since 2003/2008, as noted above.

  • Digital editions: searchable digital texts of most Vedic works are now available.

  • Religious institutions: maṭhas, temples and trusts support Vedic education.

docs.title: 11.9 Memory and the Brain
docs.text:
How do reciters memorise so much so accurately? The answer lies partly in the methods themselves, which use well-known principles of memory:

Principles at Work in Vedic Memorisation

  1. Multi-sensory learning: hearing, speaking, accent and hand movements combine;

  2. Repetition spaced over years: daily revision of everything learnt;

  3. Elaboration: the pāṭhas force the learner to process each word in many contexts;

  4. Early and intensive training: learning begins in childhood and fills most of the day;

  5. Social checking: group recitation and the teacher’s correction catch errors.

Scholarly Note: A Brain-Imaging Study of Vedic Reciters

Hartzell and colleagues compared magnetic resonance images of the brains of 21 professional reciters (paṇḍits) trained in the White Yajurveda with those of matched controls (Hartzell et al. 2016). The reciters showed greater grey-matter density and cortical thickness in several regions associated with language and memory, including parts of the right temporal lobe and the hippocampus. Because the study compares two groups at one point in time, it cannot by itself show that recitation caused the differences, but it is consistent with the view that long, intensive memory training shapes brain structure.

docs.title: 11.10 Summary
docs.text:
The Vedic oral tradition shows that a large literature can be preserved, with its sounds and accents, for three thousand years without depending on writing, provided that a society is willing to invest in it: in the years of training each reciter receives, in methods such as the pāṭhas that make errors detectable, and in the families and patrons who sustain the schools. The same investment explains the tradition’s limits. Because it was confined to initiated men of particular families, it preserved the text with great fidelity but kept it from most of the society around it; its future now depends both on continued support and on wider access.

Closing Invocation

svādhyāyān mā pramadaḥ ācāryāya priyaṃ dhanam āhṛtya prajātantuṃ mā vyavacchetsīḥ Do not neglect your daily recitation. Having brought your teacher the gift he desires, do not cut off the line of offspring. — Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.1

docs.title: Chapter 12: The Vedic Schools: Geography, History and Survival
docs.text:
Invocatory Passage

ekaśatam adhvaryuśākhāḥ sahasravartmā sāmavedaḥ ekaviṃśatidhā bāhvṛcyaṃ navadhātharvaṇo vedaḥ The Adhvaryu [Veda] has a hundred and one branches, the Sāmaveda a thousand paths; the Veda of the Bahvṛcas is twenty-one-fold, the Atharvan Veda ninefold. — Patañjali, Mahābhāṣya, introduction (Paspaśāhnika)

docs.title: 12.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The Veda has never existed as a single book. It has always been transmitted by schools, each preserving its own version of a Saṃhitā together with its own Brāhmaṇa, ritual manuals and rules of recitation. Patañjali’s figures, quoted above, are the classical statement of their number; they are conventional rather than historical, and they contrast sharply with the number of schools whose texts survive (Table 12.1).

Table 12.1. Traditional and extant Śākhās of the four Vedas. Veda Traditional Number Schools whose Saṃhitā Survives Ṛgveda 21 Śākala (complete); other schools, such as Bāṣkala, Āśvalāyana and Śāṅkhāyana, are known from ancillary texts and minor variants Yajurveda 101 White: Mādhyandina and Kāṇva (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā); Black: Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, Kaṭha, and Kapiṣṭhala (fragmentary) Sāmaveda 1,000 Kauthuma, Rāṇāyanīya, Jaiminīya Atharvaveda 9 Śaunaka, Paippalāda

The loss of most schools is a real impoverishment: each lost śākhā carried not merely a textual variant but a tradition of interpretation and ritual practice, of which fragments survive only as quotations in other texts. This chapter looks at the schools themselves: what a school was, where the different texts were composed, how the schools moved across the subcontinent and were supported by patrons, which of them survive today and in what condition, and how their manuscripts became the printed editions on which modern study depends. The method of oral transmission within the schools is the subject of Chapter 11, and the education of their pupils is treated in Volume 22, Manas and Śikṣā.

docs.title: 12.2 Śākhā and Caraṇa
docs.text:
Two terms are used for the Vedic schools. A śākhā (“branch”) is a recension: a particular version of a Veda as handed down in one line of transmission. A caraṇa (“course, conduct”) is the community that follows that line, studying its texts and performing its rites. The two words are often used interchangeably. Most schools take their names from a founding teacher—the Śākala school from Śākalya, the Kaṭhas from Kaṭha, the Taittirīyas, according to legend, from the partridges (tittiri) of Section 3.3—and Pāṇini’s grammar already contains rules for forming the names of such schools and of the texts “proclaimed” by their founders. A remark of Patañjali, that the Kāṭhaka and Kālāpaka texts are recited “in every village” (on Pāṇini 4.3.101), suggests how prominent some schools, now lost or nearly lost, once were.

A school’s identity was defined by its texts. The Caraṇavyūha, a late supplementary text attributed to Śaunaka, lists the schools of each Veda; the Brāhmaṇas and Upaniṣads end their sections with genealogies (vaṃśa) of teachers through whom the text was handed down, such as those of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (2.6, 4.6, 6.5), and the Sāmaveda has a whole Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa of this kind. Although some of the earliest names in these lists are mythical, the lists show that the schools thought of themselves as lineages of teachers and pupils. Louis Renou’s study of the Vedic schools remains the classic account of how such lineages shaped the formation of the texts (Renou 1947).

A Brahmin traditionally belongs to one Veda and one school, and is expected to study the texts of his own branch (svaśākhā) and to perform his rites by its sūtra. This affiliation is still part of a Brahmin’s formal identity: in the traditional formula of respectful greeting (abhivādana) he names his lineage (gotra) and its ancestral seers (pravara), his sūtra and his śākhā, before his own name. Affiliation to a śākhā was hereditary; it was not a matter of choice, although families sometimes adopted a locally dominant school after migrating.

docs.title: 12.3 Where the Texts Were Composed
docs.text:
The Vedic texts rarely say where they were composed, but they contain much indirect evidence: the rivers, mountains and peoples they mention, the plants and animals they know, and the features of their language. Michael Witzel has used such evidence systematically to locate the texts and schools, building on earlier work by Albrecht Weber, Hermann Oldenberg and Willem Caland (Witzel 1987, 1989, 1997). The result is a picture of movement from the north-west towards the east, and later to the south (Table 12.2). The picture is a reconstruction; individual localisations are debated, and texts often contain material of different origins.

Table 12.2. The approximate homes of the main Vedic texts and schools (after Witzel; simplified, and in part disputed). Period Region Texts and schools Ṛgvedic Greater Panjab, from the Kabul river to the Yamunā Ṛgveda, especially the family books Mantra period Kurukṣetra and the upper Ganga–Yamunā Doab (Kuru) Atharvaveda; the mantras of the Sāmaveda and Yajurveda; final arrangement of the Ṛgveda Early prose Kuru country and the north-west Maitrāyaṇī, Kāṭhaka and Kapiṣṭhala Saṃhitās Later prose Pañcāla (central and lower Doab) Taittirīya Saṃhitā and Brāhmaṇa; parts of other Brāhmaṇas Late Brāhmaṇa and early Upaniṣad Kosala and Videha (east of the Ganga–Yamunā region) Yājñavalkya’s books of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Sūtra period Spreading south and west Āpastamba, Hiraṇyakeśin and other later Taittirīya sūtras in the south; Mānava and Vārāha in the west

The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa itself contains two strata of this kind. Its books on the fire altar (6–10) are associated with the teacher Śāṇḍilya and with the western, Kuru region, while the books dominated by Yājñavalkya reflect the eastern court of King Janaka of Videha. The same text preserves a story of the eastward spread of the sacrificial fire, the legend of Videgha Māthava (ŚB 1.4.1), discussed in Section 14.3. Figure 12.1 shows some of the places and regions named in this volume.

Figure 12.1. Some places named in this volume: Harappan sites (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Rākhigṛhī); sites of the Painted Grey Ware and early historic periods in the Kuru–Pañcāla country and the Ganga plain; and Nāneghāṭ, the site of Nāyanikā’s inscription. Points are plotted by latitude and longitude; Janakpur is shown for Mithilā, the capital of Videha, by tradition only. The names in small capitals mark the regions of the later Vedic texts, and their positions are approximate (Table 12.2). The coastline is simplified, rivers are not drawn, and no political boundaries are shown.

Dialect features point in the same direction. In a well-known passage the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (3.2.1.23–24) says that the demons (asuras) were defeated because they mispronounced their battle cry, saying he ’lavo instead of he ’rayo (“O enemies”), and it concludes that a Brahmin should not speak barbarously (na brāhmaṇo mlecchet). Replacing r by l is characteristic of the eastern dialects that later became Māgadhī Prakrit, and the story shows western ritualists’ awareness of eastern speech. The Sūtra period saw the Taittirīya schools established in the south: Georg Bühler argued from the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra that the Āpastamba school originated in the Andhra region, and the later Taittirīya sūtras are all associated with the south and west of India.

docs.title: 12.4 The Schools in History
docs.text:
From the early centuries CE onwards the history of the schools can be followed in inscriptions. Kings and landholders granted villages and land to Brahmins, and the copper-plate charters recording these grants commonly identify the recipients by their gotra and their Vedic affiliation—as Bahvṛcas (Ṛgvedins), Chandogas (Sāmavedins), Taittirīyas, Vājasaneyins, Kāṇvas and so on. Such grants, and the settlements of learned Brahmins (agrahāra, brahmadeya) they created, show the schools spreading with royal patronage into central and southern India, Bengal and Odisha, and they make it possible to trace the distribution of particular schools region by region. Family and caste traditions in several regions remember a migration of Brahmins from the north at a king’s invitation; whatever their historical value in detail, these traditions reflect the real movement of Vedic schools into new territories.

Some schools prospered in particular places and vanished elsewhere. The Kaṭha school, whose texts Patañjali describes as recited everywhere, survived longest in Kashmir; its Saṃhitā and Āraṇyaka are known from Kashmiri manuscripts, and Kashmiri Brahmins have continued to follow the Kāṭhaka Gṛhyasūtra in their domestic rites long after the recitation of the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā had ceased (Witzel 1987). The Paippalāda Atharvaveda, known in the nineteenth century from a single Kashmiri birch-bark manuscript, was found in the 1950s to survive in Odisha (Section 5.3). Nepal, where the White Yajurveda predominates, preserved in its libraries many manuscripts of Vedic and ritual texts that had been lost in India.

The schools were sustained by an economy of patronage. A school survived where there were families willing to devote sons to years of memorisation, and patrons—kings, temples, monasteries (maṭha) and landholders—who supported them. Where patronage failed, as it did in many regions with political change and, in the colonial and modern periods, with new forms of education and employment, schools contracted or disappeared. The history of the śākhās is therefore also an economic and social history.

docs.title: 12.5 The Living Schools Today
docs.text:
Of the more than a thousand schools of the traditional count, the recited texts of about a dozen survive, in very unequal health (Table 12.3). The information in the table is approximate: the number of fully trained reciters of each school has never been systematically counted, and it changes from generation to generation.

Table 12.3. Surviving recitation traditions and their main regions (approximate). Veda School (and sūtra) Main regions and condition Ṛgveda Śākala (Āśvalāyana) Widespread: Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Kerala Śākala (Śāṅkhāyana, Kauṣītaki) Small groups, notably among the Nambūdiris of Kerala Black Yajurveda Taittirīya (Āpastamba, Baudhāyana, Hiraṇyakeśin and others) The most widely recited school of South India; also Maharashtra Maitrāyaṇīya A few families in Maharashtra and Gujarat; endangered Kaṭha, Kapiṣṭhala No longer recited; texts in manuscripts White Yajurveda Mādhyandina North and central India, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Nepal Kāṇva Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Odisha Sāmaveda Kauthuma Gujarat, North India, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh Rāṇāyanīya Maharashtra and Karnataka Jaiminīya Nambūdiris of Kerala and a few families in Tamil Nadu; endangered Atharvaveda Śaunaka Recitation revived in modern times, mainly in Gujarat and Maharashtra Paippalāda A few Brahmin families in Odisha; endangered

The Nambūdiri Brahmins of Kerala deserve special mention. Isolated for centuries from the rest of India, they preserve distinctive schools—the Kauṣītaki tradition of the Ṛgveda, the Baudhāyana and Vādhūla traditions of the Taittirīya, the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda—as well as distinctive styles of recitation accompanied by hand movements, which Frits Staal described in detail (Staal 1961). Their śrauta tradition, documented in the Agnicayana of 1975, is described in Section 8.10. Tamil Nadu has the largest concentration of Taittirīya reciters and preserves both Kauthuma and Jaiminīya chant; Wayne Howard’s study of Sāmavedic chant draws on traditions of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and elsewhere (Howard 1977). Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh have strong traditions of Ṛgveda and Taittirīya recitation and of the complex vikṛti patterns (Section 11.3); Gujarat and North India are the home of the Mādhyandina and Kauthuma schools, and Varanasi has long been a meeting place of reciters from all regions.

Several schools are seriously endangered: the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda, the Maitrāyaṇīya Yajurveda, the Paippalāda Atharvaveda and some of the smaller sūtra traditions depend on a handful of teachers. The forms of support on which they now rely, and the questions of access that their future raises, are discussed in Sections 11.8 and 15.10.

docs.title: 12.6 The Ancillary Literature of the Schools
docs.text:
Besides their Saṃhitās, Brāhmaṇas and sūtras, the schools produced a body of auxiliary texts that were needed to teach, recite and use the Veda correctly. The phonetic manuals (Prātiśākhya and Śikṣā) of each school are described in Section 7.2 and Chapter 11; the supplementary hymns (khila) transmitted with the Ṛgveda in Section 2.7. Several other kinds of text deserve mention.

Indexes.

The anukramaṇīs are systematic indexes of a Saṃhitā. For the Ṛgveda, a series of separate indexes of seers, metres and deities is attributed to Śaunaka, and the Sarvānukramaṇī ascribed to Kātyāyana combines them, giving for every hymn its first words, the number of its verses, its seer, its deity and its metre; the medieval commentary on it by Ṣaḍguruśiṣya adds much traditional lore. These indexes are the source of the ascriptions of hymns to seers discussed in Section 1.5, and they also served as a check on the integrity of the text, since a reciter or copyist could compare his text with the counts they give.

Legends and deities.

The Bṛhaddevatā, a long verse treatise also attributed to Śaunaka, discusses the deities of the Ṛgvedic hymns and tells many of the stories (ākhyāna) that were believed to lie behind them, such as the dialogue hymns of Section 2.10. A. A. Macdonell’s edition and translation remains standard (Macdonell 1904). The work shows how the schools explained the hymns to themselves in the period between the Brāhmaṇas and the medieval commentaries.

Practical use of the hymns.

The Ṛgvidhāna prescribes the recitation of particular Ṛgvedic verses and hymns, with fasting, offerings and other observances, to obtain specific ends—health, prosperity, protection, the removal of sin—and the Sāmavidhāna Brāhmaṇa does the same for the chants of the Sāmaveda. These texts are the Ṛgvedic and Sāmavedic counterparts of the Kauśika Sūtra (Section 9.7), and they show that the hymns were used outside the great rites, by individuals for their own purposes, much as Vedic mantras are used in later devotional and Tantric practice.

Supplements.

Many schools accumulated supplementary texts (pariśiṣṭa) on matters not covered by their main sūtras. The largest collection is the Atharvaveda Pariśiṣṭas, some seventy short texts on omens and portents, astrology, royal ceremonies, gifts and expiations, which reflect the role of Atharvavedic priests as advisers to kings. The Caraṇavyūha, the list of schools mentioned above, is itself such a supplement, as are the lists of lineages and their ancestral seers (pravara) appended to several Śrautasūtras, on which rules of exogamous marriage were later based.

Together these works show the schools as active centres of learning, not merely of memorisation. They also bridge the Vedic and the later literature: their style, their interest in legends and their practical, individual use of mantras point forward to the Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras and the ritual handbooks of later centuries.

docs.title: 12.7.1 Manuscripts and Commentaries
docs.text:
Vedic manuscripts were made by and for the schools, as aids to teaching and to ritual practice (Section 1.9). They record not only the continuous text but also the word-by-word pada text and, in some schools, the krama text, with the accents marked by lines or numerals above and below the syllables; the song-books of the Sāmaveda carry their own notation. Each region wrote them in its own script—Śāradā in Kashmir, Newari and Devanāgarī in Nepal and the north, Grantha and Malayalam in the south, Odia in Odisha—so that the manuscript record itself maps the distribution of the schools.

The great medieval commentaries also grew out of the schools and their patrons. The most ambitious was the project associated with Sāyaṇa and his brother Mādhava at the court of the Vijayanagara kings Bukka I and Harihara II in the fourteenth century, which produced commentaries on the Saṃhitās and many Brāhmaṇas and Āraṇyakas (Section 2.12). Cezary Galewicz has shown that this was a collective enterprise of a team of scholars and a deliberate act of royal patronage, intended to establish an authoritative interpretation of the whole Veda for the new empire (Galewicz 2009).

docs.title: 12.7.2 The First Printed Editions
docs.text:
European knowledge of the Vedas began with manuscripts collected in India in the late eighteenth century. H. T. Colebrooke’s essay “On the Vedas” (1805), based on manuscripts he had acquired in Bengal and Varanasi, gave the first reliable account of the contents of the corpus. The first printed Vedic texts followed in the next decades: Friedrich Rosen’s edition of the first book of the Ṛgveda (1838), Theodor Benfey’s Sāmaveda (1848) and Albrecht Weber’s Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (1852) and Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1855). Max Müller’s edition of the Ṛgveda with Sāyaṇa’s commentary, printed in six volumes between 1849 and 1874 with the support of the East India Company, was the foundation of modern Ṛgvedic studies; Müller, who never visited India, based it on manuscripts in European libraries. The Atharvaveda was edited by Rudolf Roth and William Dwight Whitney (1856), the Taittirīya Saṃhitā by Weber (1871–72), and the Maitrāyaṇī and Kāṭhaka Saṃhitās by Leopold von Schroeder (1881–86 and 1900–10).

Indian editors played a growing part. In Kolkata the Bibliotheca Indica series of the Asiatic Society published Vedic texts with Sāyaṇa’s commentaries, among them the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka edited by Rājendralāla Mitra and the Sāmaveda edited by Satyavrata Sāmaśramī. From the 1860s the government-sponsored searches for Sanskrit manuscripts in the Bombay Presidency, conducted by Georg Bühler, Franz Kielhorn, R. G. Bhandarkar and others, assembled the collection that passed to the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune; its Ṛgveda manuscripts are now on UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register. The Ānandāśrama series of Pune (from 1888) printed many ritual and Vedic texts from Maharashtra manuscripts. The critical edition of the Ṛgveda with Sāyaṇa’s commentary by the Vaidika Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala of Pune (1933–51) and the editions of S. D. Sātavalekar’s Svādhyāya Maṇḍala made the texts widely available in India.

docs.title: 12.7.3 Tools and New Editions
docs.text:
Two reference works transformed the study of the corpus. Maurice Bloomfield’s Vedic Concordance (1906) lists every mantra of the Vedic literature alphabetically with all the places where it occurs, making it possible to see how the same verse is used and varied across schools (Bloomfield 1906); and the Vaidika Padānukrama Koṣa, a concordance of Vedic words begun under Vishva Bandhu in Lahore in the 1930s and completed at the Vishveshvaranand Vedic Research Institute in Hoshiarpur after Partition, does the same for individual words. Work on the less-known schools continues: critical editions of the Paippalāda Atharvaveda based on the Odia manuscripts (Griffiths 2009), of the Kaṭha Āraṇyaka from Kashmiri manuscripts (Witzel 2004), and of several sūtras. Electronic texts of almost the entire corpus are now freely available through projects such as TITUS (Frankfurt) and GRETIL (Göttingen), which have made searching the whole Vedic literature a matter of seconds.

The history of the editions is not merely technical. Printed books standardised texts that had existed in regional and school variants; they made the Veda available to readers outside the schools, including women and non-Brahmins, for the first time; and they shifted authority, at least for scholars, from the living reciter to the printed page. Modern editors increasingly treat the reciters themselves as witnesses to the text alongside the manuscripts, a recognition that the oral and written traditions of the schools have always depended on each other.

docs.title: 12.8 Summary
docs.text: To ask where the Veda is preserved is to ask about the schools, because there has never been a Veda apart from them. Their history is one of movement and of patronage: of texts composed in a sequence of regions from the Panjab to Videha, of lineages carried south and east with royal grants, and of recitation traditions that survived where families and patrons could support years of training and vanished where they could not. That history also explains the present position, in which a dozen schools survive in very unequal health, and in which the printed and digital editions that serve scholars rest, in the end, on manuscripts and reciters that only the schools produced.

docs.title: Chapter 13: The Vedic Worldview: Cosmology, Ṛta, Dharma, and the Devas
docs.text:
Invocatory Verse

iyaṃ visṛṣṭir yata ābabhūva yadi vā dadhe yadi vā na yo asyādhyakṣaḥ parame vyoman so aṅga veda yadi vā na veda Where this creation came from—whether it was made or not— he who watches over it in the highest heaven surely knows; or perhaps he does not know. — Ṛgveda 10.129.7

docs.title: 13.1 Introduction
docs.text: The Vedic texts do not present a single, systematic worldview. They span a millennium and many schools, from the hymns of the Ṛgveda, through the ritual theology of the Brāhmaṇas, to the speculations of the early Upaniṣads. Certain ideas, however, recur and develop across this literature: a world ordered by ṛta; gods who uphold that order and are sustained by sacrifice; a cosmos of three worlds; repeated attempts to imagine how the world began; and, increasingly, the search for a single principle behind the many. This chapter surveys these ideas, which shaped much of later Indian thought.

docs.title: 13.2 Vedic Cosmogony: The Origin of the World
docs.text:
The Vedas offer not one account of creation but several, often side by side. They are best read as different images for an acknowledged mystery rather than as competing doctrines (Figure 13.1).

Figure 13.1. Some cosmogonic images in Vedic literature.

docs.title: 13.2.1 The Nāsadīya Sūkta
docs.text: The Nāsadīya Sūkta (RV 10.129) imagines a beginning before the distinction of being (sat) and non-being (asat), when “That One” breathed without wind, enveloped in darkness. It came into being through heat (tapas); desire (kāma) arose as the first seed of mind; and the poets, searching in their hearts, found the bond of being in non-being. The hymn ends in doubt: the gods are later than creation, and perhaps even the overseer in the highest heaven does not know how it arose (the final verse is quoted at the head of this chapter; the opening verse in Section 2.5).

docs.title: 13.2.2 The Hiraṇyagarbha and Viśvakarman Hymns
docs.text: RV 10.121 describes a Golden Embryo that arose in the beginning, became the lord of all that exists, and established earth and sky. RV 10.81–82 imagine the god Viśvakarman (“All-Maker”) as a craftsman, asking from what wood and what tree he fashioned heaven and earth.

docs.title: 13.2.3 The Puruṣa Sūkta
docs.text: RV 10.90 describes the world as produced from the sacrifice of a cosmic Man, a quarter of whom is all beings while three quarters are immortal in heaven. From his mind came the moon, from his eye the sun, from his breath the wind; and from his mouth, arms, thighs and feet the four social classes (Section 2.5.3). This hymn joins cosmogony to a theory of social hierarchy, a combination of lasting consequence.

docs.title: 13.2.4 Prajāpati
docs.text: In the Brāhmaṇas the creator Prajāpati produces the world by heating himself with tapas and “emitting” creatures, and is then restored through the sacrifice (Chapter 6). In the early Upaniṣads these images give way to the idea of a single self or Brahman from which all things proceed (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4; Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2).

docs.title: 13.3 Ṛta: Cosmic Order
docs.text:
Ṛta, usually derived from the root ṛ, “to fit, to go”, denotes the order of the world: what is fitting and true. It works at several levels:

  1. Cosmic: the regular rising of the sun and of the dawns, the course of the seasons, the flowing of rivers.

  2. Ritual: the correct performance of the sacrifice, which supports the cosmic order.

  3. Moral: truthfulness and the keeping of agreements.

The Path of Ṛta

ṛtasya panthām anv eti sādhu prajānatīva na diśo mināti She follows straight the path of ṛta; like one who knows the way, she does not stray from the directions. — Ṛgveda 1.124.3 (of Dawn)

Ṛta is guarded above all by Varuṇa and Mitra, the gods of oath and contract. Its opposite, anṛta, is falsehood and disorder. The concept has an exact Avestan counterpart, aša, so it goes back to the common Indo-Iranian period (Figure 13.2). Varuṇa watches human conduct through his spies (spaś), and his punishment for wrongdoing is the theme of some of the most personal hymns of the Ṛgveda, in which the poet Vasiṣṭha asks what offence he has committed (RV 7.86–89). Table 13.1 gives some key passages on ṛta and truth (satya) across the Vedic literature.

Table 13.1. Some key passages on ṛta and satya. Text Reference Content Ṛgveda 1.1.8 Agni as “guardian of ṛta” (gopām ṛtasya) Ṛgveda 10.190.1 Ṛta and satya born from kindled heat (tapas) Atharvaveda 12.1.1 Truth, ṛta, consecration, tapas, brahman and sacrifice “uphold the earth” Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.1.1.4 “The gods are truth, men are untruth”: the sacrificer takes a vow of truth Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.14 Dharma is identified with truth (satya) Figure 13.2. Ṛta and related Vedic concepts.

docs.title: 13.4 From Ṛta to Dharma
docs.text: The word dharman (from dhṛ, “to hold, support”) already occurs in the Ṛgveda, meaning “foundation” or “ordinance”. In later Vedic and post-Vedic thought, dharma gradually replaces ṛta as the key term for order. Its meaning widens to include the duties proper to each social class and stage of life (varṇāśramadharma), religious law, and righteousness in general. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (1.4.14) describes dharma as a power higher even than royal power, “through which a weak man prevails over a strong one, as with the help of a king”, and identifies it with truth: “what is dharma is truth” (yo vai sa dharmaḥ satyaṃ vai tat). In the Dharma Sūtras and Śāstras it becomes the framework of a hierarchical social and legal order; Buddhists and Jains, meanwhile, used the same word for the teaching of the Buddha or the Jina.

docs.title: 13.5 The Nature of the Devas
docs.text: The Vedic gods (devas, “heavenly ones”) are powerful beings, many of them closely linked with natural phenomena (fire, sun, dawn, wind, storm), others with social functions (Mitra with contract, Aryaman with hospitality and marriage) or with the ritual (Soma, Bṛhaspati). They are invited to the sacrifice, praised, given offerings, and asked for wealth, offspring, victory and protection.

docs.title: 13.5.1 The Three Worlds
docs.text:
The Ṛgvedic universe consists of three worlds: earth (pṛthivī), the intermediate space (antarikṣa) and heaven (dyu). Yāska later classified the gods according to these three realms (Section 2.17); Figure 13.3 follows the simpler modern grouping of Macdonell, which differs from Yāska’s lists in some details.

Figure 13.3. The three worlds of the Vedic cosmos and some of their gods, grouped after Macdonell’s Vedic Mythology.

docs.title: 13.5.2 One and Many
docs.text: Beyond the habit of praising whichever god is addressed as supreme, which Max Müller called “henotheism” (Section 2.17), a few late hymns go further and speak of the many gods as names of one being (ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti, RV 1.164.46) or of a single creator. Later Indian thinkers read these passages as the seed of Vedāntic monism or of monotheism; historians emphasise that they are exceptional within the Vedic corpus as a whole.

docs.title: 13.5.3 Devas and Asuras
docs.text:
The later opposition between gods (devas) and demons (asuras) is not found in the oldest hymns. In the family books asura is a title of honour, meaning something like “lord” or “one possessing mysterious power”, and it is given above all to Varuṇa and Mitra, but also to Agni, Indra, Dyaus and other gods. Its Avestan cognate ahura became the name of the supreme god of Zoroastrianism, Ahura Mazdā, while the Avestan daēvas, cognate with the Vedic devas, became demons (Table 1.3). In the later books of the Ṛgveda and in the Atharvaveda the word increasingly designates the enemies of the gods, and in the Brāhmaṇas the contest between the gods and the Asuras, “both offspring of Prajāpati” (BU 1.3.1), is the frame of countless explanatory stories (Section 6.4). Wash Edward Hale’s study of the word traced this shift and argued that in the oldest hymns asura is a title, “lord”, given to gods and occasionally to men, not the name of a separate class of beings (Hale 1986).

The reasons for the reversal in each tradition are debated. Older scholars imagined a religious schism between proto-Indians and proto-Iranians, each demonising the other’s gods; most scholars now regard that as too simple, and see the change in India as a gradual narrowing of the term within Vedic usage. The outcome had a long future. The serpent Vṛtra’s mother is Dānu (RV 1.32.9), and her descendants, the Dānavas, together with the Daityas, the sons of Diti, form the Asura armies of the epics and Purāṇas, the opponents of the gods in the churning of the ocean and many other myths (Volume 7, Itihāsa–Purāṇa). The Purāṇas also preserve, in figures such as the virtuous Asura kings Prahlāda and Bali, a memory that the Asuras could be wise, generous and devout.

docs.title: 13.6.1 Ātman and Brahman
docs.text: In the Ṛgveda, ātman means “breath” or “self”, and brahman means a sacred formulation and the power inherent in it. In the Brāhmaṇas and especially the early Upaniṣads, these words become the central terms of philosophy: ātman the innermost self of a person, brahman the ultimate reality. Several Upaniṣadic passages identify the two; schools of Vedānta later interpreted this identity in different ways, from strict non-dualism (Advaita) to qualified non-dualism and dualism.

docs.title: 13.6.2 Tapas
docs.text: Tapas (“heat”) is both the cosmic energy through which the world arises and the inner heat generated by ascetic effort. In the Nāsadīya Sūkta the first being comes into existence through it (tapasas tan mahinājāyataikam, “That One was born by the power of heat”, RV 10.129.3), and in RV 10.190.1 ṛta and satya are born “from kindled heat” (abhīddhāt tapaso ’dhy ajāyata). In the Brāhmaṇas the creator Prajāpati repeatedly “heats himself” before each act of creation, and the sacrificer undergoes austerities during his consecration (dīkṣā). The double meaning of the word links cosmogony and ritual with the ascetic practices that became central in later Indian religion.

docs.title: 13.6.3 Kāma
docs.text: In RV 10.129.4 desire (kāma) is the first seed of mind, the impulse that begins creation. The idea of desire as a creative and binding force recurs in the Upaniṣads and in later philosophy.

docs.title: 13.6.4 Yajña
docs.text: In Vedic thought the sacrifice is an exchange: offerings nourish the gods, who in turn grant rain, cattle, offspring and prosperity. The Brāhmaṇas extend this into the idea that the sacrifice sustains the cosmos, and the Bhagavadgītā (3.10–16) later describes a “wheel” of sacrifice linking gods, rain, food and human beings.

docs.title: 13.7 Death and the Afterlife
docs.text:
The funeral hymns of the Ṛgveda (10.14–18) give the earliest Indian picture of death. Yama, the first mortal to die, found the path to the world beyond and became king of the dead; the deceased goes along this path to join Yama and the “Fathers” (pitṛs) in the highest heaven, where they enjoy food and drink offered by their descendants. Both cremation, in which Agni carries the dead to the Fathers (RV 10.16), and burial, in which the Earth is asked to cover the dead gently “as a mother covers her son with her skirt” (RV 10.18.11), are attested. The living maintain the dead through offerings, a practice that continues in the later śrāddha rites.

The Ṛgveda has no clear doctrine of rebirth. In the Brāhmaṇas a new fear appears, of “re-death” (punarmṛtyu) in the other world, which correct ritual knowledge can avert. The doctrine of rebirth according to one’s actions (karma) and of release from the cycle first appears clearly in the early Upaniṣads: in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, Yājñavalkya teaches that “as one acts, so one becomes” (BU 4.4.5), and the “doctrine of the five fires” with its two paths of the dead (BU 6.2; ChU 5.3–10) is presented as a teaching of Kṣatriya kings, previously unknown to Brahmins. Whether these ideas grew out of Vedic ritual thought, came from other religious milieus of the eastern Ganga plain, or both, is debated. Either way, the idea of rebirth and liberation, which was to dominate later Hindu, Buddhist and Jain thought, takes shape at the very end of the Vedic period.

docs.title: 13.8 Time
docs.text: Vedic texts measure time by days and nights, the phases of the moon, the seasons and the year, and the ritual calendar follows these cycles. The great cosmic cycles of four ages (yugas) of declining virtue, and of aeons (kalpas) of creation and dissolution, are not Vedic: they are developed in the epics and Purāṇas. In Vedic texts yuga means a generation or, in the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, a five-year cycle, while the names kṛta, tretā, dvāpara and kali are those of throws in the game of dice.

docs.title: 13.9 Correspondences and Interconnection
docs.text:
A characteristic feature of Vedic thought, especially from the Brāhmaṇas onwards, is the search for correspondences (bandhus) between the cosmos, the ritual and the human person. The Upaniṣads describe these as relations between the “divine” (adhidaivata) and the “bodily” (adhyātma) domains (Table 13.2).

Table 13.2. Some recurring cosmic–bodily correspondences in Vedic texts. Cosmic Bodily Example of Source Sun Eye RV 10.90.13 (the sun born from the eye of Puruṣa) Moon Mind RV 10.90.13 (the moon born from his mind) Wind Breath RV 10.90.13; Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.2.4 Fire Speech Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.2.4 (“Fire became speech and entered the mouth”) Waters Semen Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.2.4 Quarters of space Ears Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.2.4

These correspondences imply that the person is a small-scale image of the cosmos, and that to know oneself is in some sense to know the world. The Upaniṣads carry this to the conclusion that the inner self and the ground of the world are one.

The ritual ground was read in the same way, as a model of the universe. The three sacred fires were correlated with earth, the intermediate space and heaven; the five layers of the Agnicayana altar with the seasons and other fivefold groups; and the numbers of its bricks and enclosing stones with the days, nights and divisions of the year (Staal 1983). The altar and its geometry are described in Section 3.10, and the Śulbasūtras that codify that geometry in Section 7.7.

docs.title: 13.10 Nature in the Vedic Texts
docs.text:
The Vedic hymns address many natural powers—earth and sky, the waters, rivers, dawn, sun, wind and fire—as divine (Table 13.3). The best known of these hymns is the Pṛthivī Sūkta of the Atharvaveda, with its line “The Earth is my mother; I am the son of the Earth” (AV 12.1.12), which is discussed in Section 5.4.

Table 13.3. Some Vedic hymns to natural powers. Theme Text Content Earth as mother AV 12.1 (Pṛthivī Sūkta) The earth as sustainer of all beings; prayer that what is dug from her may grow again (12.1.35) Waters RV 7.49 The divine Waters, purifying and healing Rivers RV 10.75 (Nadīstuti) Praise of the rivers of the north-west Forest RV 10.146 (Araṇyānī) The goddess of the wilderness Sun RV 1.115; 3.62.10 Sūrya and Savitṛ as the source of light and life

Modern writers often draw environmental lessons from such hymns, and the reverence they express is real. Two cautions are needed. The hymns are religious, not ecological, texts: they ask the gods for rain, cattle, sons and victory, and the Vedic economy cleared forest by fire for cultivation (the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa’s story of Agni Vaiśvānara burning his way eastward across the land is often read as a memory of this, ŚB 1.4.1.10–17). And the Vedic sacrifice included animal sacrifice. The cycle of offering and rain later formulated in the Bhagavadgītā (3.14–16) is a theology of reciprocity between gods and humans, not an anticipation of modern ecology.

docs.title: 13.11 Summary
docs.text:
No single Vedic world-view emerges from these texts, but a direction of thought does. The hymns imagine the world as an order upheld by many gods and renewed by sacrifice, and they already wonder whether anyone knows how it began. The Brāhmaṇas turn that order into a system of correspondences that the ritualist can know and use; the Upaniṣads ask what single reality lies behind all the correspondences, and find it in the self. The same movement helps to explain why ṛta gave way to dharma, why the gods came to be ranked below brahman, and why the ideas of rebirth and liberation, formed at the very end of the period, could be taken up by traditions that rejected the authority of the Veda itself.

Closing Meditation

pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idaṃ pūrṇāt pūrṇam udacyate pūrṇasya pūrṇam ādāya pūrṇam evāvaśiṣyate That is full; this is full. From the full, the full is drawn out. When the full is taken from the full, the full alone remains. — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.1.1

docs.title: Chapter 14: Vedic Society: Priesthood, Ritual, Class and Daily Life
docs.text:
Invocatory Verse

saṃ gacchadhvaṃ saṃ vadadhvaṃ saṃ vo manāṃsi jānatām devā bhāgaṃ yathā pūrve saṃjānānā upāsate Come together, speak together, let your minds be of one accord, as the gods of old, being of one accord, sit down to their share. — Ṛgveda 10.191.2

docs.title: 14.1 Introduction: Reconstructing Vedic Society
docs.text: The Vedic texts are religious works, but they contain many incidental references to social organisation, economy, family and politics. From them historians reconstruct a picture of society that changed greatly over the Vedic period. Scholars usually distinguish an Early Vedic period, reflected in the Ṛgveda (composed c. 1500–1200 BCE), centred on the Panjab, and a Later Vedic period, reflected in the other Saṃhitās, the Brāhmaṇas and the early Upaniṣads (c. 1200–500 BCE), during which the centre shifted to the Ganga–Yamunā Doab and further east (Thapar 2002; Witzel 1997). Because the texts were composed by and for priests and their patrons, they show society mostly from the top; the voices of women, of Śūdras and of the peoples the texts call dāsa are heard, if at all, indirectly.

docs.title: 14.2.1 The Early Vedic Period
docs.text:
The society of the Ṛgveda was made up of clans of cattle-herders who also practised some agriculture and moved seasonally. The basic unit was the patrilineal household (gṛha, kula); households formed clans (viś), and clans formed peoples (jana) such as the Pūrus, Bharatas and Yadus. The word grāma originally meant a mobile band or trek rather than a settled village. There were no hereditary classes in the later sense, but there were clear distinctions of wealth and status: generous chieftains and patrons (maghavan), hereditary families of poet-priests, ordinary clansmen, and captives and servants. The texts also speak of enemies called dāsa or dasyu, who spoke differently, did not perform the Vedic rites and were often, though not always, opposed to the ārya; some dāsa chiefs appear as patrons, and dāsa came to mean “slave” or “servant” (Figure 14.1).

Figure 14.1. Units of early Vedic society.

docs.title: 14.2.2 The Later Vedic Period
docs.text: In the later Vedic period, settled agriculture became the basis of the economy, iron came into use, and small kingdoms emerged, above all the Kuru–Pañcāla realm, whose kings sponsored the great śrauta rituals. Society came to be described in terms of four hereditary classes (varṇas), with the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas claiming superiority over the Vaiśyas, who produced wealth, and the Śūdras, who served. The first references to groups regarded as impure, such as the caṇḍāla, also appear in this period.

docs.title: 14.3 The Archaeological Setting
docs.text:
The Vedic texts and the archaeological record are two very different kinds of evidence. The texts were composed and preserved orally, mention no pottery styles and few datable objects, and describe a world of ritual from the priests’ point of view; archaeology recovers settlements, graves, tools and pottery, but not the language their makers spoke or the hymns they sang. Correlating the two is therefore always a matter of matching regions, periods and ways of life, and every correlation is a hypothesis (Erdosy 1995; Singh 2008). With that caution, the archaeology of north-western and northern India in the second and early first millennia BCE provides a setting against which the textual sequence of Section 1.7 can be read.

The north-west in the second millennium BCE.

After about 1900 BCE the cities of the mature Harappan civilisation declined, and the north-west was occupied by smaller, regionally diverse “late Harappan” or post-urban cultures. Several archaeological complexes of this period have been discussed in connection with the arrival of Indo-Aryan speech. Beyond the subcontinent, the Sintashta culture of the southern Urals (c. 2100–1800 BCE) has yielded the earliest known spoked-wheeled chariots buried with horses, a combination central to the Ṛgveda, and the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex of southern Central Asia (c. 2300–1700 BCE), with its fortified settlements and fire structures, has been proposed by Asko Parpola and others as a zone of contact through which Indo-Iranian speakers passed and from which they borrowed religious ideas and vocabulary (Anthony 2007; Parpola 2015). Within the subcontinent, the cemeteries of the Swat valley in the north-west (the so-called Gandhāra Grave culture, from the mid-second millennium BCE), with their cremations and inhumations and evidence of the horse, are among the cultures most often linked with early Indo-Aryans. None of these identifications can be proved, and each has its critics; the genetic evidence summarised in Section 1.8 is at present the strongest independent indication of movements of people into the region in this period.

The burials excavated at Sanauli in western Uttar Pradesh in 2018, which included wheeled vehicles dated by the excavators to about 2000–1800 BCE, have been presented by some as “chariots” of a Vedic type. Their wheels are solid, not spoked, and no horses were found with them, so that their interpretation as horse-drawn war chariots, and any connection with the Ṛgveda, remain unproven.

The Iranian side of the frontier offers a complementary perspective. The first chapter of the Avestan Vīdēvdād lists sixteen lands created by Ahura Mazdā, among them Haraxvaitī (Arachosia, in southern Afghanistan) and Hapta Hindu, the “Seven Rivers” that correspond to the Ṛgvedic sapta sindhavaḥ. Whatever its date, the list shows that the borderlands between the Iranian plateau and the Indus were known to both traditions, as the shared vocabulary of Table 1.3 would lead one to expect.

The Painted Grey Ware and the Kuru realm.

The best-known correlation concerns the later Vedic period. The Painted Grey Ware, a fine wheel-made grey pottery painted with simple black designs, is found at many hundreds of sites in Haryana, the Indian Panjab, northern Rajasthan and western Uttar Pradesh, and is usually dated c. 1200–600 BCE, with some earlier radiocarbon dates. Its distribution coincides strikingly with the Kuru–Pañcāla country of the later Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas, and at sites such as Hastināpura, Ahichchhatra, Atranjikhera and Bhagwanpura it is associated with modest agricultural villages of wattle-and-daub houses, the cultivation of rice, wheat and barley, cattle and horses, and the use of iron. B. B. Lal’s excavation at Hastināpura first suggested a link between this culture and the world of the later Vedic texts and the epic (see Volume 7, Itihāsa–Purāṇa) (Lal 1955); Witzel has connected the spread of Painted Grey Ware with the formation of the Kuru realm described in Section 14.9. The correlation is plausible in region, date and economy, but it remains a correlation: the pottery itself tells us nothing about language or ritual.

Iron.

The Atharvaveda’s “dark metal” (Section 1.7) fits the appearance of iron in Painted Grey Ware levels. Excavations in the central Ganga plain and the eastern Vindhyas have since produced iron in levels dated to the second millennium BCE (Tewari 2003), so that iron working in India began earlier and in more regions than was once assumed (see Volume 14, Rasāyana). The Vedic texts reflect its spread in the north-west and the Doab, not its first beginnings in the subcontinent.

The eastward shift.

The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.4.1) preserves a legend of this movement. Agni Vaiśvānara, carried in the mouth of King Videgha Māthava, burns his way eastward from the Sarasvatī, burning over the rivers as he goes, until he reaches the Sadānīrā, which he does not cross; the Brahmins had not crossed it either, for the land beyond was marshy and “untasted by Agni”. Now, the text says, many Brahmins live east of it, because they have made the land fit for sacrifice. The story has often been read as a memory of the extension of Vedic ritual culture, and of the clearing and settlement of land, into the eastern Ganga plain (Videha) in the late Vedic period. In archaeological terms, this is the region and period in which Painted Grey Ware gives way to the Northern Black Polished Ware (from about the seventh or sixth century BCE), and in which the towns, coinage and states of the “second urbanisation” and the new religious movements of the Buddha and the Jina emerged (Allchin 1995). The late Vedic texts and the earliest Buddhist and Jain texts thus describe neighbouring and partly overlapping worlds.

Table 14.1 summarises the main archaeological cultures discussed here and the textual layers with which they have been compared.

Table 14.1. Archaeological cultures of northern South Asia and the Vedic texts (dates approximate; all correlations hypothetical).
