Culture Date Region Relation to the texts Mature Harappan c. 2600–1900 BCE Indus and Ghaggar–Hakra basins, Gujarat Before the Ṛgveda on the academic chronology; no certain link Late (post-urban) Harappan c. 1900–1300 BCE Panjab, Haryana, Sindh, Gujarat Contemporary in part with the early Ṛgvedic period Gandhāra Grave culture From the mid-second millennium BCE Swat and neighbouring valleys Often proposed as early Indo-Aryan Painted Grey Ware c. 1200–600 BCE Haryana, Panjab, northern Rajasthan, western Uttar Pradesh Region and date of the later Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas (Kuru–Pañcāla) Northern Black Polished Ware From c. 700–600 BCE Ganga plain Late Vedic and early Buddhist and Jain texts; the “second urbanisation”

Taken together, the archaeological evidence supports the broad sequence derived from the texts: a Ṛgvedic world in the north-west in the second half of the second millennium BCE, a later Vedic world centred on the Doab in the late second and early first millennia, and an eastward extension towards the Ganga plain by the middle of the first millennium. It does not allow us to identify “the Vedic people” with any single pottery or burial type, and it is fully compatible with the mixed, multilingual society that the texts themselves imply.

docs.title: 14.4.1 Varṇa in the Ṛgveda
docs.text:
The word varṇa means “colour” or “appearance”, and hence “kind” or “class”. In most of the Ṛgveda it is used of the two opposed groups, the ārya varṇa and the dāsa varṇa: Indra, for example, “slew the Dasyus and protected the Ārya colour” (RV 3.34.9). Whether “colour” here refers to skin colour, to light and darkness as symbols of friend and foe, or simply to “kind” is debated; the nineteenth-century racial reading is no longer accepted as established. Words for priest (brahman) and ruler (rājan, kṣatra) are frequent, but a fourfold hereditary order is not.

The four classes appear together only once in the Ṛgveda, in verse 12 of the Puruṣa Sūkta (RV 10.90), a hymn of the latest layer. The verse, quoted in Section 2.5.3, says that the Brahmin was the mouth of the sacrificed cosmic Man, the Rājanya his arms, the Vaiśya his thighs, and that the Śūdra was born from his feet.

The image is one of a single body, and later writers have often emphasised this organic unity, arguing that the four classes were meant to be complementary functions rather than ranks. That reading is a later interpretation. The hymn itself places the Brahmin at the mouth and the Śūdra at the feet, and it was understood in this hierarchical sense from the Brāhmaṇas onward. Its main historical significance is that it gave a sacred, cosmic charter to social inequality.

docs.title: 14.4.2 Varṇa in the Later Vedic Texts
docs.text:
The Brāhmaṇas state the hierarchy explicitly. A well-known passage of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (7.29), describing what each class’s descendants would be like if a king consumed the wrong portion at the sacrifice, characterises the Vaiśya as “paying tribute to another, to be lived on by another, to be oppressed at will”, and the Śūdra as “the servant of another, to be removed at will, to be slain at will”. Śūdras were excluded from the śrauta ritual and from Vedic study. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (5.10.7) teaches that people of good conduct are reborn in a Brahmin, Kṣatriya or Vaiśya womb, and people of foul conduct in the womb of a dog, a pig or a caṇḍāla—an early sign of the idea that birth in a low group results from past deeds, and of the treatment of some groups as untouchable (Table 14.2).

Table 14.2. The four varṇas as described in later Vedic and Dharmaśāstra texts. Varṇa Body part (RV 10.90) Prescribed Occupations Ritual Status Brāhmaṇa Mouth Studying and teaching the Veda; sacrificing for self and others; receiving gifts Initiated (“twice-born”) Kṣatriya Arms Protection, rule, war Initiated Vaiśya Thighs Agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade Initiated Śūdra Feet Serving the other three Not initiated; excluded from Vedic study

docs.title: 14.4.3 Varṇa, Jāti and the Later History of Caste
docs.text:
The four varṇas were always a theoretical scheme. The social reality of caste consists of thousands of endogamous, often occupational groups (jātis), which the Dharmaśāstras later tried to fit into the varṇa scheme by explaining them as the offspring of “mixed” marriages. The Dharma Sūtras (c. 3rd–1st centuries BCE) and the Mānava Dharmaśāstra (c. 2nd century CE) codified the privileges of Brahmins, the disabilities of Śūdras and the exclusion of untouchable groups (Olivelle 1999). Genetic studies suggest that Indian population groups mixed extensively between roughly 4,200 and 1,900 years ago, and that strict endogamy became widespread only towards the end of that period, that is, around the time when these texts were composed (Moorjani et al. 2013).

The varṇa scheme has been debated ever since. The Buddha and the Jina rejected the claim that birth determines worth; the Bhagavadgītā (4.13) speaks of the four varṇas as created “according to qualities and actions”, a verse that modern reformers read as meaning that varṇa should depend on aptitude rather than birth; and medieval devotional poets attacked caste pride. In modern India, Dayānanda Sarasvatī and M. K. Gandhi argued for a reformed, non-hereditary varṇa, while B. R. Ambedkar argued that the system was rooted in the sacred texts themselves, and in Who Were the Shudras? (1946) and Annihilation of Caste (1936) called for its abolition (Ambedkar 1946; Sharma 1990). The Constitution of India (1950) abolished untouchability (Article 17).

Scholarly Note: Reading the Puruṣa Sūkta Today

It is possible to admire the poetry and cosmology of the Puruṣa Sūkta while recognising what it did. Two common responses should both be avoided: dismissing the whole Vedic corpus because of this hymn, and explaining away its hierarchy as “functional complementarity”. The historian’s task is to show how a late hymn became the charter of a social order that brought privilege to some and lasting suffering to many, and how that order was challenged within Indian tradition itself.

docs.title: 14.5 The Vedic Priesthood
docs.text: The great rites required specialised priests trained in different Vedas: four in the simplest offerings and sixteen, in four groups led by the hotṛ, the adhvaryu, the udgātṛ and the brahman, in the Soma sacrifice. Their division of labour, their texts and their fees are described in Section 8.3 (Figure 8.2). Socially, the priesthood became the hereditary preserve of Brahmin families, identified by their lineage (gotra) and its ancestral seers (pravara) and by their affiliation to a Vedic school (Chapter 12). The alliance between a king and his household priest (purohita), which the last book of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa treats as indispensable to royal power, became a central element of political ideology (Section 14.9).

docs.title: 14.6 The Life-Cycle Rites
docs.text: The life-cycle rites (saṃskāras) of the Gṛhyasūtras, described in Chapter 9 (Table 9.2), are also a social record. Many of them are still performed in Hindu families. But initiation, and with it Vedic study, was restricted to boys of the upper three varṇas; several rites aim specifically at the birth of sons; and for daughters the rites of childhood were to be performed without Vedic mantras.

docs.title: 14.7 Women in Vedic Society
docs.text:
The position of women in the Vedic period has been the subject of a long debate. Nationalist historians such as A. S. Altekar argued that women enjoyed high status in the early Vedic period and that it declined later; feminist historians such as Uma Chakravarti and Kumkum Roy have criticised the idea of a Vedic “golden age” and emphasised the patriarchal structures already present in the texts (Altekar 1938; Chakravarti 2003; Roy 2010). The evidence points both ways:

  • Participation: the sacrificer’s wife (patnī) was required in the śrauta ritual, with her own ritual roles (Jamison 1996); a few hymns are ascribed to women poets, and the Upaniṣads show women such as Gārgī and Maitreyī taking part in philosophical debate.

  • The household: a Ṛgvedic poet says “the wife is the home” (jāyed astam, RV 3.53.4), and the wedding hymn (RV 10.85) wishes the bride to be mistress over her husband’s family.

  • Widows: the funeral hymn bids the widow rise from beside her dead husband and return to the world of the living (RV 10.18.8); whether this implies remarriage, perhaps to the husband’s brother, is debated. There is no evidence of widow-burning in the Ṛgveda.

  • Subordination: the texts are composed from a male point of view; prayers are overwhelmingly for sons, not daughters; descent and inheritance passed through men, and a Black Yajurveda passage (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.8.2) declares women to be without strength and without a share in inheritance.

  • Later restriction: in the Dharma Sūtras and Śāstras, women were excluded from Vedic study and initiation, and their dependence on father, husband and son was made a rule.

docs.title: 14.7.1 The Evidence in Detail
docs.text:
The general picture can be made more precise from the texts themselves. On women’s role in the solemn and domestic rites, see Chapters 8 and 9; on women’s education and the later debate about it, Volume 22, Manas and Śikṣā; on women in the law books, Volume 18.

Daughters and sons.

The preference for sons runs through the whole corpus. In the story of Śunaḥśepa told at the royal consecration, a verse addressed to the childless king Hariścandra says that “a wife is a companion, a daughter a misery, a son a light in the highest heaven” (sakhā ha jāyā kṛpaṇaṃ ha duhitā jyotir ha putraḥ parame vyoman, Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 7.13). The domestic rite of puṃsavana was performed in pregnancy to obtain a male child (Chapter 9). The reasons are clear in the texts: a son continued the line, performed the offerings to the ancestors and inherited the property.

The unprotected woman.

Several images in the Ṛgveda show what a woman’s position was when she lacked a husband or brother. A poet asks Indra for a share “like a girl growing old at home with her parents” (amājūr iva pitroḥ sacā satī, RV 2.17.7), an image that works only because the unmarried daughter without a portion of her own was a familiar figure. Dawn, who goes towards men, is compared to a “brotherless” woman (abhrātā iva, RV 1.124.7), that is, one without the male kin who would normally arrange her marriage. The later law of the “appointed daughter” (putrikā), whose son became her father’s heir, addressed the case of a father without sons. A verse of a hymn to the Aśvins asks who brings them to the place of sacrifice “as a widow brings her husband’s brother to bed” (RV 10.40.2), a simile that presupposes the custom by which a widow could be taken by her husband’s brother; it is often taken as the earliest evidence for the institution that the law books later call niyoga, and it bears on the interpretation of the funeral verse discussed above.

Co-wives.

Kings and rich men had more than one wife. The horse sacrifice names four wives of the king, of different rank, each with her own part in the rite. Two late hymns of the Ṛgveda are composed in a woman’s voice about rival wives: RV 10.145, a spell with a plant to drive away a co-wife and win the husband’s undivided love, ascribed by the Anukramaṇī to Indrāṇī, and RV 10.159, the triumphant song of a woman who has overcome her co-wives, ascribed to Śacī Paulomī. The Atharvaveda has more charms of this kind. Whoever their actual authors were, these are among the few Vedic texts that speak from a woman’s position in the household.

Impurity.

The Taittirīya Saṃhitā (2.5.1) tells how Indra’s guilt for killing Viśvarūpa was taken over in thirds by the earth, the trees and women, and how women received in return the boon of conceiving children and of desire until childbirth; the guilt appears in them as their monthly impurity, and the passage goes on to prescribe restrictions on contact with a woman “in soiled garments”. The story is an early charter for the menstrual taboos of the later law books, and it shows how a myth could be used to explain and justify a social rule.

Women of learning.

The texts that name learned women also show that they were exceptions. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4.5.1) says that of Yājñavalkya’s two wives “Maitreyī was one who discoursed on brahman (brahmavādinī); Kātyāyanī had only a woman’s understanding (strīprajñā)”: the praise of the one depends on a low expectation of the other. Gārgī Vācaknavī questions Yājñavalkya twice in the debate at Janaka’s court (BU 3.6, 3.8); the first time he silences her with the warning that her head will shatter if she asks too much, a threat he also uses against male opponents. Gārgī’s name, with those of Vaḍavā Prātītheyī and Sulabhā Maitreyī, also appears in the list of former teachers to whom libations are offered in the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra (3.4.4), which suggests that the Ṛgvedic schools remembered some women as authorities in their tradition.

The honest conclusion is that women’s position was neither equal nor uniformly low, that it varied by class and period, and that it became more restricted as the Brahmanical law books took shape.

docs.title: 14.8.1 Cattle and Agriculture
docs.text: Cattle were the chief measure of wealth in the Ṛgveda. Raids for cattle were a principal form of warfare—gaviṣṭi, “desire for cows”, is a word for battle—and gotra, originally “cow-pen”, later came to mean “clan”. Agriculture is also attested: the Ṛgveda knows ploughing and the grain yava (barley, or grain in general). Rice (vrīhi) and wheat (godhūma) appear in the later Saṃhitās, as farming became the foundation of the later Vedic economy. Ploughing charms (AV 3.17) and the ploughing imagery of RV 10.101 show the importance of the field.

docs.title: 14.8.2 Crafts and Trade
docs.text:
The texts mention carpenters and chariot-makers (takṣan, rathakāra), smiths, weavers, potters, leather-workers, physicians and many others; the list of occupations in Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 30 (the Puruṣamedha) is especially rich. RV 9.112 humorously compares the different aims of the carpenter, the physician and the priest. Trade is attested, including a merchant’s prayer (AV 3.15); references to the samudra and to the Aśvins’ rescue of Bhujyu from the waters (RV 1.116) have been read as evidence of sea voyages, though this is uncertain. There was no coinage in the Vedic period; cattle and gold ornaments served as measures of value (Table 14.3).

Table 14.3. Some economic activities attested in the Vedic texts. Activity Example of Evidence Remarks Cattle-rearing RV 6.28 (hymn to the cows) The chief form of wealth Agriculture RV 10.101; AV 3.17 Ploughing; more prominent in later texts Weaving RV 10.130 The sacrifice imagined as a woven fabric Crafts RV 9.112; VS 30 Lists of occupations Trade AV 3.15 A merchant’s prayer

docs.title: 14.9 Political Organisation
docs.text:
In the early Vedic period the rājan was a tribal chief and war-leader, whose position depended on success in battle and on the support of his clansmen. The texts mention assemblies, the sabhā and the samiti, whose exact composition and functions are uncertain; a charm of the Atharvaveda asks for the help of both in winning a debate (AV 7.12.1; see Section 5.6). Some writers have described these assemblies as a form of “Vedic democracy”. This is an overstatement: they seem to have been gatherings of free men of the clan, or of its leading men, and they declined as kingship grew stronger.

In the later Vedic period, kings ruled territories rather than peoples, collected regular tribute (bali), and were surrounded by officials, the ratnins (Roy 1994). Royal rituals such as the Rājasūya, Vājapeya and Aśvamedha proclaimed their power, and the alliance between king and Brahmin chaplain (purohita) became central to political ideology.

docs.title: 14.9.1 The Kuru Realm and the Shaping of the Vedic Canon
docs.text:
Michael Witzel has argued that the first Indian “state” in a meaningful sense took shape in the Kuru realm of the upper Ganga–Yamunā Doab around the twelfth to tenth centuries BCE (Witzel 1995, 1997). Later tradition remembers the Kuru kings Parīkṣit and his son Janamejaya, the former praised in an Atharvavedic hymn (AV 20.127.7–10) as a king under whose rule the realm prospered. On Witzel’s reconstruction, the Kuru rulers and their Brahmin allies brought together the poetic traditions of the older clans, collected them into the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā in roughly its present arrangement, organised the new Yajurveda and Sāmaveda collections, and developed the elaborate śrauta ritual with its four kinds of priest, which proclaimed the king’s power and bound the clans to him. The four-class scheme of the Puruṣa Sūkta, in which priest and ruler stand above producers and servants, fits this political context.

When the Kuru realm declined, Vedic culture and its schools moved eastward. The later Brāhmaṇas and the early Upaniṣads were composed in the Pañcāla country and further east in Kosala and Videha, where King Janaka’s court appears as a centre of debate. It was in this eastern region, a little later, that urban centres, coinage and new religious movements—including Buddhism and Jainism—emerged in the second half of the first millennium BCE, in what historians call the “second urbanisation”. The reconstruction of the Kuru state is a scholarly hypothesis, not a certainty, but it offers a coherent explanation of how scattered clan traditions became a single sacred canon.

docs.title: 14.10 Education and Learning
docs.text: Education centred on the learning of the Veda by initiated boys in their teacher’s household (see Chapter 11). Besides memorising one or more Saṃhitās, students might learn the Brāhmaṇas and the ancillary sciences. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (7.1.2) gives a list of subjects known to a learned man of its day, including the four Vedas, “the fifth Veda” of history and ancient lore (itihāsa-purāṇa), grammar, rites for the ancestors, mathematics, divination, logic, ethics and the sciences of snakes and spirits. Such learning was largely confined to men of the upper varṇas, and above all to Brahmins.

docs.title: 14.11 Seasonal Rites and Recreation
docs.text:
Table 14.4 lists some seasonal rites of the Vedic calendar.

Table 14.4. Some seasonal rites of the Vedic calendar. Rite Time Description Cāturmāsya Three times a year Sacrifices at the beginning of the three four-month seasons Āgrayaṇa Harvest Offering of the first fruits Mahāvrata Near the end of the year-long session A festive rite with music, a swing, ritual abuse and a mock combat Viṣuvat The middle day of the year-long session The central day dividing the ritual year in two

The texts mention music and musical instruments—drums (dundubhi), flutes and, in later texts, the vīṇā—and dance. Chariot races featured in the Vājapeya. Dicing was a popular and dangerous pastime: the “Gambler’s Lament” (RV 10.34) is one of the most human poems of the Ṛgveda, in which a ruined gambler laments his addiction and is advised to leave the dice and plough his field (RV 10.34.13, quoted at the end of this chapter).

docs.title: 14.12 Summary
docs.text:
Vedic society changed profoundly over a thousand years: from mobile, cattle-herding clans led by chieftains to agrarian kingdoms with a developed priesthood and an articulated class hierarchy. The texts show a rich ritual life, real intellectual achievement, and ideals of concord and generosity. They also show the origins of hereditary inequality, the subordination of women and the exclusion of Śūdras and of groups later treated as untouchable. A responsible account of the Vedic heritage must keep both sides in view.

Closing Verse: The Gambler’s Lament

akṣair mā dīvyaḥ kṛṣim it kṛṣasva vitte ramasva bahu manyamānaḥ tatra gāvaḥ kitava tatra jāyā tan me vi caṣṭe savitāyam aryaḥ Do not play with dice; plough your field. Take pleasure in your property, valuing it highly. There are your cows, gambler, there your wife: so this noble Savitṛ reveals to me. — Ṛgveda 10.34.13

docs.title: Chapter 15: The Legacy and Modern Relevance of the Vedas
docs.text:
Invocatory Verse

ā no bhadrāḥ kratavo yantu viśvato ’dabdhāso aparītāsa udbhidaḥ May auspicious intentions come to us from every side, undeceived, unobstructed, breaking through. — Ṛgveda 1.89.1

docs.title: 15.1 Introduction
docs.text: This final chapter considers what became of the Vedas after the Vedic period: how later Indian traditions drew on them, argued with them or rejected them; how they were received in the modern world; and in what sense they remain relevant today. A responsible answer must avoid two temptations—treating the Vedas as a museum piece of no living importance, and claiming for them a scientific or moral authority that the evidence does not support.

docs.title: 15.2 The Vedas and Later Indian Traditions
docs.text:
For Brahmanical Hinduism the Vedas became the ultimate source of authority. The orthodox philosophical schools, the Dharmaśāstras, the epics and Purāṇas, and many Āgamic and devotional traditions claim to be based on the Veda or consistent with it. In practice, the relationship was often nominal: later Hinduism worships deities such as Śiva, Viṣṇu and the Goddess in forms barely present in the Vedas, and much of its ritual follows the Āgamas and Purāṇas rather than the śrauta texts. The Veda functioned less as a text that people knew than as a symbol of authority and orthodoxy.

Other Indian traditions defined themselves partly against the Veda. Buddhists and Jains rejected its authority, the efficacy of animal sacrifice and the claim that birth confers religious status; the materialist Cārvākas mocked the priests; and many medieval devotional poets, such as Kabīr, dismissed Vedic learning in favour of devotion. Many regional and tribal traditions had little to do with the Veda at all. India’s intellectual history is therefore not simply a story of descent from the Vedas, but of a long conversation in which the Veda was one of the central voices. Two parts of that conversation, the early Buddhist and Jain critique and the Tamil reception of the Veda, are outlined below.

docs.title: 15.2.1 The Buddhist and Jain Critique
docs.text:
The earliest sustained criticism of Vedic learning, and of the claims made for birth, comes from the Buddhist and Jain canons, composed in the same eastern Ganga plain in which the late Vedic texts took shape (Section 14.3). The Pali discourses (suttas) make their case in dialogues with Brahmins, often men learned in the “three Vedas” (tevijja), and several of these dialogues are classics (Walshe 1995).

In the Tevijja Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 13) two young Brahmins, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, dispute which of the paths taught by Brahmin teachers leads to union with Brahmā. The Buddha asks whether any Brahmin learned in the three Vedas, any teacher of theirs back to the seventh generation, or even the ancient seers who made the mantras, has seen Brahmā face to face. The seers are named—Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa and Bhagu, that is, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Bhṛgu and others of the families of Section 1.5. None has; their teaching is likened to a file of blind men, each holding on to the one in front, and to a man who builds a ladder at a crossroads to climb to a mansion he has never seen. The Buddha then teaches, as the true way to companionship with Brahmā, the cultivation of friendliness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity. The argument does not reject the goal; it rejects the claim that recited texts give access to it.

In the Ambaṭṭha Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 3) a young Brahmin sent by his teacher Pokkhara­sāti insults the Sakyans as menials; the Buddha shows that Ambaṭṭha’s own clan descends from a slave woman of the Sakyan royal house, and teaches that it is knowledge and conduct (vijjācaraṇa), not birth or lineage, that make a person excellent. The Aggañña Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 27), addressed again to Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, answers the Brahmins’ claim to be the true sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, by observing that Brahmins are plainly born from Brahmin women like everyone else—a riposte to the image of the Puruṣa Sūkta (Section 2.5.3). It then tells a counter-myth of social origins, in which beings decline from a luminous state, property and theft appear, the people choose a ruler, the “Great Elect” (mahāsammata), and the four classes arise from occupations, not from a cosmic body. Steven Collins and Richard Gombrich have read the discourse as a sustained parody of Brahmanical cosmogony (Collins 1993; Gombrich 1988). The Kūṭadanta Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 5) turns to sacrifice: a Brahmin preparing a great animal sacrifice is told of an ancient king whose sacrifice killed no animal and was completed with ghee, oil, butter, curds, honey and molasses, and of higher sacrifices still—gifts, refuge, the moral precepts and meditation—and he sets his animals free. A verse of the Vasala Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta (1.7) puts the principle in a line: na jaccā vasalo hoti, na jaccā hoti brāhmaṇo; kammunā vasalo hoti, kammunā hoti brāhmaṇo, “not by birth is one an outcaste, not by birth a Brahmin; by deeds one is an outcaste, by deeds a Brahmin” (Bhikkhu Bodhi 2017).

The Jain canon makes the same points in its own idiom. In the Uttarādhyayana Sūtra the monk Hari­keśa, born among the Śvapākas, an outcaste group, comes for alms to a Brahmin sacrifice, is reviled and beaten, and teaches the Brahmins that the true sacrifice is the fire of austerity fed by right conduct (chapter 12); and in chapter 25 the monk Jayaghoṣa, at the sacrifice of the Brahmin Vijayaghoṣa, describes the true Brahmin as one who is free from passion and harms no living being, adding that one does not become a Brahmin by uttering Oṃ (Jacobi 1895).

These texts do not simply reject the Veda. They take over its vocabulary—the true Brahmin, the true sacrifice, union with Brahmā—and give it an ethical meaning. That strategy, more than outright dismissal, was the most lasting part of the critique, and it has parallels within Brahmanical tradition itself, in the Upaniṣads’ internalised sacrifice (Section 6.6) and in the Bhagavadgītā’s definition of varṇa by “qualities and actions” (Section 14.4). The Buddhist and Jain traditions are treated in Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā.

docs.title: 15.2.2 The Veda in Tamil Literature
docs.text:
Tamil literature had its own poetic traditions, with conventions of its own, but it was never isolated from the Veda. The Sangam anthologies of the early centuries CE know Brahmins (antaṇar,pārppār) who tend the sacred fires and recite the “four Vedas” (nāṉmaṟai), and they celebrate kings for their Vedic sacrifices: a Pāṇṭiya king of the Puṟanāṉūṟu is remembered as Palyākacālai Mutukuṭumi Peruvaḻuti, “of the many sacrificial halls”, and a Cōḻa king as Rācacūyam Vēṭṭa Perunaṟkiḷḷi, “who performed the Rājasūya”. George Hart and Kamil Zvelebil have shown how Sanskrit and Tamil conventions met in this literature without either absorbing the other (Hart 1975; Zvelebil 1973). The Tirukkuṟaḷ, a work on ethics usually dated to about the fifth century CE, respects the Brahmin’s learning but values conduct above it: a Brahmin who forgets the Veda can learn it again, but one who fails in conduct is ruined (134); and in its chapter on abstaining from meat it declares that not to kill and eat a living creature is better than a thousand sacrifices with oblations poured into the fire (259). In the epic Cilappatikāram the marriage of Kōvalaṉ and Kaṇṇaki is solemnised by an aged Brahmin, the couple walking round the fire according to the Vedic rite.

The devotional movements took the relationship further. The Śaiva poets of the Tēvāram praise Śiva as the substance and meaning of the Vedas, and the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition gave the hymns of the Āḻvārs, collected by Nāthamuni in the tenth century as the Nālāyira Tivviyap Pirapantam (“Four Thousand Sacred Compositions”), the status of a Veda in Tamil. Nammāḻvār’s Tiruvāymoḻi was called the “Tamil Veda”, its author was praised as the one who made the Veda into Tamil, and from the twelfth century Śrīvaiṣṇava theologians commented on it alongside the Sanskrit Upaniṣads, a doctrine of “dual Vedānta” (ubhaya-vedānta); in temples such as Śrīraṅgam the Tamil hymns are recited in the liturgy beside the Sanskrit Veda (Carman and Narayanan 1989; Narayanan 1994). The claim was at once a tribute to the Veda’s prestige, since a text was exalted by being called a Veda, and a challenge to the Brahmin monopoly of revelation, since the Tamil hymns could be learnt and sung by people to whom the Sanskrit Veda was closed; Nammāḻvār himself was remembered as a man of the Vēḷāḷa cultivator community, not a Brahmin. Other Tamil voices were openly critical: the Siddhar poets mocked ritual and caste, and in the twentieth century the Self-Respect movement of E. V. Ramasamy (“Periyar”) attacked the authority of the Brahmanical texts. Tamil literature thus contains the whole range of responses to the Veda, from patronage and adaptation to appropriation and rejection.

docs.title: 15.3 The Later History of the Vedic Gods
docs.text: The gods of the hymns did not vanish when the great theistic traditions of Viṣṇu, Śiva and the Goddess took shape. They were given new places in a reordered pantheon: some rose, some became guardians of the directions or heavenly officials, some were absorbed into other gods, and a few were all but forgotten. The epics and Purāṇas, treated in Volume 7, Itihāsa–Purāṇa, are the main witnesses to this change; E. Washburn Hopkins’s Epic Mythology remains the fullest survey of the epic forms of the Vedic gods (Hopkins 1915). Table 15.1 summarises the fates of the principal deities.

docs.title: 15.3.1 The Gods Relativised
docs.text: The change began within the Vedic period. In the Brāhmaṇas, Prajāpati, the creator who is also the sacrifice and the year, stands above the older gods (Chapter 6). The early Upaniṣads go further. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.4.10) says that one who worships a deity as other than himself, thinking “he is one, I am another”, does not understand: he is like a domestic animal to the gods, who would not like human beings to learn the truth. In the Kena Upaniṣad (sections 3–4) Agni cannot burn and Vāyu cannot blow away a single blade of grass placed before them by a mysterious being, and it is the goddess Umā Haimavatī who tells Indra that the being was brahman. The gods remain real, but they are no longer ultimate. Buddhists and Jains took a similar view from their own premises: the gods are beings in the cycle of rebirth, enjoying a long and pleasant life as the reward of past deeds, and in need of liberation like everyone else.

docs.title: 15.3.2 Indra
docs.text:
Indra, the most praised god of the Ṛgveda, had the most varied later history. Already in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (2.5.1) he carries the guilt of killing Viśvarūpa, the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ, who was a Brahmin, and the epic develops the theme: in the Udyogaparvan of the Mahābhārata, Indra hides in the waters after killing Vṛtra, and the mortal king Nahuṣa rules heaven in his place until his arrogance brings his fall. The Rāmāyaṇa tells of his seduction of Ahalyā (Volume 7). In the Purāṇas Indra becomes an office rather than a person: each age of Manu (manvantara) has its own Indra, and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa names the Indra of the present age Purandara, “breaker of forts”, a Ṛgvedic epithet of the god. A well-known story in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa, made familiar to Western readers by Heinrich Zimmer, shows Indra humbled by the sight of a procession of ants, each of which had once been an Indra (Zimmer 1946). In the Govardhana episode of the Kṛṣṇa cycle (Harivamśa; Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas; Volume 7), Kṛṣṇa diverts the cowherds’ festival from Indra to the mountain and shelters them from Indra’s storm. The story turns the Vedic rain-god into the rival, and finally the devotee, of the supreme god.

Indra nevertheless remained a living figure. He is the guardian of the east among the eight guardians of the directions (dikpāla), riding the elephant Airāvata, and he appears in that role on temples across India (Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa). Festivals of Indra’s banner (indradhvaja) are described in the Sanskrit manuals; the Tamil epic Cilappatikāram devotes a canto to the festival of Indra at the Cōḻa port of Pukār; the Tolkāppiyam assigns Vēntaṉ, identified by its commentators with Indra, to the agricultural landscape (marutam); and the Indra Jātrā of Kathmandu, with the raising of a great pole, is still one of the main festivals of the Newars of the Kathmandu Valley. Buddhists made him Śakra (Pāli Sakka), king of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three and a devoted follower of the Buddha; for the Jains Śakra, the lord of the first heaven, honours the newborn Tīrthaṅkara with the bath on Mount Meru, and his hymn of praise (Śakrastava) is recited in Śvetāmbara worship (Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā).

docs.title: 15.3.3 Varuṇa and Mitra
docs.text: Varuṇa, the sovereign guardian of ṛta who binds the wrongdoer and forgives the penitent (Section 2.3), was associated with the waters already in the Ṛgveda. In the later texts that association prevails. Varuṇa becomes the lord of the waters and of the ocean and the guardian of the west, holding the noose (pāśa) that recalls his Vedic fetters; but his moral sovereignty, the sense of a god who sees hidden wrongdoing and can forgive it, passed to other gods. Joel Brereton’s study of the Ṛgvedic Ādityas shows how closely Varuṇa and his companions were tied to the principles of social order, which may explain why they declined when that order came to be expressed through dharma rather than through gods (Brereton 1981). Mitra, Varuṇa’s partner, almost disappears as a god of his own; his name survives as one of the names of the sun, and the series of twelve names recited with the Hindu sun-salutation begins with “Mitra”. His Iranian counterpart Mithra, by contrast, had a long career in Iranian religion.

docs.title: 15.3.4 Other Gods
docs.text:
Agni remained indispensable: every Hindu fire offering (homa) is still made through him, and he guards the south-east. The Mahābhārata makes him the father of the war-god Skanda and tells how he burned the Khāṇḍava forest with the help of Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna. Soma, whose plant was replaced by substitutes in the ritual (Chapter 8), had been identified with the moon already in the Brāhmaṇas; as the moon (Candra) he is the husband of the twenty-seven lunar asterisms, the daughters of Dakṣa, and the ancestor of the lunar dynasty of kings. Sūrya kept a cult of his own. Sun temples were built across India, as at Modhera in Gujarat (eleventh century) and Konārak in Odisha (thirteenth century); the Sāmba and Bhaviṣya Purāṇas tell how Sun-priests called Magas were brought from Śākadvīpa, a reflection of Iranian influence on the northern sun cult, whose images wear boots and a tunic. Prajāpati gave way to Brahmā, the creator, who is honoured in myth but has few temples. Bṛhaspati, the divine priest, became the teacher of the gods and the planet Jupiter, and his name was attached to the materialist school (Volume 3, Darśana Darpaṇa). The Aśvins became the physicians of the gods and, in the Mahābhārata, the fathers of Nakula and Sahadeva; Vāyu the father of Bhīma and of Hanumān; Yama the judge of the dead, with his scribe Citragupta, and the guardian of the south; and Tvaṣṭṛ, the divine craftsman, was largely merged with Viśvakarman, the patron of the craftsmen (Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru). Sarasvatī, the river goddess already identified with Speech (Vāc) in the Brāhmaṇas, became the goddess of learning and the arts, honoured by Hindus, Jains and Buddhists, and carried by Buddhism as far as Japan. Uṣas, the Dawn, whose hymns are among the most beautiful in the Ṛgveda, has had almost no later cult.

The two great beneficiaries of the change were Viṣṇu and Rudra. Viṣṇu’s three strides became the story of his dwarf incarnation (Vāmana), and Rudra’s double nature as fierce archer and healer, together with the Yajurvedic Śatarudrīya that is still chanted in Śiva temples, passed into the figure of Śiva (Section 2.3.5; Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama).

Table 15.1. The principal Ṛgvedic deities and their later roles (simplified). Deity In the Ṛgveda In the epics and Purāṇas Indra Warrior king of the gods, slayer of Vṛtra King of heaven as an office held in each manvantara; guardian of the east; rival of Kṛṣṇa; Śakra in Buddhism and Jainism Varuṇa Sovereign guardian of ṛta; binds and forgives Lord of the waters and the ocean; guardian of the west Mitra God of contract, paired with Varuṇa A name of the sun Agni Messenger and priest of the gods Fire of every homa; guardian of the south-east; father of Skanda Soma Sacred plant, drink and god The moon; ancestor of the lunar dynasty Sūrya, Savitṛ Sun; the impeller Sūrya with temples and a sectarian cult Prajāpati Late; creator (in the Brāhmaṇas) Succeeded by Brahmā Bṛhaspati Lord of the sacred formula Teacher of the gods; the planet Jupiter Viṣṇu Strider of three steps Supreme god of Vaiṣṇavas; Vāmana and other incarnations Rudra Fierce archer and healer Merged into Śiva Sarasvatī River goddess Goddess of speech and learning Yama First of the dead, king of the fathers Judge of the dead; guardian of the south Uṣas Dawn Almost no later cult

docs.title: 15.3.5 Explaining the Change
docs.text: Several reasons for this transformation can be given, none sufficient by itself. The Vedic gods were the gods of a sacrificial cult, invoked for cattle, sons, victory and long life; the new religions of devotion looked for a supreme god who could grant grace and final liberation, and they found him in Viṣṇu or Śiva, who absorbed the myths and attributes of many older gods (Gonda 1970). The doctrine of karma and rebirth made the gods themselves into beings who hold their places by merit, which is why the epics and Purāṇas can make Indra an office and Nahuṣa his temporary successor. The decline of the śrauta ritual, the setting in which Indra and Varuṇa were most at home, reduced their occasions of worship. Yet “decline” is not the whole story. Wherever the śrauta rites are still performed, the gods are invoked in their Vedic roles with the Vedic mantras; the guardians of the directions are worshipped at the consecration of every temple and house; and in literature, festival and folk practice Indra and his companions have remained vivid figures for three thousand years.

docs.title: 15.4 The Six Schools of Philosophy
docs.text: The six classical schools of philosophy (ṣaḍ darśana) are traditionally called āstika, “affirming” the authority of the Veda, but their actual relationship to it varies greatly. Pūrva Mīmāṃsā, whose root text is ascribed to Jaimini, interprets the ritual injunctions and defends the eternity and authorlessness of the Veda; Uttara Mīmāṃsā or Vedānta, ascribed to Bādarāyaṇa, interprets the Upaniṣads as the means of knowing Brahman. Nyāya (Gautama) accepts the Veda as reliable testimony composed by God; Vaiśeṣika (Kaṇāda) accepts its authority but makes little use of it; Sāṃkhya (Kapila) and Yoga (Patañjali) accept verbal testimony, but their doctrines owe little to the Vedas. Only the two Mīmāṃsās are, strictly speaking, schools of Vedic interpretation. The nāstika schools—Buddhist, Jain, Cārvāka and Ājīvika—rejected Vedic authority, and their debates with the orthodox schools shaped all of Indian philosophy. The schools are treated in Volume 3 of this series, Darśana Darpaṇa, and the Buddhist and Jain traditions in Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā.

docs.title: 15.5 Modern Interpreters
docs.text:
The nineteenth and twentieth centuries saw new Indian readings of the Vedas, often in response to colonial scholarship and to Christian missionary criticism. The responses of Dayānanda Sarasvatī, B. G. Tilak and Sri Aurobindo, and the critical editions produced by Indian scholars, are described in Section 1.11. Dayānanda’s call for a “return to the Vedas” also carried a programme of reform: the Ārya Samāj rejected image worship and hereditary caste and promoted the education of women, although its claim that the Saṃhitās contain modern scientific knowledge is not supported by historical or philological evidence. Other influential figures include:

  1. Svāmī Vivekānanda (1863–1902), who presented Vedānta to the world, beginning at the World’s Parliament of Religions in Chicago (1893);

  2. Madhusūdan Ojhā (1866–1939), a Jaipur scholar who wrote extensively on Vedic thought in Sanskrit;

  3. B. R. Ambedkar (1891–1956), who subjected the Vedic and Dharmaśāstra texts to a searching critique as sources of caste inequality (Section 14.4).

docs.title: 15.6 UNESCO Recognition of Vedic Chanting
docs.text: In 2003 UNESCO proclaimed the tradition of Vedic chanting a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, and in 2008 it was inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The recognition acknowledges the antiquity and continuity of the tradition, the fidelity of its oral transmission, the sophistication of its recitation techniques, and the endangered status of several of its schools.

docs.title: 15.7 The Vedas and Science: Achievements and Myths
docs.text:
The relationship between the Vedas and science is often discussed, and often distorted. The genuine achievements of the Vedic sciences are considerable and need no exaggeration:

  • Linguistics: the phonetic analysis of the Prātiśākhyas and Pāṇini’s grammar are among the high points of linguistic science in any culture. Modern linguists and computer scientists have found Pāṇini’s rule-system illuminating for the theory of formal grammars—a recognition of its rigour, not evidence that Sanskrit is uniquely suited to computers, a popular myth with no basis.

  • Mathematics: the Śulba Sūtras contain an early general statement of the “Pythagorean” theorem, an accurate approximation of \(\sqrt{2}\) and methods of geometric construction; Piṅgala’s prosody contains early combinatorics (Chapter 7).

  • Calendrical astronomy: the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa gives a coherent five-year luni-solar calendar, reconciling the movements of sun and moon by intercalation (see Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa).

Other popular claims do not stand up to examination. The Vedas do not anticipate the Big Bang, quantum physics, aircraft or modern medicine; the Nāsadīya Sūkta is a profound speculative poem, not a cosmological theory. The so-called “Vedic mathematics” popularised since 1965 is a set of mental-arithmetic techniques devised by Bhāratī Kṛṣṇa Tīrtha in the twentieth century; its sixteen “sūtras” are not found in any Vedic text. Such claims do the Vedas no honour: they obscure the real achievements described above and invite justified scepticism.

docs.title: 15.8 Living Traditions
docs.text:
The Vedas remain living texts in several ways:

  1. Recitation: Vedic schools (pāṭhaśālās) across India continue to train reciters, and Vedic chanting is widely heard in homes, temples and on public occasions.

  2. Ritual: Vedic mantras are used in the domestic life-cycle rites (saṃskāras), especially initiation, marriage and funerals, and in daily worship such as the sandhyā with the Gāyatrī. A small number of families still perform śrauta rituals.

  3. Philosophy: the Upaniṣads, through Vedānta, remain central to Hindu thought, and modern teachers have drawn on them in presenting yoga and meditation, although modern yoga has many other sources as well.

  4. Literature and identity: the Vedas are a powerful symbol of Indian heritage, invoked in politics and education as well as religion—a use that brings both opportunities and the risk of distortion.

docs.title: 15.9 The Vedas and the Indian Knowledge Systems Initiative
docs.text: Recent Indian education policy, including the National Education Policy 2020, encourages the study of Indian Knowledge Systems in schools and universities. This creates opportunities: to support endangered oral traditions, to train scholars who can read Vedic texts in the original, and to bring traditional experts and academic researchers into dialogue. It also brings responsibilities. The study of the Vedas in modern institutions should meet the same standards of evidence as any other field: it should rest on critical editions and sound philology, distinguish tradition from history, avoid unfounded claims of scientific priority, and give an honest account of difficult subjects such as caste and gender.

docs.title: 15.10 Challenges and the Way Forward
docs.text:
1. Declining numbers of reciters: the number of fully trained reciters, especially in rare schools such as the Jaiminīya, Maitrāyaṇī and Paippalāda, is small.

  2. Economic precarity: traditional reciters and teachers often face economic hardship, which discourages new entrants.

  3. Critical editions and translations: several Vedic texts still lack reliable critical editions or modern translations, especially in Indian languages.

  4. Access: the restriction of Vedic learning to particular castes and to men is being questioned within the tradition; how to widen access while respecting living lineages is an open question.

  5. Bridging communities: traditional scholars and academic Indologists still too rarely work together.

Promising responses include systematic recording of all surviving recitation traditions, support for pāṭhaśālās and their teachers, collaborative editing projects, and the inclusion of rigorous Vedic studies in university curricula.

docs.title: 15.11 Conclusion
docs.text:
Why do the Vedas matter? They matter historically, as the oldest literature of South Asia and as a source for the language, religion and society of the second and first millennia BCE. They matter intellectually, for the questions their poets and philosophers asked about the origin of the world, the self and the power of speech, and for the sciences of language, metre, geometry and calendar that grew up around them. They matter culturally, as texts still recited and revered by millions, and preserved by one of the most remarkable oral traditions in human history. And they matter ethically, because the social order they helped to sanctify, with its hierarchy of birth and its restrictions on women, has shaped Indian society for better and worse, and is still being argued over. To study the Vedas well is to hold all of these together.

Final Invocation: The Śānti Mantra

dyauḥ śāntir antarikṣaṃ śāntiḥ pṛthivī śāntir āpaḥ śāntir oṣadhayaḥ śāntiḥ vanaspatayaḥ śāntir viśve devāḥ śāntir brahma śāntiḥ sarvaṃ śāntiḥ śāntir eva śāntiḥ sā mā śāntir edhi Peace in the sky, peace in the intermediate space, peace on earth, peace in the waters, peace in the plants, peace in the trees, peace in all the gods, peace in Brahman, peace in everything; peace itself is peace—may that peace be mine. — Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 36.17

Here ends Volume 1 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Veda Prakāśa: The Vedic Corpus.

docs.title: Glossary of Sanskrit Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning Adhvaryu The priest who performs the ritual actions, muttering Yajurvedic formulas Agnicayana “Piling of Agni”: the building of the great brick fire altar Agnihotra The daily milk offering into the fire, morning and evening Agniṣṭoma The Soma sacrifice with a single pressing day, the model of all Soma rites Agnyādheya The rite of establishing the three śrauta fires Āhavanīya The square eastern fire, into which most śrauta oblations are poured Āhitāgni A householder who has established the three śrauta fires Anudātta “Not raised”: the low pitch of the Vedic accent Anukramaṇī An index listing the seer, deity and metre of each hymn Apauruṣeya “Not of human origin”: the doctrine that the Veda has no author Āprī A hymn of the animal sacrifice inviting a fixed series of ritual entities, one to a verse Āraṇyaka “Forest book”: text on secret or dangerous rites and their meaning Arthavāda Explanatory or laudatory passage in a Brāhmaṇa Ārya Self-designation of the Vedic people; later “noble” Aṣṭakā Domestic offering to the ancestors on the eighth day of a dark fortnight in winter Aśvamedha The royal horse sacrifice Ātman Breath; self; in the Upaniṣads the innermost self Bandhu “Connection”: equivalence between ritual, cosmic and bodily elements Brahman (neuter) sacred formulation; ultimate reality. (masc.) the overseeing priest Brāhmaṇa (1) a member of the priestly class; (2) a prose text explaining the ritual Brahmavādinī “One who discourses on brahman”: a learned woman such as Maitreyī (BU 4.5.1) Brahmodya A ritual exchange of riddles about the nature of the world Caraṇa A Vedic school as a community of teachers and pupils Cāturmāsya The four-monthly seasonal sacrifices Chandas Metre; the Vedāṅga of prosody Dakṣiṇā The fee given to the priests Dakṣiṇāgni The semicircular southern fire of the śrauta ritual Dānastuti “Praise of the gift”: verses praising a patron’s generosity, closing a hymn Darśapūrṇamāsa The new- and full-moon offerings, model of all iṣṭis Dāsa, Dasyu In the Ṛgveda, enemies of the Ārya; later “servant, slave” Deva “Heavenly one”: a god Dharma Ordinance, law, duty, righteousness Dhī Insight, visionary thought; the poet’s inspired conception Dikpāla One of the eight guardians of the directions, such as Indra (east) and Varuṇa (west) Dīkṣā Consecration of the sacrificer before a Soma rite Gārhapatya The round western “householder’s fire” of the śrauta ritual Ghana The most complex of the standard recitation patterns Gṛhya Sūtra Manual of domestic rites Hotṛ The priest who recites Ṛgvedic verses Iṣṭi A śrauta offering of cakes, milk or ghee, without Soma or an animal victim Jaiminīya A school of the Sāmaveda, surviving in Kerala and Tamil Nadu Jaṭā “Braid”: a recitation pattern (1–2, 2–1, 1–2, …) Jāti “Birth”: an endogamous caste group Jyotiṣa Astronomy and calendar; one of the Vedāṅgas Kalpa Ritual procedure; the Vedāṅga comprising the Śrauta, Gṛhya, Dharma and Śulba Sūtras Kāṇḍa A book or section of a text Kauthuma The most widespread school of the Sāmaveda Kavi A poet or sage, a person of insight; also said of gods Khila A supplementary hymn transmitted with the Ṛgveda Krama Recitation in overlapping pairs of words Mahāvedi The great trapezoidal altar ground of the Soma sacrifice Maṇḍala One of the ten books of the Ṛgveda Mantra A sacred verse or formula Muhūrta A thirtieth part of a day (48 minutes) Nakṣatra Star; one of the 27 or 28 lunar asterisms Nirukta Etymology; Yāska’s work explaining Vedic words Niyoga The appointment of a man, usually the husband’s brother, to beget a son on a widow Pada pāṭha The word-by-word recitation of a text Paippalāda A recension of the Atharvaveda, surviving in Odisha Pākayajña “Cooked offering”: the basic domestic rite Paṇi In the Ṛgveda, stingy non-sacrificers who hid the cows in the Vala cave Paśubandha The śrauta animal sacrifice Prajāpati “Lord of offspring”: the creator god of the Brāhmaṇas Prakṛti A model rite, whose procedure is transferred to its variants (vikṛti) Prāṇa Breath; vital force Prātiśākhya A phonetic manual of a particular Vedic school Pravargya Śrauta rite of the heated clay pot filled with milk Puruṣa Man, person; the cosmic Man of RV 10.90 Rājasūya The royal consecration Ṛc A verse, especially of the Ṛgveda Ṛṣi A seer or inspired poet Ṛta Cosmic and moral order; truth Śākhā “Branch”: a Vedic school and its recension Sāman A chant; a melody of the Sāmaveda Saṃhitā A collection of verses or formulas; the continuous recited text Saṃskāra A life-cycle rite Saṃsthā One of the seven forms of the Soma sacrifice Śastra A recitation of verses by the hotṛ priests, answering a stotra Sattra A Soma “session” of twelve or more days in which all officiants are sacrificers Satya Truth Śikṣā Phonetics; one of the Vedāṅgas Smṛti “What is remembered”: tradition; texts of human authorship Snātaka A young man who has completed Vedic study and taken the ritual bath Soma A sacred plant, the drink pressed from it, and its god Śrauta Relating to the solemn rites with three fires Śruti “What is heard”: revealed scripture, the Veda Sthālīpāka A pot of rice or barley cooked and offered in the domestic fire Stobha A chant syllable inserted in a sāman Stotra A chant of sāmans sung by the udgātṛ priests at the Soma sacrifice Sūkta A hymn Śulba Sūtra Manual of altar geometry Svara Accent; tone; musical note Svarita The falling tone that follows an udātta Tapas Heat; ascetic effort Udātta “Raised”: the high pitch that marks the accented syllable Udgātṛ The chief chanter of sāmans Upākaraṇa Annual rite opening the term of Vedic study (today the Upākarma) Upanayana Initiation into Vedic study Upaniṣad A text of esoteric teaching, especially on ātman and brahman Upaveda A “subsidiary Veda”: a practical science attached to a Veda Vājapeya “Drink of strength”: a Soma sacrifice with a chariot race Vala The rock cave holding the cows and the dawns, broken open by Indra or Bṛhaspati Varṇa “Colour, kind”: one of the four classes of Brahmanical society Vedāṅga “Limb of the Veda”: one of six auxiliary sciences Vedi The shallow, strewn altar-ground between the fires Vidhi An injunction Vikṛtipāṭha One of the “modified” recitation patterns Vipra An inspired poet; later, a Brahmin Vyākaraṇa Grammar; one of the Vedāṅgas Yajamāna The sponsor of a sacrifice Yajña Sacrifice, worship with offerings Yajus A sacrificial formula Yūpa The wooden post to which a sacrificial animal is bound
